#820. London City's 'bravery' paying off in top three pursuit

London City earn point in thrilling draw against Arsenal

After 10 games in the Women's Super League season, London City Lionesses have shown they are capable of finishing inside the top three.

Their narrow 2-1 defeat by Manchester City two weeks ago provided snippets of their potential but a 1-1 draw at the Emirates against an improved Arsenal on Sunday confirmed their credentials.

Eder Maestre's side sit third in the table - the last qualification spot for next season's Women's Champions League - and are six points above Arsenal.

It is a strong position to be in just shy of the halfway stage having already faced big hitters Arsenal, Manchester City and Manchester United.

Current leaders Chelsea await in December but, for now, London City's progress is moving at a pace that looks set to challenge the usual suspects.

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

Goodwin's glorious solo strike draws London City Lionesses level

A sold-out away end helped fill out the 32,000-strong crowd at the Emirates on Sunday as many hoped for an end-to-end encounter.

They were not disappointed as fearless London City showed bravery against an Arsenal side who played with a spark following their 1-1 draw with Barcelona.

The visitors were helped out by Arsenal's wastefulness - the Gunners had 17 shots and only converted one - but London City caused plenty of problems of their own.

Maestre said after their defeat by Manchester City that their opponents showed more experience and know-how but against Arsenal, his side matured.

They were under pressure early on and fell a goal down thanks to Frida Maanum's opener but it took just 98 seconds for Izzy Goodwin to equalise for London City.

That killed Arsenal's momentum and when the pressure increased again from the hosts in the second half, goalkeeper and player of the match Mary Earps stepped up to make crucial saves.

"The performance was there. We had the chances to score and get a better result but Arsenal had chances too. The game was very open," said Maestre.

"The way we faced and challenged every circumstance in the game shows we are here, and able to play with that mentality in these big games.

"We came here to take risks. Our energy was good. We were brave and weren't scared about the context or the opponent.

"We tried to play as if we were at home. I always want to feel that my teams are brave and go for the win."

That bravery showed as Alexia Putellas came close twice with long-range efforts, Goodwin could have been onside when she was played in behind later on.

London City hit the crossbar through substitute Delphine Cascarino and had 14 shots compared to Arsenal's 17, including four inside the box.

Arsenal are still yet to win at home this season in the WSL but this was still an impressive showing from London City, who came to the Emirates to play.

But while they were willing to take risks, they were smarter than they were against Manchester City, choosing when to press aggressively and when to hold off.

"We tried to match the pace of the ball and not expose ourselves as much to the players that Arsenal have," added Maestre.

"We were trying to mix the moments we were more clinical in our press. We made some adjustments at half-time and were much better at recognising those."

London City are backed by US billionaire Michele Kang and that has made a big difference in the transfer market.

They recruited superstars Alexia Putellas, Mary Earps, Mapi Leon and Kadidiatou Diani in the summer.

Such is their depth that high-flying Spaniard Lucia Corrales, the dangerous Cascarino and England international Freya Godfrey came off the bench.

Those individual talents have made a difference and on Sunday it was goalkeeper Earps who took the plaudits, claiming the player of the match award.

She made crucial saves late on as Arsenal pushed ferociously for a winner, tipping Maanum's effort onto the crossbar and blocking her shot from close range.

Earps had to bide her time for the number one shirt after making the switch from Paris St-Germain this summer but has started the past three WSL games.

"Mary is a very strong character and is much more than the things we see in terms of the performance," said Maestre.

"She has experience, and energy that you can bring to every part in the process and not just the things we see in the matches.

"I think the energy that she brings to the position is massive and has a massive impact. I'm very pleased with her."

Watching on in the stands was England boss Sarina Wiegman who will have been pleased with the display from goalscorer Goodwin.

The 23-year-old got the better of England captain Leah Williamson when she fooled her with quick feet and fired the ball into the back of the net, making it 1-1.

She is proof that competition for places in the London City starting XI is pushing players on and that their depth is improving each week.

"I think Izzy is becoming a more mature player. She has the inner competition and the signings sometimes push you to bring 100% every time," added Maestre.

"She is committed to keep pushing and, with the performances she is having, why not [earn an England call-up]?

"Izzy is moving forward in the ways she can take advantage and that commitment is the way she is reaching those performances. I'm very proud of her."

#819. Ronaldinho makes debut for Italian side Ravenna after 11-year hiatus in playing career

Brazil legend plays first half for Serie C club at age 46

‘Is this my last one? I don’t know,’ Ronaldinho says

Ronaldinho played 45 minutes on his return to professional football in Italy. The 46-year-old Brazil great announced in June that he had signed for the Serie C side Ravenna, 11 years after he appeared to have brought his illustrious career to a close with Fluminense.

Five months later, he was in the starting lineup as Ravenna faced their local rivals Forlì. Ronaldinho, wearing the No 10 shirt, entered the stadium to great fanfare, with the 5,000-capacity Stadio Bruno Benelli adding a temporary 1,800-capacity stand – dubbed “R10” – for the occasion. Flares and smoke bombs were let off in the stands while Andrea Bocelli’s Con Te Partiro blasted out of the stadium’s speakers.

Ronaldinho failed to add to his goal tally upon his return, showing some nice touches and playing a role in helping Giulio Donati score Ravenna’s opening goal, but unable to create a sight of goal for himself.

The 2005 Ballon d’Or winner acknowledged the Ravenna fans at the end of the first half and was replaced by Matteo Maggio when the teams returned after the break.

Ronaldinho, who has also become a shareholder in the club, hinted there could be more appearances to come, telling Sky Italia: “It went by too fast, that has always been football for me. Is this my last one? I don’t know. If the president keeps calling me, I will come back. It is always a pleasure. I told the president, if he needs me, then I will be here.

“It was lovely to be here, playing, having the buildup in the dressing room. Football has always been the most wonderful thing in my life.”

Ravenna, who have not played in Serie B since 2008, are second in their regional group in Serie C and came into the weekend’s fixtures six points behind the leaders, Spezia.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

It is Ronaldinho’s second spell in Italy, albeit at a much lower level, after three seasons with Milan from 2008 to 2011, where he won one Serie A title. He also played for Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona in a trophy-laden career that included claiming the World Cup with Brazil in 2002. He scored 94 goals in 207 matches for Barcelona and 33 times in 97 games for Brazil. He has also played for Brazilian sides Grêmio, Flamengo and Atlético Mineiro, and for Querétaro in Mexico.

#818. Ronaldinho makes comeback in Ravenna win

Ronaldinho played the first 45 minutes for Ravenna against Forli

Brazil legend Ronaldinho made his comeback aged 46 for Ravenna in their 2-0 win over Forli in an Italian third-tier derby.

The 46-year-old came out of retirement for the Serie C club he joined as an investor in August, having last played in 2015 for Fluminense.

He started Sunday's game and showed some bright touches, and he was involved in the opening goal.

The former Barcelona superstar held off a defender before playing the pass that came before the assist for Giulio Donati's drive from outside the box.

He had earlier set up a chance for Donati from a corner, with the defender having his header saved.

At half-time there was a media circus around Ronaldinho, with journalists surrounding him, and former Brazil and AC Milan team-mate Dida joined him on the pitch.

Ronaldinho was substituted at the break with the score at 1-0.

A temporary stand, named the R10 in reference to Ronaldinho and his familiar shirt number, was built for the sold-out fixture at the Stadio Bruno Benelli.

The game was streamed in several countries around the world.

Ronaldinho trained once with the team, on Saturday, before Sunday's debut.

A team graphic beforehand showed him on the left side, but he mostly played centrally.

In his peak playing years, Ronaldinho was one of the best players in the world - as well as one of the most popular for his joyful demeanour and exuberant skill.

He won the 2002 World Cup with Brazil, the 2006 Champions League with Barcelona, and league titles with Barca and AC Milan - plus the Ballon d'Or and Fifa World Player of the Year awards in 2005.

He also played for Paris St-Germain as well as Gremio, Flamengo, Atletico Mineiro and Fluminense in his homeland, plus Mexican side Queretaro.

Ronaldinho scored 299 goals in his regular career and had been hoping to have a chance for number 300 for Ravenna. He would have taken a penalty had they been awarded one.

"It was lovely to be here, playing, having the build-up in the dressing room," Ronaldinho told Sky Sport Italia.

And asked if he might play again for Ravenna, who are second in their Serie C group, he said: "If the president calls me, I'll be back."

All of Ravenna's players - and not just the starting XI - posed with Ronaldinho in the team photo before kick-off

#817. Mary Earps frustrates Arsenal as London City Lionesses earn battling draw

Arsenal’s fifth draw from five home games in the Women’s Super League left them frustrated once again but this was a wholly different story to the previous four, as they played out an entertaining 1-1 draw with a London City Lionesses side inspired by their goalkeeper Mary Earps.

Aston Villa, Birmingham, Manchester United and Crystal Palace all came to this stadium for a point, defending resolutely and exposing Arsenal’s inability to break down low blocks, whereas London City came to play and were rewarded with a draw that maintains their six‑point advantage over Arsenal in the race for a European place, and moving within six points of the leaders Chelsea.

Earps, producing her best performance to date for the team she joined in the summer, repeatedly denied Frida Maanum and Lisa Baum and was named player of the match in a contest where both goals were scored inside the space of 99 seconds. The impressive Maanum finished off a superb team move for Arsenal to open the scoring in the 10th minute but her goal was cancelled out by a terrific finish from Isobel Goodwin whose head coach, Eder Maestre, said: “We came here to take risks. We really wanted to win.

“Our identity is playing with bravery – we were brave today. We weren’t scared about the context, the opponent, the stadium, nothing. We tried to play as we play at home.”

Arsenal had secured an impressive result in Barcelona on Thursday, drawing with the European champions, but this game against the WSL’s third-placed side felt as though it was of even greater importance, particularly if Arsenal wish to continue visiting venues such as the Camp Nou next season, and they were unable to find a way past Earps to win and close the gap in the table.

Just like they had done away at Anfield last Sunday, Renée Slegers’s team made a bright start with energy, pace and the threat of Alessia Russo. Emily Fox’s shot was deflected wide, after a good move that included some excellent Maanum buildup play, before Ona Batlle’s long-range effort bounced wide. It was not long before Maanum tucked in the opening goal after an intelligent cutback from Russo.

The visitors struck back almost immediately, though, as Goodwin did superbly to turn inside Leah Williamson and then demonstrated strength and composure to hold off Baum and fire a lethal finish past Misa Rodríguez with power and precision. It was a timely moment of class from the English striker in front of the England head coach, Sarina Wiegman, who was in the stands before naming her next England squad on Tuesday morning.

Earps then twice saved from Baum from range. After the break, Earps did well again to dive low to her left to divert a Caitlin Foord strike wide, and what followed was a sustained spell of London City possession, territory and chances. Maestre’s team spent a good part of 20 minutes firmly camped in Arsenal’s half and they carved open a good chance for Kadidiatou Diani but her relatively tame, low, near-post effort was saved by Rodríguez.

Diani’s 62nd-minute replacement from the substitutes’ bench, Delphine Cascarino, drew gasps from the crowd as she unleashed a dipping strike that bounced off the top of the crossbar. It was a lucky escape for Arsenal, who had won all seven of their previous meetings with London City across all competitions but were denied by two more fine Earps stops, firstly from a Maanum close-range effort and then from Maanum’s curler, which looked destined for the top corner before Earps touched it on to the bar.

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

Viviane Asseyi scored twice as West Ham secured back-to-back WSL home wins after beating rock-bottom Charlton 2-0.

Asseyi’s curled finish put the Irons in front just ahead of the break and she then scored a 25-yard free-kick early in the second half. The defeat saw Charlton, who remain without a point, become the first WSL team to lose all 10 of their opening matches of the season.

Mathilde Harviken’s late goal gave Aston Villa a 1-0 win over derby rivals Birmingham, which gives Brian Sørensen his third win since stepping in as interim manager and leaves his side seventh. Press Association

Slegers’s 50th WSL match in charge of the north London side almost ended in defeat late on but Alexia Putellas’s rising, stoppage-time strike flew narrowly over the bar. Regarding lying sixth in the table after 10 games, Slegers said “the season isn’t over, it’s still November”, before praising her team’s resurgence in their past three matches.

“The team is in a very good place,” she said. “The preparation, the dedication, the hunger for details, doing everything they possibly can – that’s the standard. Things are clicking well. But also the [opponents], they’re teams that spend time on the ball and that are brave and want to dominate games, so the types of games have been different.”

It certainly was different but the end result was the same for an Arsenal team still unable to find that elusive home win.

#816. I used the Vaonis Vespera 3 for weeks and here’s who I would recommend it to — full review

The Vespera III is a premium smart telescope that delivers powerful features like multi-night observation and mosaic technology, rewarding avid astrophotographers who have a serious interest in capturing the night sky.

Excellent deep-sky images with rich colors

Multi-night imaging makes ambitious targets easier

Much more expensive than many of its rivals

Why you can trust Space.com Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test and review products.

I’ve spent a lot of time with smart telescopes, from relatively inexpensive Seestar models to the original Vaonis Vespera and the Vespera Pro. They all promise essentially the same thing — you put a telescope outside at night, choose something interesting on your smartphone and let the technology take care of the rest. The Vaonis Vespera 3 does that exceptionally well, but after spending several nights with it, I’m convinced it’s designed for a rather different kind of buyer.

At $2,490/£2,199, this is hardly an impulse purchase for the beginner who’s curious about astronomy – you could buy several perfectly capable smart telescopes for the same money. Yet I found myself increasingly impressed by what the Vespera 3 could achieve, particularly when I returned to the same object over several nights. The images were sharp, the colors were excellent and I almost never had to think about the battery.

That doesn’t mean the experience was flawless. I sometimes spent longer than I’d have liked waiting for the telescope to get ready, but once it began photographing the sky, the Vespera 3 reminded me why I love smart telescopes so much.

One of my favorite things about smart telescopes is watching a photograph develop as more light is collected. What begins as a fairly ordinary patch of stars gradually becomes something much more interesting. First a faint cloud of gas appears, then more structure emerges, and eventually you have an image that, only a few short years ago, would have been difficult to capture without specialist equipment.

With the Vespera 3, I spent several nights photographing the Pleiades (M45), the famous star cluster in Taurus. The Pleiades make an excellent subject for testing a telescope because the stars are bright, but the surrounding nebulosity is much harder to capture convincingly. The Singularity app used to control Vespera 3 stacks each image as it goes, but keeps them in sight as an optional time-lapse, so you can see exactly why you’re spending so much time on one object.

Even better, the Vespera 3’s PerseverENS feature lets you add data to an existing observation over multiple nights (it’s actually called multi-night observation in the app). Instead of having to call it a night or start again every time the weather interrupts an imaging session, you can return to a target and continue building the image over weeks — or years. This is excellent for faint nebulas, but also for anyone who lives somewhere with unpredictable weather.

The Vespera 3 also has CovalENS, Vaonis’s mosaic imaging system, which captures adjacent sections of sky to produce a larger image. That’s helpful for objects such as the Pleiades and large nebulas, which occupy a substantial area of the sky.

Mosaics inevitably take longer than conventional images — if it images six sections of the night sky, it takes six times longer for the same image quality — but they also make the telescope more versatile than its native field of view (2.5 x 1.4 degrees) might suggest.

Smart telescopes are particularly useful for people living under light-polluted skies. A conventional optical telescope can show you the moon, the planets and some brighter star clusters, but faint nebulas are largely out of reach. The Vespera 3 tackles that problem by taking repeated short exposures and combining them automatically. As the exposures accumulate, faint details become clearer, and the image becomes less noisy.

I photographed the Orion Nebula (M42), one of the most rewarding deep-sky targets for almost any telescope. Its bright central region makes it a quick capture, but the surrounding clouds of gas give a camera plenty more to uncover. The color in M42 via the Vespera 3 was particularly striking: stars looked sharp, the background was pleasingly clean, but the colors had a richness you don’t always see from less expensive models.

The Vespera 3 uses a 50mm refractor telescope and an 8.3-megapixel Sony IMX585 camera sensor. Those specifications are identical to the Vespera 2, but the Vespera 3 has a new optical system, which uses four lenses in three groups, including two extra-low-dispersion elements. Vaonis has also introduced internal baffling to reduce unwanted reflections from nearby artificial lights. For urban astronomers, every little helps. I wouldn’t claim that the Vespera 3 makes dark skies unnecessary. It doesn’t — and if you do take a trip to dark skies with the Vespera 3, your images will improve — but it can produce extremely satisfying images even from a city.

For anyone who wants more control over their images, the Vespera 3 also saves lossless TIFF files that can be exported to a PC or Mac using a USB-C cable. That means you can take the images into your preferred editing software for further processing, rather than relying entirely on the results produced by the Singularity app.

There’s something wonderfully simple about looking at a map of the night sky, spotting an interesting object and tapping it to point your scope in that direction. It’s one of the reasons I enjoy using Seestar smart telescopes. I did miss that experience with the Vespera 3.

Vaonis’s Singularity app has an extensive catalog of galaxies, nebulas, star clusters and other targets, but I found myself browsing lists when I’d rather have been exploring an interactive sky chart.

There is a section devoted to constellations, which initially got my hopes up. I thought it might allow me to photograph an entire constellation, capturing its familiar star pattern as a wide-field image. Sadly not — each constellation has a diagram showing where the catalog’s deep-sky objects are located. That’s useful if you already know what you’re looking for, but it isn’t the same as being able to see the sky overhead and choose a target visually.

However, the telescope can still find and photograph the objects in its catalog, and the automated tracking works well once you’ve made your choice.

That smart telescopes give you instant gratification is something of a selling point — but it’s also a myth. Yes, they save an enormous amount of work compared with traditional astrophotography equipment. There’s no separate tracking mount to align, no camera to attach and no laptop required to control the imaging process. However, automation doesn’t necessarily mean instant results.

For example, every time the Vespera 3 is switched on, it needs to establish its position by identifying stars overhead. Its Star Zone Search and autofocus procedure took around five minutes, with a percentage displayed in the app to show how far it had progressed. That’s not an unreasonable wait for a sophisticated astronomical instrument, but it felt a little drawn-out when I was eager to begin photographing something. If there are clouds, expect it to take much longer.

Once the Vespera 3 had aligned itself, I could choose a target and leave the telescope to work. The optical arm moved into position, the camera began collecting exposures and an image gradually appeared on my smartphone.

I was less impressed by the touch-sensitive power button. Its softly illuminated indicator didn’t always make it obvious whether the telescope was switched on. More than once, I had to check my phone’s available Wi-Fi networks to establish whether it was on or off.

Vaonis claims the Vespera 3 can operate for up to 11 hours. I didn’t run it continuously until the battery was exhausted, but it lasted longer than every observing session I attempted. That did change how I used it, because I could concentrate on the target instead of keeping an eye on the remaining charge or wondering whether I should connect a portable battery.

The new, improved tripod also makes a difference. It’s tall, adjustable and reassuringly stable, with a useful canopy strung between its legs for holding any accessories — perhaps filters, a red torch or snacks.

The Vespera 3 is capable of photographing the moon and the sun, although solar photography requires a properly fitted optional solar filter. Unfortunately, that costs a further $179/£159, which is rather steep.

It’s also not the best choice for detailed planetary images. The 245mm focal length is ideal for framing many galaxies and nebulas, but Jupiter and Saturn remain small subjects.

Another omission is an equatorial tracking mode. Some cheaper smart telescopes — such as the Seestar S50 Pro and the DwarfLab Dwarf 3 — offer EQ mode for more advanced imaging, but the Vespera 3 relies solely on its motorized alt-azimuth mount. That doesn’t stop it from producing excellent photographs, but it does mean more experienced users have one less option to experiment with.

The biggest question surrounding the Vespera 3 isn’t whether it works — it’s whether it’s worth the money. After all, it costs far more than the Seestar S50 Pro, which also has built-in imaging filters, whereas the Vespera’s light pollution ($229/£219), dual-band ($399/£370) and solar (£179/£159) filters are optional purchases. They do, however, make a significant difference — with the dual-band filter giving nebulas more contrast, color and detail.

Overall, the Vespera 3 offers a slightly more polished imaging experience than the many entry-level smart telescopes on the market. I enjoyed its clean, colorful images and appreciated the ability to work on the same subject over several nights, while the excellent tripod and battery endurance make it particularly well suited to longer observing sessions.

I wouldn’t recommend it to everyone, but I can see why someone who already loves photographing the night sky might happily pay extra for the Vespera 3.

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#815. Aberdeen appoint Liechtenstein's Frick as head coach

Mario Frick has been announced as the new head coach of Aberdeen, taking over from the sacked Stephen Robinson to become the club's fourth manager in 2026.

Capped 125 times as a striker for Liechtenstein, the 52-year-old was last in charge at Luzern, leaving the Swiss club in the summer after five years.

He follows Robinson, Peter Leven and Jimmy Thelin in leading the side in this calendar year and will take charge for the first time against Scottish Premiership bottom side Kilmarnock on Saturday.

"Throughout our discussions, he demonstrated a clear vision, strong leadership qualities and a deep understanding of what is required to build a successful team," said Pittodrie chief executive Adrian Bevington.

"He was also exceptionally well regarded by the many people across the game we consulted during the process, and the board was unanimous in its belief that he is the right person to lead Aberdeen forward."

Former Motherwell and St Mirren boss Robinson was dismissed on 9 November, with Aberdeen second bottom of the table and having lost four games in a row in all competitions.

'Aberdeen hunt yet another manager after ill-fated Robinson reign'

Latest Aberdeen news, analysis and fan views

Watch new Aberdeen boss Frick score against Scotland in September 2010

Frick, who also managed Vaduz in the Swiss Super League, will be assisted by Roman Matter and is the seventh permanent manager since Dave Cormack took control of the club in November 2019.

As a player, his former clubs include FC Basel, FC Zurich, St. Gallen and Grasshopper, while his 16 international goals make him Liechtenstein's all-time top scorer.

"Mario is a strong personality with clear ideas about how he wants his teams to play," added sporting director Lutz Pfannenstiel. "He brings energy, ambition and a winning mentality, and knows how to build a strong team environment.

"We were looking for the right person to lead the next chapter of Aberdeen FC, and I'm convinced Mario has the qualities, character and vision to make a real impact."

Frick got Vaduz promoted in 2020 before helping Luzern avoid relegation following his move there in 2021.

The next again year he guided them to a fourth-placed finish and European qualification, although they were knocked out of Conference League qualifying by Lee Johnson's Hibernian.

Aberdeen say Frick "has built a strong reputation for transforming teams, handing top-flight debuts to more than 30 academy players during his coaching career".

Hibs striker Thibault Klidje and current Aberdeen goalkeeper Marius Muller both played under him.

Aberdeen did not disclose contract details for Frick as he takes over a side with just three wins from 12 Premiership outings this season.

One of his international goals came at Hampden Park in 2010 when a late Stephen McManus header rescued a 2-1 win for Scotland.

#814. Kate Middleton Reveals Theme of Her Annual Christmas Carol Concert

As Kate Middleton and Prince William prepare for the holidays, the theme for her annual “Together at Christmas” carol service at Westminster Abbey has been revealed.

Kate Middleton is already preparing for the most wonderful time of the year.

This December will mark the sixth time that the Princess of Wales has held her annual “Together at Christmas” service at Westminster Abbey, marking the holidays with an evening of carols and giving back.

Over 1,500 people attend the service every Christmas at the same location where Kate and Prince William tied the knot back in 2011. And the Abbey has continued to serve as an important landmark in the couple’s journey as a family, with their children Prince George, 13, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, 8, often joining their parents for the annual holiday celebration.

In addition to being an evening of carols, however, every year “Together at Christmas” also honors individuals around the United Kingdom who have gone above and beyond to help support those in their local communities and make them “feel supported, connected and less alone.”

This year’s event, according to an announcement from Kate and William’s The Royal Foundation, will “celebrate the power of love and kindness to bring people together, creating hope, connection and a shared sense of community during the Christmas season.”

“At the heart of this year’s services is the belief that small acts of care can have an extraordinary impact,” the announcement continued. “Whether through friendship, volunteering, neighbourliness or simply being there to listen, the services will recognise the many ways people help create environments where others feel safe, valued and able to reach out when they need support.”

In addition to the event at Westminster Abbey, there will be 15 carol services happening concurrently in local communities across the U.K., ensuring individuals who have gone above and beyond across all four nations are recognized for their efforts.

The announcement confirmed the “cherished” tradition will air in the U.K. on ITV1 and ITVX on Christmas Eve.”

The annual celebration marks a rare instance in which William and Kate step out as a family of five, with all three of their children. And not only does it provide a sweet look at their family bond as George, Charlotte and Louis grow older, but the event also allows for the couple’s children to show off their special talents.

In fact, last year’s broadcast saw a special duet from Charlotte and Kate, the mother-daughter duo sitting side by side at the piano to perform "Holm Sound" by Erland Cooper.

Alongside the piece of music, narration from Kate shared an emotional message about the spirit of the holidays.

"At its heart, Christmas speaks of love taking form in the simplest, most human ways," she said. "Not in sentimental or grand gestures, but gentle ones: a moment of listening, a word of comfort, a friendly conversation, a helping hand, presence. These simple acts of care might seem small, but they contribute to the beautiful tapestry of life to which we all belong."

For more updates from the royal family this year, read on.

Kate Middleton & Prince William's Son Prince George Starts School at Eton College

On Sept. 8, the Prince and Princess of Wales' oldest son started his first day of school at Eton College, a boarding school Prince William attended in his youth.

Prince Harry, Meghan Markle Return to U.K. for Extended Stay

Six years after stepping away from their senior royal duties and moving to California, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex returned to the U.K. for an extended stay.

While the move is not permanent, the couple—who touched down in England Aug. 26—reportedly enrolled their children Archie and Lilibet in a British school.

The king of Norway died after 35 yearts on the throne.

"It is with deep grief that we announce that His Majesty King Harald has passed away," the palace shared. "King Harald died peacefully at Oslo University Hospital Rikshospitalet Friday 28 August at 6:35 AM.

His son, Crown Prince Haakon, asceneded following his father's death.

King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV Dies at 34

After taking the throne in 1995 at just 3 years old following the death of his father, King Rukidi tragically died Aug. 27 at the age of 34.

“It is with profound sadness and a heavy heart that I announce the passing of His Majesty the Omukama of Tooro, King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, at approximately 10:00 p.m. this evening,” Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki wrote in a statement. “This is an immeasurable loss for the Royal Family, the people of Tooro, and the nation of Uganda."

The British royal welcomed her third baby—a daughter named Adelaide Elizabeth Annina Brooksbank—with husband Jack Brooksbank in August.

“Named after three people we love and admire past and present, including her Great-Grandmother who we hold close in our hearts,” Eugenie, who is also mom to son August and Ernest, wrote in an Aug. 17 Instagram post. “Her name is part of English and Portuguese history, two places we love and call home."

Meghan Markle's Show With Love, Meghan Scores Daytime Emmy Nomination

Meghan earned her first-ever Daytime Emmy nod on July 14 for the 2026 award show after her series With Love, Meghan was nominated for Outstanding Lifestyle Program.

On July 7, British Justice Matthew Nicklin ruled against a group of high profile figures—including the Duke of Sussex, Elton John and Elizabeth Hurley—in a lawsuit accusing the Associated Newspapers, the publisher of the Daily Mail, of unlawful information gathering.

In the lawsuit, filed in 2022, the plaintiffs accused the newspaper organization of mobile phone hacking, landline bugging and even home bugging in 97 separate allegations.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew, was arrested on Feb. 19, his 66th birthday, on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

The arrest came amid renewed controversy over Andrew's alleged ties to Jeffrey Epstein. (Andrew has denied any wrongdoing.)

Prince William and Kate Middleton Break Silence on the Epstein Files

The Duke and Duchess of Wales spoke out amid the release of millions of documents in connection with Jeffrey Epstein, sharing their support for the victims of the late convicted sex offender.

"I can confirm The Prince and Princess have been deeply concerned by the continuing revelations," a Kensington Palace spokesperson shared in a statement obtained by MS NOW Feb. 9. "Their thoughts remain focused on the victims."

Marius Borg Høiby, Son of Norway's Crown Princess, Arrested Ahead of Rape Trial

Marius Borg Høiby—the eldest son of Crown Princess Mette-Marit and step-son of Crown Prince Haakon—was arrested Feb. 1 for assault, threats with a knife and violation of a restraining order, Oslo police confirmed in a statement to The Associated Press.

The 29-year-old—who does not carry a royal title or official duties—is being kept in detention for up to four weeks over risks of reoffending after the Oslo district court granted the request. His attorney Petar Sekulic told the outlet that they are considering appealing the decision.

Høiby is expected in court Feb. 3 as part of a separate indictment regarding four alleged rapes between 2018 and 2024, as well as two alleged acts of violence against a partner and violating a restraining order.

His defense team addressed the allegations in a statement to the AP, saying that Høiby "denies all charges of sexual abuse, as well as the majority of the charges regarding violence."

Flora Vesterberg, Queen Elizabeth's Cousin, Announces Pregnancy

Flora Vesterberg, the granddaughter of Queen Elizabeth II's first cousin Princess Alexandra, announced that she is pregnant with her and husband Timothy Vesterberg's first baby.

"Delighted to share that Timothy and I are expecting our first child," she wrote on Instagram Jan. 19. "We're truly over the moon."

Prince Harry Appears in Court for Lawsuit Against U.K. Tabloids

Harry appeared at London’s High Court Jan. 19 for the start of what is expected to be a weeks-long trial against Associated Newspapers—the media group that publishes the Daily Mail, The Mail on Sunday, and Mail Online—over allegations of unethical newsgathering tactics

Other stars including Elton John, Elizabeth Hurley, and Sadie Frost are also taking aim against the publishing company in the lawsuit.

Associated Newspapers has “vigorously denied” the claims, according to the BBC.

Meghan Markle and Prince Harry Celebrate 10 Years Together

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex celebrated ten years together by sharing a romantic black and white video of themselves dancing in their backyard.

Set to Olivia Dean’s “So Easy (To Fall In Love),” the couple revealed that the clip was recorded by none other than their 4-year-old daughter Lilibet.  Alongside a camera emoji, Meghan—who also shares 6-year-old son Archie with Harry— added in the caption of the Jan. 16 Instagram post, “cred: our daughter.”

The couple also shared a throwback photo from their first year of dating. In the adorable snap, the pair embraced each other during a nature-filled getaway.

“When 2026 feels just like 2016….,” Meghan wrote in the caption. “You had to be there.”

The Greek royal family’s private office announced Jan. 15 that Queen Sofia of Spain’s sister died at the age of 83.

As the statement read, "It is with deep sadness that the Greek Royal Family announces that HRH Princess Irene, beloved sister and aunt, passed away on Thursday, January 15th 2026, at 11:40 local time, in Zarzuela Palace in Madrid surrounded by loved ones."

Her funeral was held Jan. 19 at the Metropolitan Cathedral in Athens following her death, with the burial at the Royal Cemetery of Tatoi.

Kate Middleton Celebrates Her Birthday With Moving Message

On her 44th birthday, the Princess of Wales shared a message on the power of nature to heal.

“Even in the coldest, darkest season, winter has a way of bringing us stillness, patience and quiet consideration,” Kate said in a voiceover alongside footage of snowy landscapes in her Jan. 9 video. “Where the stream slows just enough for us to see our own reflection, to discover the deepest parts of ourselves, alongside the whispers and the pulse of every living thing.”

She added, “I find myself reflecting on how deeply grateful I am. For the rivers within us flow with ease, fears washed away, cleanse and purify, come to peace with our tears and discover what it means to be alive, to be at one with nature—a quiet teacher and a soft voice that guides in memory helping us to heal in.”

Kate Middleton Makes Surprise Appearance With Prince William

The Princess of Wales marked her first public appearance of 2026 as she joined her husband during an engagement at the Charing Cross Hospital in London. The outing in support of healthcare workers came almost a year after she announced she was in remission following her cancer diagnosis.

#813. England fend off fiery Spain fightback after Anderson’s red to top Nations League group

It was the game to show Thomas Tuchel where his rebooted England team had got to; surely the ultimate test in international football. Spain in Spain. A world champion team who, in Tuchel’s words, had “forgotten how to lose.” Before this Nations League group decider, they had been beaten only once in 43 matches – on penalties against Portugal in the final of this competition last year.

What England produced for 65 minutes was extraordinary. What followed was equally so for different reasons. When it was over, England had made the most sensational of statements. Back in 2018, on their previous visit to Spain, England won 3-2 in Seville in the Nations League; it was one of Sir Gareth Southgate’s most famous results, an ignition point. It was the same scoreline and the same feeling for Tuchel on Sunday night.

England led 3-0. It was Harry Kane, of course, who put them in front from the penalty spot; the best player in the world damaging the best team. When Ezri Konsa and Ben White added the others, the travelling supporters were pinching themselves. With Jude Bellingham to the fore, England had run riot.

It was not over. Far from it. Everything changed when Jarell Quansah made a big error as the last man, robbed by Lamine Yamal, who got into the area and was fouled by Elliot Anderson. It was a red card for the England midfielder and a penalty for Spain. When Mikel Oyarzabal converted, it was the prompt for a siege.

Spain knocked hard at the door. They scored again through the substitute Nico Williams, created by an assist from the frankly ludicrous Lamine Yamal, a talent who sprinkles his magic liberally, and England were placed in grim survival mode. We have been here before under Tuchel and the equaliser looked on. The manager made a couple of defensive changes – Myles Lewis-Skelly for Kane and Djed Spence for Anthony Gordon. Bellingham was removed, too, and he departed shaking his head. Dan Burn came on towards the very end.

England held out. One of Tuchel’s major selection calls was to start James Trafford over Jordan Pickford in goal and he produced a remarkable stoppage-time double save to ensure England got the result they needed to leapfrog Spain and advance to the quarter-finals as the group winners. The second part of it was to deny Aymeric Laporte. It was a breathtaking moment; one to advance Trafford’s claim on the No 1 jersey. There were many others on a night that pulsed wildly from the outset – pretty much from when Spain paraded the World Cup trophy before kick-off. Had they not already had their homecoming with the gold? It was a power play.

England brought the swagger. They pressed hard on to the front foot. It was thrilling to see how they took on those in red and beat them, creating the sense of possibility. It was worth mentioning a spin move by Lewis Hall on halfway in the eighth minute when he could not afford to lose the ball. He did not, getting England up the field. There were other examples of the proactivity from other players; the desire to drop shoulders and surge forward, to be direct.

It was England who looked likely to score first and Spain needed a superb save from Unai Simón to deny Bellingham in the early going. He ran on to a Declan Rice corner, centrally placed and, with the ball slightly behind him, he had to dig out the half-volley rather than hit it more cleanly. Simón’s reflexes were nevertheless impressive. Gordon had a shot blocked by Martín Zubimendi. Kane fizzed another one just wide.

Spain kicked out a foothold in the 15th minute. It was Lamine Yamal, inevitably, who dragged them back into it. He nutmegged Hall and blasted away from him, Rice bringing him down to pick up a yellow card. What Hall did next spoke volumes about England’s approach, not to mention his courage. It was a slicing run from him, on a diagonal towards goal, which laid waste to a host of Spain players. He almost found Morgan Rogers with his cross.

It was an excellent first half for England; Rogers bristled with confidence on the ball, Bellingham threatened. They deserved to take a lead into the interval. Bellingham appeared to be fouled by Marc Cucurella, but Anderson did not stand on ceremony, driving a first-time pass up the inside right channel for Kane, who cut inside Pau Cubarsí to set up the shot.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Kane cleverly got his body between Cubarsí and the ball; the Spain centre-back had a problem. His challenge was necessary but clumsy; it was a clear penalty. Kane had a long wait while the video assistant referee checked for an Anderson foul on Cucurella as he followed through after his pass. It was accidental but nasty. Anderson got away with it. Kane had missed decisively in England’s 3-2 defeat against Spain at Wembley at the start of this competition. He made no mistake this time. It was his 93rd England goal.

England continued to push after half-time, especially Bellingham. He won the corner that led to Konsa heading in unmarked from a Rice outswinger and it was Bellingham who played in White, who was adventurous all night, for the third.

Pio Esposito gave Italy ⁠an early lead but their joy was short-lived as Belgium scored ​three times before the ​interval through Maxim De Cuyper, ​Nathan Ngoy and Jérémy Doku (pictured). Diego Moreira made it 4-1 in the 80th minute.

England and Spain had already confirmed qualification to the quarter-finals before Sunday's dramatic clash between the sides in Madrid, which England won 3-2, but the remaining match in Group A3 saw Croatia beat Czechia 2-1, thanks to Lovro Majer's 87th-minute winner.

Nothing silly, Tuchel had to have thought. Quansah did something silly and the entire mood changed. Spain went right to Lamine Yamal and his low cross for Williams was perfect.

#811. How did England cling on against Spain and what did Tuchel do differently?

James Trafford (right) kept Spain out in the latter stages

England held on to beat Spain 3-2 with a backs-to-the-wall finale in the Nations League to finish top of their group.

But many observers would have been feeling a sense of deja vu from the World Cup semi-final when England sat back and were beaten by Argentina.

So what was different this time? BBC Sport has a look.

First of all the context of the two games was entirely different.

England were 1-0 up against Argentina in the 55th minute on neutral territory in Atlanta - and still had all their players.

Anthony Gordon had put them ahead but Lionel Messi set up Enzo Fernandez and then Lautaro Martinez late on.

But against Spain the best performance of Thomas Tuchel's reign had them 3-0 up through goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White.

Elliot Anderson then fouled Lamine Yamal for a penalty, which Mikel Oyarzabal scored - and that began the siege at a partisan Riyadh Air Metropolitano.

Nico Williams made it 3-2 but Spain could not find an equaliser, thanks in part to England keeper James Trafford.

"Half an hour feels like two hours against a team like this [with 10 men]," Tuchel told ITV afterwards. "That's the way it is. Without the red card we were clear winners."

60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages

England cling on to stun world champions Spain in thriller

Making defensive subs is fine when it works - but when it does not, boy will a manager hear about it.

In the World Cup last 16, England had been 2-1 up against Mexico in the Azteca when Jarell Quansah was sent off.

Tuchel brought on three defenders for a defender, a midfielder and a forward.

But England won 3-2 and Dan Burn's cameo was the stuff of legend.

However, nine days later with England 1-0 up against Argentina, Tuchel did the same again - three defenders on for a defender, midfielder and forward.

The first of those subs, with Konsa replacing Anthony Gordon, was in the 72nd minute.

And England just sat back until Argentina broke their resistance.

However, against Spain this time, despite England being down to 10 men and facing incessant pressure, Tuchel was not so quick with defensive subs.

Myles Lewis-Skelly, replacing Harry Kane, was the first on after 78 minutes - 15 minutes after Anderson's sending off. And then five minutes later he brought on two more players - but one of them was a striker in Dominic Calvert-Lewin.

Burn replaced fellow defender White in the 89th minute.

"Harry played 78 minutes, Jude [Bellingham] 83 minutes and then just defending and defending, it's tiring," explained Tuchel.

"So we needed fresh energy. I was asked yesterday what happens if there needs to be a critical or crucial substitution. And I said, I feel free enough to take any substitution if I think it is necessary to help the team and to influence the game.

"I feel free enough to do that and I think there was a lot of defending needed. So we just went for some fresh legs."

Dan Burn usually comes on when England are trying to hang on - but he was only introduced for the last few minutes

England actually faced more of a siege this time than against the Argentines, the stats confirm.

In the final 30 minutes they faced 19 shots from Spain, with seven on target and an expected goals (xG) total of 2.53.

Argentina, in that time, had 10 shots, with four on target and an xG of 1.41.

In terms of passes from England the numbers were similar with 65 against Argentina and 61 against Spain - both times with an accuracy rate of about 64%.

In Thursday's 2-1 win against Croatia, as a comparison, they tried 557 passes with accuracy of 89%.

"For half an hour it was Mexico reloaded and it felt like we were back in the Azteca. We had to overcome 30 minutes which, against Spain, felt like three hours," Tuchel told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"The difficult thing is it's not only a red card, it's a red card, and a goal so that makes a completely new game. Thirty minutes against the world champion feels like three hours. I said it before in the stadium and wave after wave after wave."

England were criticised for blowing a 2-1 half-time lead at Wembley in their first Nations League game with Spain.

But on that day their final 30-minute figurers were much better - with only five shots faced and 176 attempted passes with a 90% accuracy.

So what was different this time? Perhaps the team showed more resilience and unity?

After Spain had pulled one back England's players had a huddle.

"I love the fact the team went into a huddle and if anything the manager's stepped back because he wants to see the player reaction," said ex-England defender Matt Upson on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I almost think that the trauma from that sending off of Elliot Anderson has almost been a positive thing for England because it's given the team a chance to get together and cope in what is an incredibly difficult situation and come through the other side.

"There was so much going on in this game. England had to suffer and came through the other side."

Defender and goalscorer White was asked about the huddle after the game.

"Just stay calm, when you're one down it becomes more difficult and things change so it was all about managing that," he said.

Another factor was the performance of England keeper James Trafford, who made six saves - with four of them coming in the final 12 minutes of the game with the score at 3-2.

He made an incredible double save to deny Fermin Lopez and Lamine Yamal in injury time.

Upson said: "I think that double save was the moment for Spain and Trafford had the answers."

A commercial satellite has spotted the International Space Station (ISS), giving us a unique view of the orbiting lab from above.

Most of the time, when we see the ISS, it is from down here on Earth or from the viewpoint of the astronauts onboard, peering out the windows at the station's limbs, solar arrays and instruments.

But in this snapshot, which was posted on X on Nov. 9 by the Australian company HEO, we can see the station stretched out in all its glory.

HEO specializes in using satellites in low Earth orbit to capture images of other spacecraft, though longer-term the company aims to capture observations far out into the solar system. HEO doesn't build the satellites that take these photos; rather, the company's software tasks the spacecraft to image targets as they come into range.

This great photo of the ISS from above, for example, was taken by a satellite operated by BlackSky, a Virginia-based company that holds a non-Earth imaging agreement with HEO.

So far, HEO and its partners have captured imagery of a variety of spacecraft in orbit, including the ISS, China's Tiangong space station and the European Space Agency's ERS-2 satellite (while it was hurtling back to Earth in 2024).

While it might seem that satellites are just hovering above Earth, the space station and other spacecraft in LEO are hurtling through space at roughly 17,500 mph (28,160 kph), hundreds of miles above our planet's surface.

A snapshot of a satellite from above is therefore far from mundane. Rather, it requires incredible coordination and technical skill; satellite operators must know precisely when their target will present itself, and their equipment must be capable of getting the shot.

#808. 60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages

Harry Kane scored for a record-equalling seventh England away game

Thomas Tuchel went with bold words when reminded about the caution that sabotaged England's World Cup hopes and left them with so much to prove against Spain in the Nations League on Sunday.

In a media theatre at the Metropolitano in Madrid, head coach Tuchel's sixth sense led him to go public with what he was convinced England would produce against the world champions.

Tuchel looked his inquisitors in the eyes and declared: "We are up for something spectacular."

To say Tuchel and England kept their word was a masterpiece of under-statement after the finest night of the head coach's reign resulted in a 3-2 victory that was large parts magnificent, some parts madness - and all parts spectacular.

It also ended Spain's 43-game unbeaten run - setting aside their penalty shootout defeat by Portugal in the 2025 Nations Cup final.

If England and Tuchel could be accused of being cowed by pressure when they led Argentina in the ill-fated World Cup semi-final, they were thrillingly positive in this unforgiving Madrid environment.

The question being asked when England held a one-goal advantage through Harry Kane's penalty at half-time was 'what would theirs and Tuchel's reaction be?' Stick or twist?

Would Tuchel tell England to press their foot on the pedal for acceleration? Or would he take the approach of going into reverse gear, as he did to ill-fated effect against Argentina?

How did England cling on against Spain and what did Tuchel do differently?

Who swaggered around like he owned the place? Spain v England ratings

England hold on to stun world champions Spain in thriller

The answer was delivered when they added goals from Arsenal duo Ezri Konsa and Ben White in the first 12 minutes of the second half.

This being England, they then created a mess for themselves when Elliot Anderson was sent off for fouling Lamine Yamal in the area after 65 minutes, although the main culprit was Jarell Quansah for initially conceding possession.

Mikel Oyarzabal scored from the spot and, when Yamal set up Nico Williams for Spain's second with 15 minutes left, it looked like more than an hour of faultless England football might be wasted.

But not a bit of it, as goalkeeper James Trafford produced heroics and England defended with every fibre to close out this landmark win.

Was this the statement victory that was almost demanded of Tuchel as recompense for the World Cup disappointment, a performance to convince the doubters?

"We're fully aware what we put out there," said Tuchel afterwards. "What a performance we put out for 65 minutes to be deservedly 3-0 up.

"Of course, the red card and the penalty changed the momentum and the characteristics of the game... but we know, and the players know very, very well, what they put out there. That is the statement - and that is the significance of this victory."

Simple details of the game barely touch the sides of a night filled with quality and glorious chaos, vindication for Tuchel and England's positive approach.

Spain opened with an ostentatious parade of the World Cup in front of England's players as the teams lined up, perhaps a psychological reminder of the superiority that has seen them dominate international football.

What followed, at times literally, reduced Spain's supporters to stunned silence and their players to a shell-shocked shambles chasing the shadows that were overpowering them.

England's white shirts were everywhere but Spain could not get near them. The tormentors had become the tormented.

It was alien territory for a Spain side that has carried all before them, while England's fans tucked away high in a corner of this vast arena were equally unbelieving as a dream unfolded in front of them.

England, for 65 minutes, were in a different class to Spain. And, yes, you have read that right.

From the first whistle, employing a suffocatingly high press, England ran all over Spain.

When White crowned a superb move with the third goal four minutes after Konsa's second, it looked, remarkably, to be a case of how big England's victory margin would be.

In the end, the margin was narrow but the stature and significance of England's victory was huge.

Tuchel labelled this meeting with Spain as "proof of concept at the highest level".

There was no doubt the German manager and England were under fierce scrutiny after the manner of the collapse, mentally and tactically, against Argentina at the World Cup.

Here they delivered the proof they can match the best then beat them.

If the vital signs were being forensically examined for evidence Tuchel has learned lessons from a chastening World Cup, that England have improved after that harrowing experience, this game delivered these conclusions.

Of course, England must do it again. Do it when the pressure and expectation in at its highest.

The Nations League is competitive but cannot be compared to a World Cup and European Championship, both titles currently in the possession of the team they beat here.

But England's world-class players delivered - Kane inevitably with his 93rd international goal, but Jude Bellingham was on a level of his own, the outstanding performer on both sides with an individual display simply confirming he is the player with everything.

And Tuchel got his big calls right, especially selecting Trafford, who responded superbly in a frantic closing phase. White, making a strong claim for the right-back berth, not only scored a goal but produced crucial challenges in the face of relentless, albeit belated, Spain pressure.

"This was the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness," said Tuchel. "It was on the highest level football wise in all aspects of the game. We did everything that needs to be done together.

"The deep build-up. The high press. The counter-attack. The tracking. The defensive phases. This was an excellent performance and of course a wonderful feeling for us in the dressing room.

"We overcame some difficult moments in the end. That's how it is. But we are very well aware which steps we took now through after the World Cup."

England's win means they top their Nations League group, but the importance spreads much wider than simply a league table.

The first 65 minutes were simply breathtaking. Spain wilting under attack after attack. Spain rattled until they shook as England refused to allow them meaningful possession.

After Anderson's dismissal, bad memories were revisited as England were forced into a rearguard action, but any other result than the one that was eventually delivered would have been a huge injustice.

England survived 29 nervous minutes, including added time, to make a powerful statement about their current status, which is much healthier than when recriminations about Tuchel's approach provided the post-World Cup narrative.

"I'm very impressed with the steps that we took after the World Cup", said Tuchel. "We wanted to get better, better in a deep build-up, get better in defending in a low block and, on top of it, we wanted always to impose our identity and the way we want to play against every opponent.

"I think this was clearly visible throughout the whole group phase. The results followed with an excellent group phase."

Was this the finest performance of Tuchel's time in charge? Most observers felt so, but the head coach was best placed to answer.

"Yes, given the circumstances," he said, "and the pressure, the quality, where we played in this building against the reigning world champions, unbeaten in 43 matches. Putting a performance out there in Madrid, and in this environment, was a very complete performance."

Tuchel will, of course, need repeat performances - but the outstanding ability and character England displayed here to beat the World Cup holders will deliver a huge injection of confidence and self-belief.

One of the most anticipated fall TV series, "Blade Runner 2099," recently dropped its final neon-tinted trailer, and now we’ve finally got a handle on the plot dynamics of this dystopian thriller set in the cyberpunk world of Ridley Scott's original.

Prime Video's bold and brooding 8-episode series lands Nov. 25 as a tangential sequel to Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049," unfolding some 50 years after the 2017 feature film. Now the artificial inmates are running the asylum when violent replicant uprisings flip the script, causing humanity to become second-class citizens.

"In Los Angeles 2099, Cora (Hunter Schafer) lived her entire life on the run, a chameleon forced to adopt numerous identities," states Prime Video's synopsis. "To secure a stable future for her brother, she assumes one final identity and is forced to partner with Olwen (Michelle Yeoh), a Blade Runner who’s confronting the end of her life. The two are pulled into a widening conspiracy that poses an existential threat to a city that’s fighting to be reborn."

This engrossing final trailer reveals more of the detailed noir world and Cora's plight to blend into society as a Blade Runner who links up with Olwen, an aging replicant exterminator, for an uneasy partnership. Here, a tense scene plays out in this preview as Cora undergoes an intense police station screening while being used as a resistance pawn to help take back the city from usurping androids. But another deep mystery lies hidden in plain sight!

"You have to see the lie that is in front of you," warns Yeoh's dying synthetic cop.

"Blade Runner 2099" sports a spirited cast that includes Dimitri Abold ("The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes") and Lewis Gribben ("Somewhere Boy”) in collaboration with Katelyn Rose Downey ("The Nun II"), Daniel Rigby ('Renegade Nell"), Johnny Harris ("A Gentleman in Moscow"), Amy Lennox ("Only Child"), Sheila Atim ("The Woman King") and Matthew Needham ("House of the Dragon”).

Delivered by creator and showrunner Silka Louisa ("Shining Girls"), and executive produced by Silka Louisa and Ridley Scott’s Scott Free Productions, "Blade Runner 2099" lands on Prime Video beginning Nov. 25, 2026.
