#806. Phil Collins Walks With 2 Canes During Rare Public Appearance

Phil Collins made his first major public appearance in months at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame on Nov. 14, using the assistance of two canes during the evening.

The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame marked another day in paradise for Phil Collins fans.

After all, the beloved rocker made an ultra-rare public appearance for the Nov. 14 induction ceremony in Los Angeles, marking his first major event since May amid his ongoing health challenges.

For the occasion—which saw Collins inducted as a solo member, having previously been included as part of Genesis 2010—the 75-year-old walked the carpet in an elegant black suit which he paired with a white button-down shirt, the collar of which he left loose, and with the assistance of two wooden canes.

Collins was joined for the evening by three of his five children; Joely Collins, 54, whom he shares with ex-wife Andrea Bertorelli; Lily Collins, 37, whom he shares with ex-wife Jill Tavelman; and Nicholas Collins, 25, whom he shares with ex-wife Orianne Cevey. (The drummer is also dad to Simon Collins, 50, with Bertorelli and Matthew Collins, 22, with Cevey.)

In fact, during his speech on stage, Collins proved there will always be gratitude in his heart for his former wives, reserving a special shoutout for them.

"They loved me through the years, but more importantly, they have given me five great children," he said, per USA Today. "They are incredibly talented, and I made life tough for them growing up. But they have turned into such wonderful human beings. I love them to death."

The “Son of Man” artist—who in recent years has been navigating challenges with his kidneys, nerves and spine, in addition to type-2 diabetes—also took a moment to address his health after first taking to the stage.

“Thank you so much, I'm really not as bad as it looks," he told the audience, holding his canes aloft. "I'm much better."

And he thanked his longtime assistant Lindsay Evans for helping his health get back on track.

"Without her, I wouldn't be here. I'd be in a box, six feet under," he noted, saying Lindsay was able to show him his lifestyle choices were "bad, and she showed me what to do to make it better."

As for his musical legacy, Collins is still thanking his lucky stars for everything that has come his way.

"I've really been just very, very lucky," he said. " I grew up just wanting to play the drums. That's all I wanted to do. Everything else has been a very happy accident."

And when it comes to his future, and whether that includes a return to the stage, Collins teased there might be something in the air for fans.

“You haven't heard the last of me," he noted, "I can promise you that.”

For more stars who have spoken about their health challenges publicly, read on.

The Blink-182 drummer stopped smoking weed after being diagnosed with "precancer of the esophagus."

"I loved blunts and I would smoke too much," he shared on a November 2026 episode of the Big Bro with Kid Cudi podcast, recalling how his doctor said it was a "serious case. "He’s like, ‘This is your warning shot. Don’t f--l around. You’ve got to stop smoking."

The Jessie alum opened up about her "hellish" migraines, sharing how they've worsened after suffering five concussions over the course of her life.

"The brain injuries make things significantly worse," Ryan shared during a September 2026 episode of Mythical Kitchen’s Last Meals. "I had a pretty crazy, life-altering brain injury a few years ago, and I was out of commission for six months."

While Ryan described her first four concussions as "incidents," she said her fifth one was trauma caused by "sustained shaking over a minute of time."

Now, the former Disney Channel star needs to close her eyes to "think better."

"Quite often the world is really loud. It’s really too bright. There’s a lot going on," she explained. "The visual data that I'm taking in can be so distracting and so loud. Then, with the migraines—which are significantly worsened by that—it sort of is too much."

Brianna "Chickenfry" LaPaglia's Ovarian Cyst

In May 2026, the BFFs podcaster underwent emergency surgery after doctors discovered a large ovarian cyst that had been twisting her organs and causing internal bleeding.

"There was a half a liter of blood in my pelvic floor," Brianna shared in a TikTok video after the operation. "I have five incisions all over my stomach. They went in through my belly button with a camera so they could find all the blood."

The Total Bellas alum revealed that one of her breast implants shifted after an elbow slam from fellow WWE star Piper Niven during a July 2025 wrestling match.

"It's OK," she told sister Bella Garcia at the time. "We're going to get it fixed one day. I told the doctor, I go, 'Newly divorced, so the minute the boots are hung up, I'm going to come back to you and we're going to make these girls look real good, because these girls are going to get some action in the future and that can't look like that.'"

In October 2026, the former The Bachelorette star detailed how she cracked a vertebra in her spine after setting her vibration plate—a motorized platform that rapidly moves back and forth to promote muscle activation and circulation—to "level 30, supersonic speed."

"Seemingly, subtly, somewhere on the way to 30, maybe 10 or 20, my vertebrae turn crooked and rub against each other," Windey shared in a Substack essaye aptly titled "Broke back, no mountain."

"It was too fast vibrations I guess, and too many vibrations maybe, and too much pressure to shake," she continued. "And it broke. Broke right off, like your ex-boyfriend’s bumper. Well, technically, it cracked."

The injury left her with what she described as "insatiable" paresthesia—a medical term for a tingling, pins-and-needles sensation.

"This is the greatest sense of condemnation; of persecution, I’ll ever feel," she added. "And I do wish it on my worst enemy If only they hadn’t wished it on me first."

The 12 Years a Slave star was diagnosed with uterine fibroids—non-cancerous growths that develop in or around the uterus—in 2014, the same year she won an Oscar for performance in the movie.

However, it wasn't until 2025 when she disclosed her diagnosis, writing on Instagram that she had been "suffering in silence" for more than a decade.

"When we reach puberty, we're taught periods mean pain, and that pain is simply part of being a woman," she shared. "We're struggling alone with something that affects us most."

The Beverly Hills, 90210 alum revealed in April 2025 that he was recovering from surgery after his appendix nearly burst.

“Last week, I started feeling some pain in my stomach,” Brian said in an Instagram video at the time. “I ended up going to the emergency room, and I had a perforated appendix. Not quite burst, but just before.”

He added, “I'm on the road to recovery. It's not an easy process. This is my first major surgery.”

In July 2025, the Daisy Jones & The Six star shared that she had been hospitalized due to a hernia—a gap in the muscular wall that's commonly found in the abdomen or groin area—caused by wearing tight pants.

"'Suki you never tweet anymore,'" she wrote on X, formerly known as Twitter. "Have you ever considered I wore pants so tight 6 months ago it caused a hernia & I’ve been too scared to tell you?"

Savannah DeMelo's Mid-Game "Medical Emergency" Mid-Game

The Racing Louisville midfielder collapsed just a few minutes into her soccer team's September 2025 match against Seattle Reign at Lumen Field in Seatle.

The United States Women’s National Team player could be seen slowly sitting down on the field with a teammate by her side, per Reuters, as the referee called for trainers to check her out. She collapsed seconds later.

“Savannah received immediate on-field care from medical personnel and was transported to a local hospital for further evaluation,” the National Women’s Soccer League wrote on X later that night. “She is stable and alert."

Adam Devine's Long-Term Injury From Childhood Accident

Adam Devine shared that injuries he sustained after getting hit by a cement truck when he was 11 years old are still affecting him to this day.

“It’s been a nightmare,” Devine said in a 2025 episode of the In Depth With Graham Bensinger podcast. “I have spasms all over. For a while, [the doctors] told me I was dying—literally, within this last year.”

He noted that pain comes and goes, adding, "My body has all these things that are a little wonky and a little wrong with it."

The Bachelor Nation alum shared that he went to the hospital “crawling on all fours” due to overwhelming back pain that was aggravated during an RV trip with a friend.

“Right now, knees to my toes, it’s, like, still tingly, which is crazy,” he said on a March 2025 episode of his Trading Secrets podcast. “And to put in perspective, I don’t know, man, like not to sound douchey, but like two, three weeks ago, maybe a month ago, I was squatting probably like 295 pounds. And right now, I can’t do a squat on my foot. I can’t do a one legged squat, I fall. It’s like I had a stroke or something.”

But with the help of a back specialist and some steroids, he added, “We’re on the mend.”

Real Housewives of Orange County’s Gina Kirschenheiter shared her ex-husband Matt Kirschenheiter suffered a heart attack in March 2025, but thankfully survived the ordeal.

The 30 Rock star suffered a health scare at a New York Knicks basketball game in March 2025, leading to him being wheeled out of Madison Square Garden.

However, the comedian shared an update on social media the following day, noting it was a case of food poisoning and that he was on the mend.

The Even Stevens alum shared in February 2025 that she was shot in the face while on a trip to shoot clay pigeons to celebrate husband Brendan Rooney's birthday.

"There was another party with us and they unsafely fired in the wrong direction and shot me in the face," she wrote on Instagram. "@thebrendanrooney immediately sprung into action, assessed me, and rushed me to the hospital. I was hit in 5 places, one was less than an inch from hitting me directly in my right eye."

The Kim Possible alum continued, "Unfortunately a fragment got lodged behind my eye and it is too risky to remove surgically at this time. Doctors will continue to monitor me (I can see normally at the moment)."

The actress said she was grateful to be alive. "I love my daughters, husband, family, and friends so much," she said. "I saw my life flash before my eyes and I’m telling you, hug the people around you every chance you can. Life can change in an instant."

While the internet isn't always a kind place, Amy Schumer is happy that, in this case, it helped her get answers."The internet really came for me after doing a bunch of press, and I was like, 'OK everybody, relax,'" Amy recalled of her "puffier" face on a January 2025 episode of Call Her Daddy. "But then doctors were chiming in in the comments and they were like, 'No no, we think something’s really up. Your face looks so crazy that we think something’s up. And I’m like, ‘Wait, I’m getting trolled by doctors?’"After these doctors said they thought she had Cushing syndrome and that it may be caused by spiking coritsol levels or steroid injections, the Life & Beth creator thought, "Wait, I have been getting steroid injections in my scars.""I had a breast reduction, a C-section, whatever, and so I was getting these steroid injections," Amy said. "So it gave me this thing called Cushing syndrome, which I wouldn’t have known if the internet hadn’t come for me so hard."Toda, Amy is just relieved she's OK. As she shared in a February 2024 News Not Noise newsletter, "Finding out I have the kind of Cushing that will just work itself out and I'm healthy was the greatest news imaginable."

Casey Fitzgerald's Neck Injury From Hockey Skate Blade

The AHL player was cut by a fellow player's skate during a game in December 2024 and received 25 stitches. His father, New Jersey Devils general manager Tom Fitzgerald later told ESPN after his son was fully recovered, "We're very lucky. I don't wish that on any parent."

Hailey Bieber had the "scariest moment" of her life when she was having breakfast with husband Justin Bieber and started experiencing stroke-like symptoms in March 2022."Justin was like, 'Are you OK?'" the Rhode skincare mogul shared a month later on YouTube, "and I just didn't respond because I wasn't sure. And then he asked me again and when I went to respond, I couldn't speak. The right side of my face started drooping. I couldn't get a sentence out."While Hailey said the facial drooping stopped and her speech came back, she went to the hospital to make sure she was OK."They did some scans and they were able to see that I had suffered a small blood clot to my brain," the model added, "which they labeled and categorized as something called a TIA [Transient Ischemic Attack]."Later, Hailey went to the University of California, Los Angeles, where she found out she had a hole in her heart called a patent foramen ovale (PFO).She explained the blood clot had traveled into her heart, "escaped" through the hole and went to her brain, leading to the TIA.Hailey said she had a successful PFO closure procedure and was now feeling great.

The same year Hailey had her health scare, Justin experienced one of his own.In June 2022, the "Baby" singer shared he was diagnosed with Ramsay Hunt syndrome, a condition that caused temporary paralysis to parts of his face and forced him to cancel the remainder of his Justice World Tour."It is from this virus that attacks the nerve in my ear and my facial nerves and has caused my face to have paralysis," Justin explained in an Instagram video at the time. "As you can see, this eye is not blinking. I can't smile on this side of my face. This nostril will not move. So, there's full paralysis on this side of my face."In fact, he told his followers it had gotten "progressively harder to eat." But after a while, the paralysis went away."He's doing really well," Hailey said on a June 2022 episode of Good Morning America, later adding, "He's feeling a lot better. Obviously, it was just a very scary and random situation to happen, but he's going to be totally OK and I'm just grateful that he's fine."

While Jamie Foxx initially kept details of his April 2023 hospitalization private, he later opened up about what he went through.One day in Atlanta, "I was having such a bad headache, so I asked my boy, I said, ‘Listen, I need an aspirin,’” the Oscar winner said in his 2024 Netflix special What Had Happened Was... “Before I could get the Aspirin, I went out. I don’t remember 20 days.”Jamie said he was initially taken to a doctor who gave him a cortisone shot and then sent him home. However, his concerned sister Deidra Dixon then drove him to a hospital, where they got an answer: He had a brain bleed that led to a stroke.Twenty days after undergoing an operation, the Django Unchained woke up May 4 in a wheelchair and couldn’t walk. He then went to Chicago for rehabilitation and therapy."All I can tell you is that I appreciate every prayer,” he said, “because I needed every prayer.”

Tracey Yukich's Medical Emergency on The Biggest Loser

The reality star revealed that she "died" while running a mile during the first challenge of the NBC competition series.

“I don't remember a lot,” she explained on Fit for TV: The Reality of The Biggest Loser. “I remember hearing the helicopter. I just felt like I was floating. And then my grandpa was there. And then I saw darkness. But then I saw light. So I knew, I knew I died that day.”

“My organs were literally shutting down,” she continued. “I didn't realize that I had rhabdomyolysis. And rhabdomyolysis is your body's way of saying, ‘I'm going to shut down on you.’”

Emilia Clarke filmed battle scenes for Game of Thrones, but in 2019, she published an essay in The New Yorker titled "A Battle for My Life."Having a bad headache at the gym, "I reached the toilet, sank to my knees, and proceeded to be violently, voluminously ill," the actress wrote. "Meanwhile, the pain—shooting, stabbing, constricting pain—was getting worse. At some level, I knew what was happening: my brain was damaged."She was taken to the hospital for a brain scan."The diagnosis was quick and ominous: a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), a life-threatening type of stroke, caused by bleeding into the space surrounding the brain," the Emmy nominee added. "I’d had an aneurysm, an arterial rupture."Emilia had immediate surgery to seal the aneurysm, calling the pain "unbearable." While she was recovering, she continued, she experienced aphasia and was "muttering nonsense."A week later, "the aphasia passed," Emilia added, and she left the hospital a month after being admitted. At a 2013 brain scan, she learned a growth "doubled in size" and that she needed surgery again."When they woke me, I was screaming in pain," she wrote. "The procedure had failed. I had a massive bleed and the doctors made it plain that my chances of surviving were precarious if they didn’t operate again. This time they needed to access my brain in the old-fashioned way—through my skull."Thankfully, Emilia shared, she's now "at a hundred per cent."

Snoop Dogg's daughter Cori Broadus is grateful for her family.Because after she suffered a "severe stroke" in January 2024, her loved ones rushed to be by her side."I texted them that I just had a stroke and sent them a picture," she told E! News correspondent Will Marfuggi in December 2024. "Everybody just came to my rescue."Because of other medical concerns, Cori ended up staying in the hospital longer than she initially expected."I could have went home after my stroke, but my lupus wasn't doing so well," the Snoop's Fatherhood: Cori and Wayne's Story star continued. "My kidneys were failing. It was a lot going on."Today, Cori is on the mend."I'm doing great," she added. "I just had a little bit of motor skills that I had to work back on. But other than that, I was fine."

Shailene Woodley’s early 20s were not an easy time health-wise.“It got to the point where I was losing my hearing. I couldn’t walk for longer than five minutes at a time without having to lay down for hours, and hours and sleep. Everything I ate hurt my stomach,” the actress said on a September 2024 episode of the SHE MD Podcast. “It was this conflation of issues and diagnoses and different doctors telling me different things.”So Shailene—who chose to keep the exact condition private—set out to find answers. “I come from a very holistic background and study herbalism,” she added. “So I was very keen on, ‘I’m going to work with real MDs, [and] I’m also going to work with independent kind of healers.’ Just trying to search for some sense of comfort in my own skin.”It was a long journey—one that lasted for 10 years.“Throughout that decade, a lot of other things came from feeling so much discomfort physically,” the Big Little Lies star noted, “which was, ‘My gosh, if everything I eat hurts my stomach, I’m now suddenly afraid of food.’ And then going into the kind of mental f--ckery that can happen with that of body dysmorphia and confusion about identity and feeling safe in my own capsule, in my own skin, what that meant, and what that should be.”After tending to both her physical and mental health, Shailene is feeling much better.“It was a journey that ultimately physically resolved itself, and I am very healthy,” she shared. “I’m so happy to be able to say that."

#805. Garbage Wraps 2026 Tour With Mariachi-Infused Free Show at Mexico City’s Zócalo: 5 Best Moments

Shirley Manson became the first non-Hispanic woman to conquer the iconic venue on Nov. 14.

Garbage wrapped up their 2026 tour on Saturday (Nov. 14) with a free concert at Mexico City’s Zócalo, paying tribute to a country they have visited for three decades with a nod to its culture.

The Scottish-American band performed their song “The World Is Not Enough” from the James Bond film of the same name with a mariachi arrangement. They also invited Paulina Villarreal, drummer of the Mexican rock band The Warning, to sing their iconic track “I Think I’m Paranoid.”

Garbage frontwoman Shirley Manson, 60, made history by becoming the first non-hispanic woman to headline the Zócalo, drawing a crowd of 90,000 people, according to official figures. Before her, superstars Rosalía and Shakira had packed Mexico’s most important public square in 2023 and 2026, respectively.

“It’s one of the biggest honors of our entire career [to play at the Zócalo], and the whole band is very excited,” Manson told Billboard Español before taking the stage. “Really, we’re all really emotional, and we’re so proud to be here tonight, and it’s an extraordinary… It’s a culmination of 30 years of coming to Mexico and playing in this amazing city.”

The Scottish-born artist noted that her outfit — featuring a white veil, a floral tricolor headdress and braided hair — paid homage to Mexican culture, particularly the legendary Mexican painter Frida Kahlo, whose life and work have inspired her.

During their performance, the band — also including drummer Butch Vig, guitarists Duke Erikson and Steve Marker, as well as guest bassist Nicole Fiorentino — surprised fans with their own rendition of The Cure’s classic “Lovesong.”

The setlist kicked off with “No Future,” followed by “Hold,” “Have We Met (The Void),” “Vow,” “The Men Who Rule the World,” “Chinese Fire Horse” and “Run Baby Run.” The group also performed “The Day That I Met God,” “Control,” “Fix Me Now,” “Special” and “Stupid Girl,” taking fans on a journey through 30 years of their career and eight studio albums, including Garbage (1995), Version 2.0 (1998), Beautiful Garbage (2001) and Let All That We Imagine Be the Light (2025).

Garbage joins an exclusive list of acts who have performed at Mexico’s Zócalo, the second-largest public square in the world after Tiananmen Square in Beijing. This iconic venue has hosted legendary artists and bands, such as Paul McCartney, Roger Waters, Justin Bieber, Manu Chao, Shakira, Rosalía, Café Tacvba and the late icon of Mexican regional music Vicente Fernández. The concert was organized by Mexico City’s government through its local Department of Culture.

The record for attendance at free Zócalo concerts is held by Colombian superstar Shakira, who drew over 400,000 people in March 2026, according to city authorities. She is followed by the Argentine rock band Los Fabulosos Cadillacs, who brought in 300,000 attendees in June 2023, and Grupo Firme, who gathered 280,000 fans in September 2022.

Here are the five standout moments from Garbage’s show at Mexico City’s Zócalo.

The traditional Mexican shout to express brotherhood also reached Manson, who went down into the crowd twice to make the encounter more intimate. With the Mexican flag tied around her neck, the performer sang “Chinese Fire Horse” while greeting and hugging some fans. The chant “¡Shirley, hermana, ya eres mexicana!” (“Shirley, sister, you’re already Mexican!”) echoed through the city’s iconic plaza also known as the First Square, moving her to tears.

One of the most anticipated moments of the night came with the appearance of Paulina Villarreal, a member of The Warning, whom Manson had already announced as a guest. The Mexican rocker joined the band during “I Think I’m Paranoid,” a song that has become one of Garbage’s signature tracks. The performance sealed a moment between two female rockers from different generations who have made history.

A surprise the group prepared for this special night was a heartfelt rendition of “Lovesong” by the iconic British band The Cure. The opening chords sparked euphoria among the audience, who joined Manson in singing at the top of their lungs, creating a unique and deeply moving moment.

Manson, who has stood out for her activism in favor of women’s rights and the LGBT community, took a moment during the concert to express her support for Palestine upon noticing some flags waving in the Zócalo square.

“It makes me happy that people are fighting for those who don’t have very much in life and who are in need of protection and who are struggling against a power that is threatening to completely destroy them,” the artist said. “The important thing I think to remember is that we’re all absolutely exactly the same. Doesn’t matter if you come from f—ing Palestine, whether you come from Mexico City, whether you come from Edinburgh, Scotland, or Madison, Wisconsin, or from Boston, Massachusetts. We’re all the f—ing same”.

Garbage took the iconic theme song “The World Is Not Enough,” which they originally recorded in 1999 for the James Bond film of the same name, to another level by transforming the symphonic orchestra sound into traditional Mexican music, accompanied by the Mariachi Fiesta de México. The arrangements for the piece were crafted by sound sculptor Héctor Ruiz, who elevated it to a dramatic and festive level. The performance served as the finale to a concert by a band that helped define the sound of rock in the 1990s.

#804. Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Download the Nature Podcast 13 November 2026

The past year has been... a lot. Record-breaking temperatures, devastating floods and catastrophic wildfires have brought the realities of climate change into sharp focus for people around the world. At the same time, many governments and organisations have scaled back on their climate action.

If you’re anything like me you might be feeling it’s all a bit ‘doom and gloom’. So in this series I decided to face my climate anxiety head on and set out in search of reasons for optimism.

In this first episode of Cooked? I talk to experts around the world about what the data really show and why there are still reasons to hope.

00:00 How climate change feels overwhelming

21:49 How are the world’s nations doing on climate change?

Nature: COP31 kicks off as planet faces imminent overshoot of 1.5 °C climate target

Nature: How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown

Nature: Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change

This episode was written and produced by Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was the editor. Music was by Daniel Knowler, Akio Jefferson, Lionel Cohen and The Conductor, and was provided by Triple Scoop Music via Getty Images. Thanks to Hannah Ritchie, Ketan Joshi and Niklas Höhne for featuring in this episode.

I’m going to be honest with you. I worry a lot.

I worry about all sorts of things. Money, friends, family, if my voice is weird as you’re listening to it... but there’s one thing I’ve been worried about since I was a teenager in the early 2000s. The climate.

Those anxieties have only gotten worse. In recent years, it has felt like climate action has stalled. In 2024, the world passed the 1.5˚C ‘threshold’ set in Paris for the first time. Shortly thereafter, Donald Trump returned to the White House and on the first day of his Presidency set about reversing climate policies of the previous administration, vowing to promote fossil fuels. In Europe, right-wing politicians have taken aim at climate goals, with the EU weakening previously ambitious environmental policy. All while it’s getting hotter and hotter. In May there were record breaking temperatures in my home of the UK , then in June those records were broken again, twice in the same week in fact, with temperatures in some places across the continent more than ten degrees hotter than they were between 1991-2020. That was the story all over Europe. Without climate change, it’s extremely unlikely Europeans would have had to endure these heatwaves. And globally, scientists of all stripes have expressed doubts that any government has done enough to avoid the worst impacts of climate change.

So, it feels like we’re failing on climate, heck, I can even look outside my window and see evidence for that. But what’s weird is that even as climate change is affecting me more, I find it harder to engage with.

As things get worse, I’m having trouble staying optimistic that we, you me and everyone, can do anything about it. And that’s an odd position to be in, as a science journalist. Climate change is one of the biggest stories of our time.

Every week, we pick out stories to cover on the podcast. And I always want to report the latest climate science, and I do, but I find it hard. Sometimes it just feels like more bad news at a time when our audience, and I, could do with less. I feel hopeless.

But is that actually right? Am I justified in that feeling? As the one thing I know about science is often the truth is a bit more complicated than we think. So, while the narrative can feel overwhelming negative, is that really what the data says?

To try and shake myself out of this climate funk, talking to some of the scientists and campaigners on the front lines of climate research, and what I found was a story of: Tipping points…

That has the potential to move this energy transition over the edge.

I don't think we've had this level of uncertainty about a technological shift before.

I think there's this positive feedback loop by which all of our individual level actions can lead to bigger collective actions.

The system is changing at exponential speed.

This is Cooked? a three-part miniseries for Nature, where I try and find out whether we are well… cooked. Is it game over for climate or are there reasons for hope? I’m your host Nick Petrić Howe. And in this first episode, I decided to start with the data, and I had a good idea of who might be able to help me with that.

As a data scientist, I'm biased. And I would say, look at the data to understand for these big problems, where they're coming from, why they're happening, and importantly, what we can do to solve them.

In the past year or so, I’ve found myself struggling with anxiety about the climate. But a couple of years ago a book came out that seemed to fly against what I had assumed was the case, as it stated, backed up with oodles of data, that it isn’t the end of the world. So, I knew I wanted to speak to its author — Hannah Ritchie.

What I wanted to do in that book was, think, twofold.

That’s Hannah, the author of ‘Not the end of the world’ and a data scientist at our World in Data and the University of Oxford.

One was that I was trying to write it to my former self, who was very, very pessimistic, wasn't sure if there was really a future there for me and present where we are now. And the point is not that these problems are solved in any way, they're still huge problems, but we have started to make progress and there's lots of opportunity for us to make more progress. My point is not that we should be complacent and optimistic that these problems will solve themselves. I think it's to kind of maybe get rid of a bit of the cynicism that there's nothing that we can do and actually no one is doing anything because I don't think that's true. And I think the second kind of motivation for doing that is to look at the data and understand if we want to solve these problems, what are the really key and big things that we need to do to solve them?

The book looked at seven huge challenges that humanity faces, including climate change, examining each through the lens of data, to understand the progress we have and haven’t made on them, and what we should do. So I was curious to hear from Hannah about how we were actually doing on climate change.

If you go back 10 years, the world we were sitting in when the world signed the Paris Agreement was that the alternatives to fossil fuels were much more expensive than fossil fuels. For solar and wind were way more expensive. Batteries were extremely expensive. Electric vehicles were basically not on the radar at that point. So it seemed very, very hard to me at the time to see how the world would actually progress on this. What we've seen over the last decade is this huge drop in the costs of these low-carbon energy sources. And that now means that they're cost competitive with fossil fuels, right? So you have the kind of short-term incentive of picking the low-cost solution, now adding up and aligning with the long-term issue we're trying to solve, which is climate change.

These days renewable energy is very cheap. Let’s take solar energy as an example. Between 2009 and 2025, estimates from the investment firm Lazard suggest solar energy prices have dropped to less than a sixth of what it used to cost on average. This number even includes the continued costs of running solar plants, making them, along with wind, the cheapest form of energy.

This change has helped Hannah go from pessimistic to optimistic about the future of climate change. It’s not just that the costs have tumbled, more and more this ‘clean’ energy is actually being implemented as well.

We now also see that many countries are now rolling out clean energy at an increasingly fast pace. So it's not like it's just that the cost has dropped. You can actually now start to see that translating into action.

Hannah also thinks that this electrification of the world has other benefits too.

What's really key about that electrification lever, and I think is under appreciated, is how much you gain there in terms of efficiency. You know, it's not just we want to do this because it saves us carbon emissions, which it will if we were powering that through low carbon power, but also you get huge efficiency gains from this. like driving in an electric car uses about a third of the energy of driving in a petrol car, right? So you actually also get rid of lots of this energy waste that we currently have in the system.

Worldwide, adoption rates of electric vehicles are increasing. Around a quarter of every new vehicle sold is electric, and in some countries this rate is much higher. In Norway 97% of new cars sold were electric, while in China 53% were. Now, many people are critical of electrical vehicles for various reasons. Mining of lithium for use in batteries can be very environmentally damaging, for instance. And using public transport is better than having a personal electric vehicle most of the time. But when it comes to their climate credentials, electric cars beat conventional every time.

The world has also been built in many places to favour vehicles and in some areas public transport is not a viable option. So if we want the most people to use the least climate emission causing form of transport, electric vehicles will be part of the mix.

But it’s not just data on clean energy and electrification that gives Hannah hope. She also points to progress that’s been made in making steel and concrete production more climate conscious. They’re maybe a bit less obvious in our day to day lives, as most of us don’t work on big construction projects, but these core components of buildings come with big emissions. Cement production, for example, accounted for around 6% of global carbon emissions as of 2024 according to the International Energy Agency.

But this is down from a peak in 2021, due to slowed growth in construction, and is projected to decrease further as improvements are made to the recipe for cement, or alternatives to it entirely are created.

These solutions haven't been scaled yet. They're at a very, very small level, but I think we still have made progress there and there are actually solutions starting to come online and starting to get cost competitive, but it will take some time for them to build up to a kind of level where you would actually start to see dents in the data.

As Hannah said, the point of her book and this examination of the data is not to allow us all to pat ourselves on the back and say ‘job’s a good ‘un’. There’s still a lot that we need to do, and in many ways some of these changes aren’t happening fast enough. Rather the point is to not make us feel despondent and hopeless, as that helps nobody.

And there are actually reasons for optimism. Falling prices in renewables, increased electrification and more climate-conscious construction are all starting to make dents in the data according to Hannah.

So maybe I don't need to be so worried after all. assuming of course that we can keep this up.

Renewable energy growth has continued in the US, but all it's doing is making the rise in emissions less bad.

There's a new disruptive and energy-intensive technology out there that could stall climate progress. Artificial intelligence.

The level of debate about this technology is massive. It's actually really fascinating because I don't think we've had this level of uncertainty about a technological shift before.

Whenever I open social media these days, I see a lot of scepticism about artificial intelligence. I don’t have to scroll far to come across a video of someone pretending to be a large language model powered chatbot who says silly things while chugging litres of water. But the backlash against the technology is spilling out of social media and pouring into real world legislation. We've seen the first moratoriums on the building of data centres, the facilities that house the infrastructure for AI and other internet services. And often the cited reasons are environmental — water and electricity use.

So that got me wondering, if AI is so energy intensive could it stall climate progress? Especially as many of these data centres are using fossil fuels to meet their energy needs. For the sake of this podcast, I’m just going to focus on energy demands, as that’s what’s more relevant to the climate, and put other environmental concerns to one side for now.

To do so, I wanted to put those memes aside as well and find out what the data actually says. So, I reached out to an expert on data centres and their energy use to go through some of the numbers.

My name is Ketan Joshi. I'm an independent researcher and analyst, working on energy and data centres and fossil fuel phase-out.

Ketan has been working as energy analyst for many years, but more recently has been focusing on how much energy data centres consume, particularly for artificial intelligence. I wanted to know how a growth in data centres would affect the climate, but he explained to me that that’s a quite a difficult thing to work out.

We have thousands of projections of data center growth into the near future. But the level of variation that you see in these projections makes me almost want to never use them. and the reason behind that is really because some projections basically take a linear pathway, you know, it'll grow to maybe four to five percent by twenty thirty. I've seen ones that are up to like twenty percent of global energy consumption for data centers, you know, in the coming decades. And I find that to be a little bit silly. And the reason behind that is really because some projections basically take a linear pathway. You know, it'll grow to maybe 4 to 5% by 2030. I've seen ones that are up to like 20% of global energy consumption for data centers, you know, in the coming decades. And I find that to be a little bit silly. And the reason behind this wild skew of future projections is because there is an inherent assumption about the future of artificial intelligence and the shape and form that it takes in the near future. The way that we tend to formulate projections just falls apart with something like this where there is an inherent uncertainty as to what the technology is, what it's going to be used for, whether it's hype, whether it's real, whether we go for high energy consumption models or low energy consumption models. There's like 10 crisscrossing vectors of uncertainty that make it really, really hard to say what's going to happen.

The future is, unfortunately, unpredictable. It’s hard to know what AI will look like in 10 years, or even 10 days for that matter. So, it’s tough to fit into our projections of the future and how it may impact the climate. As a result, Ketan likes to focus on the here and now to see what we can understand about the technology. To start, it’s important to note that while AI gets a lot of attention, it currently forms a small part of energy usage. The International Energy Agency, for instance, estimates that data centres use — for everything, not just AI — around 2% of the world’s energy. As Ketan says, that may grow — perhaps by a lot, perhaps by not so much. It’s part of the uncertainty with the technology.

According to Ketan’s analyses, though, AI and by that, I mean the generative kind that powers chatbots, may be particularly energy intensive.

Something that I've found in the past few weeks actually, having looked at some of the new newer corporate statements. So for instance, Microsoft analyzed their latest statement, I analyzed Google and Amazon. And all three of those companies are using more energy to earn the same amount of revenue, if that makes sense.

Rather than working towards more efficiency as computing has done in the past, Ketan thinks that companies are using more and more energy to try and make cleverer chatbots, or autonomous AI agents. Google and Microsoft for example, have acknowledged that they’ve increased their energy usage as they build out AI capacity.

One thing to note here is that different use cases of AI have different energy demands. Techniques like Machine Learning which often gets labelled AI, don't use as much energy as generative AI like Large Language Models. And then within generative AI, things like a written response from a chatbot needs a lot less energy than generating an image or a video.

But the concern for the climate is that all this energy needs to come from somewhere. And if there isn’t sufficient renewable energy in place, it will come from fossil fuels.

Figuring out how much data centres may be using fossil fuels, though, is not easy. Ketan explained to me that when companies report their power consumption it’s not quite as simple as them just stating what proportion of renewable energy versus fossil fuels they’ve used. Similarly to carbon offsets, companies can purchase certificates from renewable energy providers and then use them to show that their emissions are lower than they are. Microsoft recently stopped using this method, which has been widely criticised, and in their most recent report there was a large rise in their emissions.

The companies can also have positive effects on renewable energy. With their vast resources they can fund new wind and solar farms. Microsoft, for example, has announced a $6 billion agreement to build AI infrastructure powered by renewables in Norway. Deals such as these can also then be included in companies’ reports on what kinds of energy they use.

So, untangling all of this is pretty tricky. With that in mind, Ketan explained how energy use has changed in the US, where there’s the most data centres in the world.

There's a new report from the energy information administration, updating on 2025 data. And of course, you know, emissions have gone up. They haven't gone up crazy. Like they haven't gone, you know, it's not like it’s skyrocketing, you know, right angle, but they have gone up and renewable energy growth has continued in the US, but all it's doing is just making the rise in emissions less bad.

The report Ketan mentioned says that US energy-related CO2 emissions went up by about 2% in 2025. That may not sound like a lot, but it’s against a backdrop of emissions falling, so any rise is a cause for concern for the climate. And like Ketan says, renewable energy adoption has continued apace, so the fact that there were more renewables, but emissions still went up implies that more energy was coming from carbon-emitting fossil fuels.

This is backed up by a report from the Energy Institute, a UK-based professional body that monitors energy use. The report said that US emissions had increased in 2025 due to higher coal use, and that electricity demand had risen faster than supply driven in part by data centres and artificial intelligence. An independent research firm, the Rhodium group, also identified a rise in carbon emissions in the US and cited a particularly cool winter, more coal use and increased demand in electricity from data centres as reasons.

Of course, data centres could be powered by renewable energy, but building this supply takes time and if we have a sudden increase in energy demand, due to AI for instance, then fossil fuels could be used to plug the gap. Google, for example, has acknowledged that it’s expanding its AI development on a grid that is undersupplied with clean energy, but still remains a large funder of clean energy projects. Google still plans to reduce their emissions, but right now, they’re using more fossil fuel energy.

Ketan would like to see more transparency from the tech companies creating AI on its environmental impacts, so it can be scrutinised more easily, along with more regulation from governments. He also thinks that everyone has a role to play deciding on what terms we use this technology.

Ketan is actually optimistic about the future, as it seems that the general public are beginning to understand that they do have the power to demand better from these companies. Environmental, cost and climate concerns are being raised against AI, and politicians are listening — you can look to the growth of moratoriums on data centres to see that. To be clear this isn’t just because of climate, opponents of data centres describe them as being ugly, straining local resources and not providing many tangible benefits to their residents. These are issues that affect people no matter what side of the political divide they sit on. And this bipartisan opposition has meant that politicians have started taking action.

But that touches on another thing I wondered about. What are governments and nations actually doing? Are they meeting the goals they’ve set out for climate? And it’s certainly felt to me like there’s been some backsliding recently — with right-wing politicians taking aim at climate goals.

So, what does the data say about how the nations of the world are doing?

Well, it's better than we used to think 10 years ago, but it's definitely not there where it should be.

If you’ve ever engaged with climate change, you’ll know that it’s a global issue. The whole world is getting hotter and that affects all of us. Because of that, nations often get together and come up with various pledges on what they’re going to do about that. What comes out of these pledges is ultimately what we, as a global society, are doing about climate change.

And I knew a scientist who keeps close tabs on this, so I gave him a call.

Hello. Niklas Höhne, New Climate Institute, calling in from Cologne, Germany.

I met Niklas a few years ago at COP26, the enormous climate conference run by the UN. He co-founded the New Climate Institute, a non-profit that works on climate policy, where he oversees analyses on climate policy. I was there reporting for Nature and I asked him, even back then, if things were hopeless. I remember that he didn’t coddle me or make me despair. He gave a nuanced picture. So, I caught up with him to see where we are now.

So while 10 years ago we thought global greenhouse gas emissions would rise forever and would lead to a temperature increase of three and half degrees by the end of the century, we now think that with currently implemented policies, they will stabilize and decline and then lead to around two and a half degrees by the end of the century. So a full degree better than we thought only 10 years ago. So that's remarkable. That's really good. But it's not enough. The Paris agreement says well below two or in the direction of 1.5 and there we are far away from it. And also, we have to say that in the past years, global greenhouse gas emissions have still increased. So despite all of the efforts, is still more fossil fuels being burned each year and therefore we have more greenhouse gas emissions each year and that means not only are we not stopping climate change, we are fuelling climate change. So, we are accelerating the speed of change each year by adding more greenhouse gases to the atmosphere than we had in the year before.

The main driver of this drop in the projected temperature increase

is something that Hannah already touched on — the speed of renewable energy production.

Prices are falling and Niklas thinks this may push us to precipice to start some exponential change.

Niklas Höhne: I think the last 10 years we've been surprised each year about the speed of renewable energy, electrification and the transformation that has been started. So, I assume that also next year and the years after we will be positively surprised because the end of that development of the technologies is not there. Yeah. So, prices still decline. New battery technologies are invented. Renewables are incredibly cheap compared to 10 years and are still declining. And what we as humans often underestimate is exponential change. The system is changing at exponential speed. And that means each year more solar is implemented than we thought before or more batteries are implemented, more electric cars. And most of the models, they are still kind of assuming a linear change and underestimate the speed of the transformation. And that's why I think I'm quite optimistic about our future projections that this renewable energy transformation will actually win against the fossil fuels because it's simply exponential change. And that always has to win over a linear trend, which is the one described by the fossil fuels.

You can see a similar exponential change if you look at the history of cars.

At the turn of the twentieth century there was blight on cities — horses. According to the London Transport museum in 1900 there were 300,000 horses in London. But just 14 years later they’d all but disappeared. This sudden departure of the city’s workhorses helped humanity solve a pretty relevant problem for a climate podcast — pollution

Horses produced a lot of… waste — you know the kind of waste I'm talking about — that was very literally clogging up streets. The solution, ironically, given the topic of the podcast, was cars. Motorized vehicles had actually been around for a few years in the early 20th Century, but it wasn’t really until 1908 when the Model-T ford came out, the first car affordable to a large number of people, that they really took off. In 1910 there were 8000 cars registered in London, in 1920 there were 190,000, the next year there were 250 000 And as cars took off, streets once clogged with horse manure instead became roads for motorcars.

That may seem like a pretty inevitable change, but if you were a Londoner in 1900, you’d probably wouldn’t have believed that the world could be so different in a few decades.

Perhaps renewable energy will be the same for us. It may seem like we’ll never overcome our addiction to fossil fuels, but as prices tumble, maybe we’re standing on the cliff edge of that exponential change.

So there are certainly positives for the climate. The speed of the energy transition has taken many experts by surprise. But beyond that, there’s still a long to go. And when it comes to how countries are actually sticking to their climate pledges, it was a bit of a mixed bag.

We regularly look at who is basically the best, which is the best country around the world. And the places one, two, three are always empty. So, no country is doing everything correct. But in each area, you can see quite positive things. We have electric mobility, which is shooting off and was shooting off in Norway because Norway supported it significantly with a lot of money. But now it's basically the better way of doing things. So even countries like Vietnam or Nepal have very high adoption rates for electric cars. They sell more electric cars than conventional vehicles in these countries. And that is remarkable because it shows that this is the most economic way of having individual mobility. Then there's other areas, buildings and industry, which really are a bit behind. And it's very difficult to find really good examples where countries are really doing well. But OK, I think also in buildings and in industry, this idea of electrification is something that will now take off as well. So in buildings, it's heat pumps for heating, which are the new normal. So, there's huge opportunity to do more in those areas as well.

You may have noticed that some of the biggest emitters haven’t been mentioned there. And to be honest, they were some of the ones I was most worried about. China and the US.

China is the world’s top emitter according to the International Energy Agency, but it seems that their emissions are finally starting to peak — meaning that the greenhouse gases they emit may be starting to reduce. According to some analyses, they have already peaked. This is likely because they have implemented a huge amount of renewable energy. Last year, China installed more solar capacity than the rest of the world combined, although this boom in installation is slowing down a bit now.

And as Niklas explained to me, China has also been instrumental in producing what the world needs for renewable energy — they’re the leading manufacturer of solar, wind and battery technology. But he did impress on me that that wouldn’t have been possible without the policies of several countries, especially in Europe, promoting renewables and therefore creating the right market conditions for China.

And then there’s world’s second biggest emitter and the largest historical contributor to climate change. The US. There I was worried about the influence of the most recent administration. Trump’s Team has dealt a severe blow to the world’s ability to tackle climate change, by walking away from Paris Agreement on Climate, for the second time. They also repealed the ‘endangerment finding’ that set out that climate change is a public threat and has been used to enact climate policy. And they have spent billions trying to undo climate projects, giving the companies behind them refunds if they instead invest that money in fossil fuels. These actions, the administration say, would save the United States money by removing excess regulations, lower bills for families and help maintain the US’s leadership. But they are counter to what climate scientists say we should be doing — we need to stop burning fossil fuels and rein in our emissions.

So, I was expecting a pretty negative response from Niklas when I asked about how the US is doing. But he had a few surprises for me.

So for the US as such, it's the second largest emitter and the Trump administration has basically dismantled all climate policies that were there from the federal government in the US. And that means now that the emissions in the US will still continue to decline, but will decline slower.

This first surprise, is that while the actions of the Trump administration will likely increase the emissions that the US will produce, that is against a backdrop of overall decline. Even though there's been a recent uptick in emissions in the past year, the US's emissions have been steadily falling since the early 2000s and that will likely continue. Albeit not as fast as it would if the Trump administration was more pro climate. Ultimately, the economics of clean energy are hard even for the most powerful country in the world to fight against — it’s getting harder and harder to justify the use of fossil fuels when the alternatives are cheaper.

The second surprise was an unexpected way that the current US administration may have unintentionally pushed for a move away from fossil fuels.

Which is the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. And that created a significant energy crisis with very, very high fossil fuel prices for oil and gas. And that created a push towards energy efficiency and renewable energy. And that effect will be significant. It's very difficult to quantify that right now. But from our point of view, it's very clearly that that will has the potential to move this energy transition over the edge, so to say, and over the tipping point that it will be self-propelling because all the countries that currently suffer significantly from fuel shortage is not even a price, a high price is really a shortage that simply have not enough. They will now really, really think about alternatives and have already. So, some countries have already increased their renewable energy targets. China has reduced their oil consumption by 10 to 20%, depending on which source you look at within only 12 months. So, there's significant changes on the way that will reduce global greenhouse gas emissions.

As Niklas mentioned, data on this is hard to get, and this is still an evolving story. Time will tell what the impacts of the war in Iran may be. There have in fact been moves towards and away from renewable energy as a result of surging oil and gas prices — with nations like India and South Korea burning more coal in response to the higher gas prices, while people in the Philippines have taken to installing rooftop solar panels at record rates to avoid the high oil prices. So, a true accounting of the effect of the closure of the strait of Hormuz will take some time. But Niklas’s assessment is backed up by an increased sale of electric vehicles and a record high in solar exports from China, and an analysis by Carbon Brief that suggests that global emissions may fall in 2026. This has led some to wonder whether the war in Iran will be a tipping point for energy — that it will finally end humanity’s addiction to fossil fuels.

Overall, while there are clearly some areas in which the world is behind on its targets, it’s perhaps not as dire as I thought. In terms of renewable energy, adoption is accelerating. True, the current pace won’t be enough to meet our climate goals. We need to stop emitting carbon altogether, and soon if we're to meet the 1.5° target set in Paris, and even then we'll probably have to take some carbon out of the atmosphere. But Niklas, even with all the caveats, was optimistic about the future.

We have all the tools at hand and even now it's economic and the obstacle is not technology, the obstacle is not cost. The obstacle is our inertia in the system and that some lose something and some others gain something. And that is something we as a society really have to overcome.

So, while there’s still a long way to go, there are reasons for optimism. Renewable energy has outperformed many researchers expectations, and continues to do so, in spite of the backlash against it in some quarters. Which, I’ll be honest, does make me feel better. The data tell me that it’s not completely hopeless. When cities were overwhelmed by horses and their waste, cheap motor vehicles changed things in a matter of decades. I’m hopeful that renewable energy can do the same here.

But this is what the data says, largely about what we’ve already done. I was also curious about what we should do in the future. What are some of the big ideas that can help tackle climate change? That’s next time.

We could sit here and say well people should just do this because they should just care about the climate and reducing their emissions. But I think having very good affordable substitutes for people to switch to is just really, really crucial.”

This episode was written and produced by me, Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was my editor. And thanks to Hannah Richie, Ketan Joshi, and Niklas Höhne for speaking to me for this episode.

#803. Michael J. Fox Steps Out With All 3 Daughters for Rare Family Outing

Michael J. Fox and Tracy Pollan’s daughters Aquinnah, Schuyler and Esmé joined their parents for the Michael J. Fox Foundation’s annual gala, marking a rare family outing.

Where Michael J. Fox is going, he just needs his family’s love.

The Back to the Future star was not only joined by his wife Tracy Pollan for the Michael J. Fox Foundation’s A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to Cure Parkinson’s gala on Nov. 14, but also by three extra special guests.

When Fox and Pollan stepped out at the Waldorf Astoria in New York City for the fundraising event, they were accompanied by 31-year-old twins Aquinnah and Schuyler, as well as 25-year-old Esmé. The three girls each wore elegant gowns and big smiles as they posed on the event’s red carpet alongside their parents. (Fox and Pollan are also parents to 37-year-old son Sam, who was not in attendance.)

Pollan, for her part, donned a calf-length black shift dress and heels, while Fox wore a black blazer over a navy t-shirt and black slacks.

The gala featured performances from John Mayer and Brad Paisley, as well as comedy sets from Josh Johnson and Tom Papa, while actor Denis Leary helmed the night as emcee.

Fox started the Michael J. Fox Foundation in 2000, nine years after he was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. In the time since, the organization has become an important player in the fight to cure the disease—with the annual gala acting as a way to thank the many hands who make executing the mission light work.

As Pollan told People at the event, “It celebrates everybody who’s worked with us for 20-plus years. Just the huge and amazing amount of money that’s been raised that goes directly into the scientists’ pockets, and they can just do all the work that’s necessary [to finding a cure]. We really are seeing so much progress.”

The 66-year-old also shared insight into how she and her family navigate Fox’s health challenges.

“I think you just have to do it day by day,” she reflected. “You have to look at what’s in front of you, and you have to stay in the moment.”

As for Fox, the Shrinking star has been candid about how grateful he is for his family walking beside him on his health journey.

In fact, when the 65-year-old accepted the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award at the 2026 Emmys, he specifically thanked his wife and kids “for their sacrifices, for their patience, and for their love.”

For a closer look at the special bonds celebrities across Hollywood share with their kids, read on.

An astronaut from Pakistan is set to launch on China's Shenzhou 24 mission in the coming weeks and become the first-ever international visitor to the Tiangong space station.

A pair of astronaut candidates from Pakistan have been training at the Astronaut Centre of China in Beijing, following an agreement reached between China and Pakistan in Islamabad in February 2025 and a subsequent selection process.

China's human spaceflight agency confirmed in a Nov. 7 press statement that the upcoming Shenzhou 24 mission will carry one of the astronauts. The agency also released a mission patch.

"China and Pakistan are all-weather strategic cooperative partners," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Nov. 9. "Having the Pakistani astronaut on board China's spaceships will mark the first-ever joint mission of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program."

It is not yet known which of the two candidates will fly on Shenzhou 24. They were named in Pakistani press reports as Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud, both pilots from the country's military forces. The pair were chosen from a wider pool of around 20 finalists.

The chosen candidate will fly as a payload specialist on Shenzhou 24 along with two Chinese colleagues, while the other will be on standby as a backup. While the Chinese astronauts will be starting a six-month-long stay in space, the Pakistani astronaut will spend roughly a week in orbit aboard Tiangong during a standard crew rotation period. He will then return to Earth aboard the departing Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, along with two Chinese astronauts who will have completed a six-month-long stay in orbit.

The arrangement means changes to China's usual "three in, three out" Tiangong crew rotations. One of the three Shenzhou 23 astronauts, who arrived at Tiangong on May 24, will stay aboard and complete China's first-ever year-long stay in orbit, while the Pakistani astronaut will take their seat aboard Shenzhou 23 to return home.

During his stay in space, the Pakistani astronaut will be responsible for four research payloads selected from more than 300 proposals, according to Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO.

China has not announced a timeline for the launch of the Shenzhou 24 mission, but it is expected to lift off before the end of November. The Shenzhou 23 astronauts currently aboard Tiangong are closing in on 180 days in orbit, nearing an end to their six months in space.

Shenzhou 24 will launch from Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in the Gobi Desert on a Long March 2F rocket. The identities of the crew for China's human spaceflight missions are typically closely guarded, and will only be revealed in a press conference a day ahead of launch. Shenzhou 24's Long March 2F rocket will be rolled out to the pad around a week ahead of launch.

The partnership between the two countries has already produced Chinese-launched Pakistani satellites, including a lunar cubesat, and a Pakistani-built rover due to fly on the Chang'e-8 lunar landing mission.

Andrew is a freelance space journalist with a focus on reporting on China's rapidly growing space sector. He began writing for Space.com in 2019 and writes for SpaceNews, IEEE Spectrum, National Geographic, Sky & Telescope, New Scientist and others. Andrew first caught the space bug when, as a youngster, he saw Voyager images of other worlds in our solar system for the first time. Away from space, Andrew enjoys trail running in the forests of Finland. You can follow him on Twitter @AJ_FI.

#801. Paleontologists discover “one-in-a-million” fossil with 450-million-year-old soft tissue

A fossil dating back more than 450 million years has revealed something scientists almost never find: delicate soft tissues from an animal that lived hundreds of millions of years before dinosaurs appeared. The extraordinarily rare discovery is giving researchers a new understanding of how some of Earth's earliest marine animals lived, fed, and evolved.

The fossil belongs to an ancient crinoid, a marine animal related to modern starfish. Crinoids often resemble underwater flowers, with branching arms extending from a central body. More than 450 million years ago, these unusual creatures were among the animals thriving in Earth's earliest coral reefs, long before plants and animals had become widespread on land.

Although scientists have discovered millions of crinoid fossils, nearly all preserve only hard skeletal structures. Delicate body parts usually decay long before fossilization can occur, leaving major gaps in our understanding of how these ancient creatures functioned.

Now, paleontologists at the University of Oklahoma have identified an exceptionally rare specimen that preserves soft tissue structures, providing an extraordinary opportunity to investigate life in Earth's ancient oceans.

"After an animal dies, soft tissues like skin, eyes, or internal organs are the first things to decay," said Dr. Lena Cole, OU paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History. "Most fossils are only made up of hard parts like bones, teeth, or shells. Soft tissues are only preserved when the environment acts almost like a natural refrigerator or vacuum‑sealer -- conditions that are incredibly rare."

A 450 Million-Year-Old Fossil With Exceptionally Rare Soft Tissue

The remarkable specimen belongs to Dendrocrinus simcoensis, an extinct species of crinoid. Its preserved tube feet represent only the second known example of fossilized soft tissue in crinoids and the oldest such discovery ever documented.

Tube feet are small, flexible structures found in echinoderms, a group of marine animals that includes starfish, sea urchins, and crinoids. Because these structures are soft and easily destroyed after death, finding evidence of them in fossils is extraordinarily unusual.

"Preservation like this is truly one in a million," Cole added. "Crinoid fossils number in the millions, and this is only the second time soft tissues have ever been found."

The age of the specimen makes the discovery even more remarkable. These delicate structures have been preserved in the fossil record for nearly half a billion years, offering direct evidence of anatomy that would otherwise have disappeared.

"It's incredible these soft tissues have survived more than 450 million years," said Dr. David Wright, another OU paleontologist and assistant curator of invertebrate paleontology at the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, who co‑authored the study with Cole. "For reference, these soft tissues are more than 200 million years older than the oldest dinosaur."

Ancient Feeding Structures Reveal Evolutionary Secrets

The fossil's preserved tube feet are especially valuable because they provide clues about how crinoids obtained food and interacted with their surroundings.

Unlike the teeth and jaws that many familiar animals use to eat, crinoids rely on specialized structures to capture food particles from seawater. Their tube feet play an important role in feeding and in how these animals interact with ocean currents.

The size, arrangement, and shape of these structures can differ between species, reflecting adaptations to particular habitats and feeding methods. By studying those differences, paleontologists can reconstruct aspects of an extinct animal's lifestyle, even when no living examples of that species exist.

"Since crinoid tube feet are used for feeding, you can think of them in a similar way to how we think about teeth in mammals," Wright explained. "Differences in their structure tell us about what kinds of environments a species lived in and how it fed."

Researchers also compared the ancient fossil with crinoids living in today's oceans. Those comparisons revealed notable anatomical differences, suggesting that the feeding structures of these animals have undergone substantial evolutionary changes over hundreds of millions of years.

"Comparisons with living crinoids show that the anatomy of this ancient species was very different," Cole added. "This gives us new insight into how crinoids evolved and how their feeding strategies changed over hundreds of millions of years."

A Rare Window Into Earth's Earliest Ocean Ecosystems

Beyond revealing details about one ancient species, the discovery could help scientists piece together how marine ecosystems developed during the early Paleozoic Era.

The Paleozoic was a vast chapter of Earth's history that began about 541 million years ago. During its early stages, marine environments supported an expanding variety of complex animals, while life on land was still relatively limited.

Crinoids were among the creatures that became established in early reef communities. Their fossils provide important evidence of how marine animals occupied different ecological roles and adapted to changing environmental conditions.

However, studying only living species cannot reveal the full range of forms and adaptations that existed in the distant past. Some extinct animals possessed anatomical features that have no close equivalent among their modern relatives.

"Fossilized remains of long‑extinct species can show features well outside the range of variation we see in living species," Wright said.

"By comparing ecological ways of life for extinct and modern species, we can understand how patterns of adaptive evolution have changed through time and what factors shaped the modern biosphere."

The biosphere includes all living organisms on Earth and the environments they inhabit. Understanding how it developed requires scientists to examine not only which species existed, but also how they interacted with their surroundings and one another.

Because soft tissues are so rarely preserved in ancient echinoderms, discoveries like this one provide evidence that conventional fossils cannot offer. They can help researchers identify previously unknown feeding strategies, understand ancient ecosystems, and trace evolutionary changes that eventually shaped modern marine life.

An Extraordinary Discovery Hidden in a Museum Collection

Perhaps one of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is where the fossil was found.

Although major paleontological breakthroughs are often associated with expeditions to remote locations, valuable scientific evidence can also remain unnoticed for decades in museums.

Fossil collections contain enormous numbers of specimens, many of which have never been examined by specialists with the expertise needed to recognize their most important features. As scientific knowledge and research methods improve, these collections can reveal discoveries that earlier generations overlooked.

"New fossil discoveries ultimately come from fieldwork, but museum collections play a significant role in this kind of integrative research," Wright said. "We don't always know the full significance of the specimens we collect. New technologies, ideas or expertise often find surprising ways to utilize existing specimens to make new discoveries."

The Dendrocrinus simcoensis fossil had been housed for years at Montréal's Musée de paléontologie et de l'évolution, a small museum that operates entirely with support from community donations.

Its remarkable scientific value became apparent when Cole and Wright, both specialists in crinoids, visited the museum and examined the specimen more closely.

Their investigation revealed that the fossil preserved an extraordinarily rare record of ancient soft tissue, transforming a specimen already held in a museum collection into an important source of new evolutionary evidence.

"This discovery highlights the importance of museum collections and the community support that keeps them alive," Cole said. "Without the dedication of many people caring for these collections, this research would never have been possible."

More Discoveries May Be Waiting in Museum Drawers

The finding also demonstrates why preserving and maintaining fossil collections is essential for future research.

At the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, Cole and Wright oversee invertebrate paleontology collections containing more than one million specimens. Additional fossils are added every year, creating new opportunities to investigate ancient organisms and identify previously unrecognized species.

With collections of this size, no individual researcher could possibly examine every specimen in detail. A fossil that appears ordinary today might become the focus of a major discovery when studied by someone with a different specialty or new scientific tools.

Making collections available to researchers around the world increases the chances that these overlooked treasures will eventually receive the attention they deserve.

"This is why we work to make our collections accessible to researchers around the world," Wright said. "There are simply too many fossils to study over one person's career. There's more than a lifetime's worth of discoveries waiting to be found."

The extraordinary crinoid fossil is a reminder that some of the most revealing clues about Earth's distant past may already have been collected. They are simply waiting for someone to recognize what makes them special.
