#778. A mysterious 93-billion-mile cosmic structure may be the wreckage of colliding worlds

A mysterious structure stretching roughly 93 billion miles across space is giving astronomers new clues about the violent events that shape young planetary systems. Known as the "Cat's Tail," this enormous cloud of dark material lies about 63 light-years from Earth, in the faint constellation Pictor (which is Latin for "painter"). For the past two years, its unusual appearance and uncertain origins have puzzled scientists.

The structure is part of a vast disk of dust and debris surrounding Beta Pictoris, a young star system that resembles our own solar system during its early development. Now, using NASA's Hubble Space Telescope, astronomers have captured previously hidden details of the Cat's Tail in visible light for the first time.

The discovery is described in a study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. Led by University of Arizona planetary scientist Arin Avsar, the research team combined the new Hubble images with observations spanning more than 14 years. Their findings provide a clearer picture of the structure's composition, location, and shape, along with additional evidence that a massive collision may have created it.

A Possible Collision Between Pluto-Sized Worlds

"The Cat's Tail is thought to be the aftermath of a collision between large bodies - think something like Pluto," said Avsar, a doctoral student working with the research groups of Daniel Apai and Kevin Wagner at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and Steward Observatory.

"Oddly, this feature had previously only been seen with the James Webb Space Telescope, which detects infrared light, but remained invisible at shorter wavelengths, which has puzzled the community for a while."

The mystery becomes even more interesting when viewed in the context of how planetary systems form.

Today, our solar system appears relatively orderly. Planets follow established paths around the Sun, while many smaller rocky objects occupy "designated" regions such as the asteroid belt. But 4.6 billion years ago, the situation was dramatically different.

A young sun was surrounded by a swirling disk of gas and dust. Rocky objects repeatedly collided, sometimes breaking apart and sometimes combining into larger bodies. Over time, some accumulated enough material to become planets, while countless others were destroyed or scattered.

Astronomers study younger systems like Beta Pictoris because they offer an opportunity to observe processes that unfolded in our own cosmic neighborhood billions of years ago. Its debris disk, consisting of dust and fragments left behind during planetary development, is believed to be approaching the final stages of planet formation.

Why Hubble Could Finally See the Mysterious Cat's Tail

One of the most intriguing questions about the Cat's Tail is why it was previously detectable in infrared light but so difficult to observe in visible light.

The answer may lie in the unusual material that makes up the enormous structure.

"We think the Cat's Tail has eluded our observations in visible light until now because of what it's made of," Avsar explained. "It consists almost entirely of we call organic refractory material, which is heavily carbon-based. These long chains of carbon atoms absorb visible light, so they're quite black."

Organic refractory material consists of complex carbon compounds that can withstand relatively harsh conditions in space. Because these compounds absorb much of the visible light that strikes them, they can make the surrounding dust appear exceptionally dark.

The Hubble observations also support another unusual finding: the Cat's Tail appears to be composed of extremely small, surprisingly porous dust particles.

Individual grains measure only about a micron across, roughly one millionth of a meter. Yet instead of being compact and solid, they appear remarkably "fluffy," with substantial empty space within their structures.

The scale of the entire cloud is difficult to imagine. It may stretch as far as 1,000 astronomical units, with one astronomical unit (AU) defined as the average distance between Earth and the Sun. That corresponds to approximately 93 billion miles, or the equivalent of lining up around 200 trillion house cats from tail to nose.

"How you can get dust grains that small that are as porous as we see here, no one really understands, and that's part of why we study this feature," Avsar said.

How a Violent Collision Could Create Fluffy Cosmic Dust

If the Cat's Tail really formed when large planetary bodies smashed into each other, researchers still need to explain how that destruction produced such tiny, porous particles.

One possibility is that the collision was powerful enough to vaporize some of the material involved.

"It's possible that the velocities involved in the collisions were so high that the carbon grains vaporized, turned into gas, and then recondensed as they cooled, and that's how they became so porous," said co-author Wagner, a NASA Sagan Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Arizona's Steward Observatory.

In this scenario, the intense impact would have transformed solid carbon material into gas. As the material cooled, it could have condensed back into solid particles with unusually open, lightweight structures.

However, the precise process remains uncertain, and additional observations will be needed to determine whether this explanation is correct.

A 93-Billion-Mile Structure With an Unexpected Shape

The new research also challenges previous assumptions about where the Cat's Tail extends in space.

By combining visible light observations from Hubble with infrared measurements from the James Webb Space Telescope, the researchers used computer modeling to reconstruct the structure's possible three-dimensional arrangement.

Earlier observations suggested that the Cat's Tail extended outward from Beta Pictoris and far behind the star from Earth's perspective. Because the surrounding debris disk is viewed nearly edge-on, it was difficult to determine how much of the structure extended away from us rather than across our field of view.

The new analysis points to a different explanation.

"We find that instead of extending for 1,000 astronomical units behind the star, the Cat's Tail may extend straight sideways relative to us, and there is no third dimension to it," Avsar said. "It's essentially in the same plane of the sky as the star and possibly extends a little bit behind it."

This suggests the structure may be spread mainly across the sky as seen from Earth, rather than projecting deep into space behind the star.

The revised geometry gives astronomers a better understanding of where the dust is located and could help them reconstruct the event that produced it.

Hubble Discovers a Strange Warp Caused by a Giant Planet

The Cat's Tail was not the only unusual feature revealed by the new observations.

Using Hubble in a different observational configuration, Avsar and his colleagues also identified an unexpected distortion in the broad halo of dust surrounding Beta Pictoris.

The researchers suspect this strange warp may be caused by the gravitational influence of Beta Pic b, one of three planets in the system.

Beta Pic b is a massive gas giant estimated to be about 10 times the mass of Jupiter. Its powerful gravity may be disturbing the surrounding debris, altering the paths of dust particles, comets, and other icy objects across enormous distances.

"This gives us another line of evidence into how giant planets influence comets through their immense gravitational force," Avsar said. "It's a testament of how much these massive planets really influence their surrounding dust and icy bodies out to hundreds of astronomical units."

The finding highlights how giant planets can shape their environments far beyond their immediate orbits.

A Glimpse Into Our Solar System's Violent Past

For researchers, Beta Pictoris offers more than an opportunity to investigate an unusual cosmic structure. It may also provide a window into the early history of our own solar system.

Consider the Kuiper Belt, the distant region beyond Neptune that contains Pluto and numerous other icy bodies.

When the Kuiper Belt was only about 20 million years old, astronomers believe it was much more crowded than it is today. It may have contained hundreds of objects comparable in size to Pluto.

Over billions of years, the gravitational influence of the solar system's outer giant planets likely changed that environment dramatically. By disturbing the orbits of smaller bodies, these planets may have pushed many objects into new regions or expelled them from the solar system entirely, effectively "clearing out" much of the original population.

The strange dust tail and newly identified warp around Beta Pictoris may offer clues to similar processes unfolding in another planetary system.

By studying these distant structures, astronomers hope to better understand how violent collisions, migrating debris, and the immense gravity of giant planets helped transform the chaos of the early solar system into the planetary arrangement we see today.

#777. Chad Lowe's Daughter Mabel Celebrates Late Sister Fiona’s Birthday

Chad Lowe and Kim Painter's eldest daughter Mabel Lowe honored her late sister Fiona Lowe as she marked the teen's first birthday since her death at 13 on Sept. 29: "I miss you."

Content warning: This story discusses suicide.

Mabel Lowe is remembering her late sister Fiona on an emotional day.

Nearly two months after Chad Lowe and Kim Painter’s middle child died by suicide at the age of 13, her older sister shared a touching tribute to Fiona on what would have been her 14th birthday.

“Happy birthday fiona,” Mabel wrote on her Instagram Stories Nov. 14 alongside a photo of her younger sibling smiling while holding up a Harry Potter movie poster. “I miss you.”

The 17-year-old continued to honor her late sister, sharing sweet photos of her and Fiona, including a throwback shot of the two holding hands while wearing matching shirts with an illustration of a cat on them.

Over the photo, Mabel referenced both of their respective zodiac signs, including a Scorpio and Taurus emoji, adding the word “forever.”

The teen also looked back at more memories, sharing a pic of her and Fiona wearing cowboy hats and another seemingly more recent photo of the sisters posing for a mirror selfie.

On Sept. 29, Chad and Kim announced Fiona’s tragic death in a statement to People, sharing they were “deeply heartbroken by the loss,” while also remembering the teen as a "loving young girl who was smart, creative, and loved to dance.”

The couple—who also share daughter Nixie, 10—added that Fiona was “adored by her sisters” and “deeply loved by her parents,” describing their late daughter as “the light of our lives.”

Fiona’s manner of death was ruled a suicide, according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner, per People.

A few days after Chad and Kim confirmed Fiona’s death, Mabel mourned the devastating loss of her sister in an emotional statement.

“I love you so much Fiona,” Mabel wrote in a since-deleted Oct. 3 Instagram post alongside photos with her younger sister. “I wish your short time here was easier and i hope your mind is at ease now. I will honor you forever and keep your memory alive. I love you, i hope you knew just how much.”

#776. Fans Choose U2 & Dolly Parton’s ‘Torn’ as This Week’s Favorite New Music

Parton's posthumous collaboration with U2 brought in 40% of the vote.

“Torn,” Dolly Parton‘s posthumous duet with U2 frontman Bono, tops this week’s new music poll.

Listeners voted in a poll published Friday (Nov. 13) on Billboard, choosing the track from U2’s Carnaval De Luz as their favorite new music.

The collaboration topped new releases from acts like ATEEZ, Snoh Aalegra and more, plus the multi-artist The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping – The Album. At the poll’s closing time on Sunday, “Torn” had 40% of the vote.

“Torn” closes U2’s Carnaval De Luz (“Carnival of Light”), the Irish rock band’s sixteenth studio album, which arrived on Nov. 13.

The song is the country legend’s last recorded vocal performance; she recorded her vocals in June and approved the final mix before her Aug. 25 death, and producer Garet “Jacknife” Lee recalled that she was “thrilled with it.” “Torn” is co-written U2, Parton and Snow Patrol‘s Johnny McDaid.

Bono told Rolling Stone that Parton “sang her heart out.”

“When she got ill, she got out of her bed to sing this song. And you can hear that. And I can’t even listen to it now,” he said.

“It’s very moving to have had these intimacies with such a figure,” said Bono. “The fact that they’re not there now, in any way you can call back, other than through her songs, is very sobering.”

Trailing behind “Torn” on this week’s poll is ATEEZ’s Golden Hour : Part.6, with 10% of the vote. Snoh Aalegra’s Legendary Love and The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping – The Album each received 4% of the vote.

James Gunn's new DC universe might be done, but the follow-up to 2025's Superman is still on the way.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It feels like yesterday when we were discussing Superman, the first big-screen entry in James Gunn's rebooted DCU. Now Gunn is out, and Skydance (the company formed by the merger of Warner and Paramount) is already dismantling his grand plans for the DCU.

That means that Man of Tomorrow, which arrives next summer, will be the final entry in Gunn's ambitious, and occasionally divisive, DC experiment. The DCU's first chapter — officially titled 'Gods and Monsters' — gave us Supergirl and Clayface (as well as TV shows like Peacemaker S2 and Lanterns) in the run-up to Clark Kent and Lex Luthor's return.

Man of Tomorrow looks to be upping the stakes from Earthly villains to intergalactic baddies with the introduction of Brainiac, and it may well have been the herald of the first Justice League movie in the rebooted DCU.

Gunn has yet to prove audiences actually care about more than Batman and Supes, which might explain why this follow-up is also an ensemble of sorts. As the Marvel Cinematic Universe prepares to unleash Avengers: Doomsday, Secret Wars, and even a fresh X-Men reboot, their DC counterparts have always struggled to get their dream team off the ground.

We'll never know what might have been, but we can still enjoy Gunn's DC swansong when it lands in 2027. Here's everything we know about James Gunn's Man of Tomorrow.

Man of Tomorrow will be released theatrically in the United States on July 9, 2027. Most international territories are expected to get it around the same time.

Only a few months after Superman's release and successful box office run, DC Studios and Warner Bros. Pictures confirmed the sequel would be coming two years after Clark Kent's return to the big screen.

Man of Tomorrow isn't out yet, but you can watch the rest of the DCU so far (it's pretty good for the most part) in preparation first.

When the movie hits theaters on July 9, 2027, it'll likely remain exclusive to big screens for at least two or three months, depending on how successful it is.

With that said, we know Warner Bros. (now part of Skydance) isn't the most patient when it comes to theatrical runs based on its track record, so the chances are Man of Tomorrow will hit HBO Max sooner rather than later, probably by early autumn 2027.

Watch Superman and the rest of the DCU on HBO Max:

Basic (Ads): $10.99/month or $109.99/yearStandard (No Ads): $18.49/month or $184.99/year Premium (4K): $22.99/month or $229.99/year

No, we're still waiting for the first Man of Tomorrow trailer. Looking at the timeline of Superman's fantastic marketing campaign, however, we can guess the sequel will get a first trailer before 2026 ends, probably in time for Christmas.

Yes, James Gunn has officially confirmed Brainiac is the main threat Earth is facing in Man of Tomorrow. This explains why other heroes will be joining Superman in a fight against the alien mastermind, but the plot is looking a bit more complex.

In typical comic book fashion (and somewhat reminiscent of Thor: The Dark World), the main hook in Man of Tomorrow appears to be a reluctant alliance between the first movie's villain, Lex Luthor, and Kal-El (aka Clark Kent). "Enemies to allies" is always a fun dynamic to have in a sequel, especially when stars David Corenswet (Superman) and Nicholas Hoult (Lex Luthor) delivered strong and memorable performances the first time around.

The actual plot remains under wraps, but we can guess Brainiac — one of DC's biggest and most iconic alien villains — will be a tough nut to crack, thus requiring some sort of unofficial team-up that will include returning heroes like Mister Terrific, Guy Gardner, Hawkgirl, John Stewart, Blue Beetle, and even Kara Zor-El (Supergirl). There are other names circling the project that could lead to even bigger appearances, but don't expect to learn much about them before the movie's marketing kicks off.

Why should you care about Brainiac? Well, he's a super-intelligent techno-organic alien from the planet Colu with an obsession with knowledge and self-improvement. A perfect foe for Luthor, Earth's greatest mind, but also a breath of fresh air for Superman, who's been stuck battling either Kryptonian menaces or just Luthor too long on the big screen.

As a direct continuation of Superman, Man of Tomorrow is bringing back plenty of actors in both main and supporting roles, including:

New cast members with publicly announced (or previously established) characters include:

Last but not least, we also know Adria Arjona, Andre Royo, Matthew Lillard, and Sinqua Walls are part of the cast, but their parts remain a secret for now.

Much of the current Man of Tomorrow speculation centers on Adria Arjona's role in the story. While many have theorized she could be playing Wonder Woman — something that neither Gunn nor Arjona has straight-up denied — the earlier reports and rumors suggested she could be Maxima.

Such a role would fit Gunn's penchant for throwing lesser-known comic book heroes and villains into his movies wherever possible. If you're not an avid reader or longtime DC fan, all you need to know is that Maxima is an alien conqueror from the planet Almerac obsessed with Superman as her perfect mate and king. She's also morally ambiguous, at least when she first appeared, so that makes her a particularly interesting character to bring in for a more complex and nuanced sequel.

With Brainiac spearheading the roster of new DC icons joining Man of Tomorrow, it also isn't hard to imagine another alien figure factoring into the plot, though the flick is getting extremely crowded as it is.

Yes, James Gunn is the sole writer and director of Man of Tomorrow.

Despite his previous role as co-chairman and co-CEO of DC Studios, Gunn is extremely hands-on when it comes to most DCU projects. In fact, it seems he had already begun working on his next movie after Man of Tomorrow, though his unceremonious exit will almost certainly mean the end of those plans.

He's also co-producing alongside Peter Safran, who was also ousted in November 2026's DC Studios shakeup.

The rest of the crew includes Sam McCurdy (Peacemaker, Shogun) as cinematographer, Fred Raskin (Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3, Supergirl) as editor, and David Fleming (Superman, Anaconda) as the main composer, among others.

#774. Russell Brand’s Wife Breaks Silence on His Conviction, Prison Sentence

Russell Brand's wife Laura Brand shared her first public comments since her husband was sentenced to 10 years in prison after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

Russell Brand’s wife Laura Brand is adjusting to a new reality.

Days after the British comedian was sentenced to over 10 years in prison following his rape and sexual assault conviction, his wife spoke out in her first comments since the news, sharing the fate of their weekly faith podcast Sunday Service with The Brands.

“I’m here to continue the good work that was being established here in this Sunday Service community,” Laura told the camera on the Nov. 15 episode. “Something very close to mine and Russell's hearts.”

“It may look different,” she continued, “but the ambitions are very much the same.”

The 39-year-old—who shares three kids with Russell—admitted that she’s turning to her faith as she moves forward with the show without her husband.

“We trust God, and we trust his plan, and we trust everything He’s doing right now, even though it’s painful,” Laura shared. “And obviously [it] will take some getting used to for me to even sit here and not have my companion and my person with me.”

After thanking fans for their “support,” the mom of three noted that she’s been speaking with Russell.

“He’s OK and he’s praying, unsurprisingly,” Laura told the camera. “He’s praying and we decided for me to continue.”

Laura’s video comes on the heels of Russell’s conviction and prison sentencing.

On Nov. 5, the 51-year-old—who had pleaded guilty to all charges—was convicted by a London court on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault for events that allegedly occurred between 1999 and 2009.

Although Russell was convicted of four charges, he was cleared of two separate counts of rape and one count of indecent assault.

However, days later, on Nov. 9, judge Joel Bennathan sentenced Russell to 10 years and six months in prison, according to The Telegraph.

While the Forgetting Sarah Marshall actor’s sentencing concludes his case that began in April 2025, his legal battle may not have reached its end.

Following Russell’s Nov. 5 conviction, the Metropolitan Police of London confirmed to E! News an investigation into the former reality TV presenter is still ongoing after two additional allegations of rape were brought forward.

“The suspect has previously been interviewed under caution in connection with the allegations,” the statement noted. “Files have been submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service in relation to both complainants. Detectives remain in close contact with prosecutors as enquiries continue and further investigative work is carried out.”

For a detailed look back at Brand’s trial, keep reading…

Russell Brand was charged with rape and sexual assault in April 2025.

The London Metropolitan Police charged Brand for one count of rape, two counts of indecent assault and one count of indecent assault in April 2025 for events that transpired between 1999 and 2005.

At the time, Brand immediately denied the allegations in a video response, noting he was receiving “egregious attacks” from the media in addition to the allegations.

“Amidst this litany of astonishing, rather baroque attacks are some very serious allegations,” Brand said in a video shared to social media at the time, “that I absolutely refute.”

Russell Brand pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Though the Forgetting Sarah Marshall star had previously written in a 2007 essay for The Guardian that he had a “sexy addiction” and “disregard for social conventions of sexual protocol,” he vehemently denied the charges against him.

In his video statement, Brand admitted he had been a “fool” in the past, although maintained he never partook in “non-consensual activity.”

“I was a fool before I lived in the light of the Lord,” Brand said in a video shared to his X account in April 2025. “I was a drug addict, a sex addict and an imbecile, but what I never was, was a rapist.”

In the same video, Brand noted he was “grateful” to have the opportunity to fight the allegations in court.  He pleaded not guilty to all five charges in May 2025.

Russell Brand was served with two more sexual offense charges in December 2025.

In December 2025, the London Metropolitan Police charged Brand with one additional count of rape and one additional count of sexual assault regarding incidents that took place with two separate women in 2009.

Brand responded to the charges in a separate video posted to his social media.

“I pray Lord, anyone that I’ve harmed or hurt in my years of mindlessness and sin would be healed, Lord,” he said in the clip. “And I pray, Lord, for the absolute truth of who I am to be abundantly revealed.”

With the additional allegations, Brand was charged with three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault involving six women for events that transpired between 1999 and 2009. He later pleaded not guilty to the additional charges.

Russell Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

In a November 2026 ruling, a London court found Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was cleared of two additional counts of rape and one count of indecent assault.

During the trial, Brand maintained his innocence and said that while he dedicated much of his life to “beyond reckless philandering,” per the New York Times, he never engaged in non-consensual activities.

Russell Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison.

After confirming he would sentence the Get Him to the Greek alum with “significant custodial time,” during the ruling and denying him bail, presiding judge Joel Bennathan sentenced Brand to 10 years and six months in prison.

During the Nov. 9, 2026 sentencing, Bennathan called Brand a “sexual predator,” and commended the women who testified for their “determination and bravery.”

Bennathan said he considered Brand’s family in his ruling, calling his decision a “sad loss” for Brand’s three children, whom he shares with wife Laura Brand.

However, the judge noted that Brand had brought the decision “upon himself,” noting the comedian had acted with “casual, arrogant disregard,” for women.

Russell Brand legal team said he is a “fundamentally different person” now.

Prior to the sentencing, Brand’s lawyer Ian Winter KC said his client is “fundamentally a different person today,” than he was when the incidents took place, per CBS News.

Winter noted that the rape for which Brand was found guilty—which took place in 2009—was a “momentary total failure.”

Brand is also represented by Oliver Schneider-Sikorsky. His legal team will have the opportunity to appeal.

#773. Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon

Far below the ocean's surface, a constant snowfall drifts through the darkness. But unlike the frozen flakes that fall from the sky, this underwater snow consists of tiny clumps of waste, dead organisms, and other debris. Known as marine snow, these particles contain everything from mucus and animal feces to silt and the remains of microscopic plankton.

As this material sinks, it carries enormous quantities of carbon from the upper ocean toward the seafloor. Researchers estimate that marine snow removes more than 10 gigatons of carbon from surface waters each year. Yet only about two gigatons reach depths where that carbon can remain stored for hundreds or even thousands of years.

Why so much carbon fails to make it into the deep ocean has long puzzled scientists. Now, researchers from UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the University of Lincoln have identified a surprisingly important factor: how sticky the marine snow is.

Their findings, published October 8 in the journal Science, show that the viscosity, or thickness and gooeyness, of marine snow influences how quickly bacteria break it apart and how far it can sink. According to the researchers, the stickiest particles can transport more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as particles with a thinner, less viscous consistency.

Marine snow plays an important role in Earth's carbon cycle, the natural movement of carbon among the atmosphere, oceans, land, and living organisms. By transporting carbon into deep water, sinking particles can keep some of it isolated from the atmosphere for centuries or longer.

However, not every particle survives the journey. Bacteria feed on marine snow as it descends, gradually breaking down the material and affecting how much carbon reaches the ocean's depths.

The new research provides the first detailed look at how living bacteria interact with the physical structure of marine snow and, more broadly, mucus itself. These interactions are important well beyond the ocean's carbon cycle. Similar relationships between bacteria and mucus help sustain coral reefs, kelp forests, plant root systems, and the digestive systems of humans and other animals.

Until recently, scientists lacked the technology to observe these interactions at the microscopic scale needed to understand them.

A Four-Year Quest to See Inside Marine Snow

The project began in 2021, when Bryce Inman, then a postdoctoral researcher at Scripps Oceanography, set out to explore what he calls "the muscoscape."

"Observing individual bacteria interacting with the physical structure of mucus had never been possible," said Inman.

Together with colleagues including Farooq Azam, a microbiologist and professor emeritus at Scripps, Inman spent four years trying to overcome that limitation. Multiple attempts were unsuccessful before the team finally developed a working technique in 2025.

Their solution combined 3D confocal microscopy with specially designed fluorescent molecules. Confocal microscopy uses light to capture detailed images at different depths within a sample, allowing researchers to reconstruct its structure in three dimensions. The fluorescent molecules helped make features of the material visible.

For the first time, the scientists could examine the "physical terrain" of individual marine snow particles while watching how living bacteria moved through and interacted with them.

The images revealed a surprisingly intricate microscopic environment, complete with structural differences that affect where bacteria can settle and how easily they can reach the material inside.

Much like snowflakes in the atmosphere, marine snow particles vary considerably. Each contains its own mixture of organic and inorganic materials, creating differences in composition, structure, and viscosity.

The researchers' new imaging approach, described in a companion study published in Nature Communications, revealed that bacteria preferentially colonize areas near a particle's surface where the material is less viscous.

The denser, stickier regions deeper inside are much harder for bacteria to penetrate.

"Bacteria can latch on to less viscous portions of each particle, but cannot reach more viscous regions until they break it down," said Inman. "Think of it like a worm in an apple: the flesh is easy to penetrate, but the core is tough to chew through"

This difference has important consequences for how long marine snow remains intact.

In laboratory experiments, the scientists observed that particles with greater viscosity resisted bacterial degradation and fragmentation for longer periods. Computer simulations further suggested that these stickier particles can descend to greater depths before breaking apart.

Based on these results, the team estimates that highly viscous marine snow can deliver more than six times as much carbon to the deep ocean as less viscous particles.

The findings help explain why some sinking material transports carbon much farther into the ocean than other particles, even though both begin their journeys near the surface.

"How far marine snow can sink is a surprisingly complicated problem, and we have added another - very gooey - piece to the puzzle," said Inman.

A Discovery With Implications Beyond the Ocean

Although the research focuses on marine snow, its implications extend to many environments where bacteria interact with mucus.

Mucus is often regarded as a relatively simple, slippery substance. But the new imaging technology reveals that it has a complex internal landscape, with microscopic structures that can influence how bacteria behave.

Understanding these physical features could help scientists investigate biological processes in settings ranging from human digestive health to the recovery of damaged coral reefs.

The method also opens opportunities to explore interactions that previously could not be observed directly, providing researchers with a new way to study the microscopic environments inhabited by bacteria.

Mucus, slime, whatever you want to call it, "has a surprising amount of structure," Inman said. "There are bulges, crevasses, all this sort of structure to it that we really had no idea about at a scale smaller than bacteria. This is the first time we're really examining this physical habitat."

The discovery adds an important missing piece to scientists' understanding of how carbon travels through the ocean. It also demonstrates that something as seemingly ordinary as the thickness of underwater slime can have far-reaching consequences for the planet's natural systems.

Additional funding for the research was provided by the Simons Foundation and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council.

Brittany Mahomes made her first appearance since revealing she's pregnant with her and Patrick Mahomes' fourth baby by supporting her husband at the Kansas City Chiefs game Nov. 15,

Brittany Mahomes is entering her pregnancy season once again.

Five days after the wife of Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes revealed she’s expecting the couple’s fourth child, she made her first public appearance since sharing the exciting news, stepping out to cheer on her husband in his NFL game against the Atlanta Falcons in Atlanta Nov. 15.

For the occasion, Brittany—who shares kids Sterling, 5, Bronze, 3, and Golden, 21 months, with Patrick—wore a Chiefs red jacket and oversized black sunglasses, styling her blond locks in a wavy ponytail.

And, of course, the 31-year-old brought her winning team to support Patrick on the field.

After all, Brittany shared fun videos of her kids enjoying some family fun before the Chiefs and the Falcons faced off.

In an adorable clip posted to her Instagram Stories Nov. 15, the Kansas City Current co-owner carried Golden through the stadium tunnel out onto the field, noting her daughter didn’t arrive empty-handed.

“This child literally walked into the stadium with [a] waffle in hand,” Brittany shared as her youngest ate her snack. “No waffle left behind!”

And just like her mom, the toddler arrived at the game in style, wearing a white jacket that featured her dad’s name and jersey number in red on her back, along with matching red ruffled leggings.

Golden matched with her older sister Sterling, who also sported Chiefs red leggings under a pink dress.

And as the Mahomes crew huddled up to watch Patrick score another win for the Chiefs, they are continuing to celebrate the exciting news of adding another player to their team.

On Nov. 10, Brittany and Patrick announced they’re expecting their fourth baby together.

“Another blessing from God,” the couple wrote in a joint Instagram post alongside sweet family photos, including a shot of their kids with their hands on Brittany’s baby bump. “& then there were 6.”

Though the pair—who tied the knot in 2022—haven’t shared whether they’re expecting a boy or girl, Patrick joked that he has one play he may prefer.

“Obviously, it’s a blessing to have another baby on the way,” he shared. “I’m excited for it.”

#770. Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk

A higher dose of the annual flu vaccine may offer older adults an unexpected benefit: a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.

In a large study led by researchers at UTHealth Houston, adults ages 65 and older who received a high-dose influenza vaccine were less likely to develop Alzheimer's than those given the standard-dose version. The findings, published in the medical journal Neurology, suggest that the strength of a flu vaccine could matter for more than just protection against influenza.

The discovery grew out of an unexpected conversation between a UTHealth Houston physician and local public health officials. What began as a visit to discuss earlier vaccine research eventually led scientists to investigate whether different flu vaccine doses might be associated with different levels of Alzheimer's risk.

A Surprising Connection Between Flu Vaccines and Alzheimer's

Alzheimer's disease is the leading cause of dementia and an increasingly serious public health concern. In 2025, more than 7 million Americans ages 65 and older were living with the disease, representing approximately 1 in 9 people in that age group. That figure is projected to more than double by 2050.

Researchers have been exploring whether common vaccines might influence the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's. In a 2022 study, a team led by Paul Schulz, MD, found that flu vaccination was associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's among adults 65 and older.

Schulz is a professor of neurology at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston and director of the Neurocognitive Disorders Center at UTHealth Houston Neurosciences.

Three years after that earlier investigation, Schulz and his colleagues published new research examining a more specific question: Could receiving a stronger flu vaccine be associated with an even greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk?

The idea came from public health officials who had learned about the team's previous findings and invited Schulz to discuss them.

"The public health department had seen our vaccine research and asked if I could come down to talk to them about it," said Schulz, who is the senior author of the study and the Rick McCord Professor in Neurology and Umphrey Family Professor in Neurodegenerative Diseases at McGovern Medical School. "We went through the findings, and they asked if there was a difference with different dosages; I was confused."

Why Older Adults Receive Stronger Flu Shots

As people grow older, their immune systems gradually become less effective at recognizing and fighting infections. This age-related decline can make influenza particularly dangerous for seniors.

To help address that vulnerability, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends high-dose influenza vaccines as a preferred option for adults ages 65 and older. These vaccines contain four times as much influenza antigen as standard-dose shots. Antigens are the components of a vaccine that stimulate the immune system to recognize and defend against a virus.

The higher dose is designed to produce a stronger immune response in older adults, whose immune systems may respond less effectively to conventional vaccines.

Schulz had not previously realized that this stronger formulation was available.

"I was stunned that, as a physician, I didn't know a higher dose was offered," Schulz said.

Annual flu vaccination is recommended broadly, but preventing influenza is especially important for people with Alzheimer's disease. Flu infections and their complications can pose serious health risks for individuals already coping with cognitive impairment.

Before 2022, the CDC did not express a preference for one type of injectable influenza vaccine over another for people ages 65 and older. Instead, the guidance emphasized receiving a flu shot every year, regardless of the specific formulation.

Previous research from UTHealth Houston had already linked inactivated influenza vaccines, which use viruses that cannot cause influenza infection, to a 40% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. However, researchers had not yet determined whether a higher vaccine dose might be associated with additional benefits.

Another practical issue made the question particularly relevant. As the population of older Americans continues to grow, demand for high-dose flu vaccines sometimes exceeds the available supply. Consequently, some seniors receive standard-dose vaccines instead.

This variation gave researchers an opportunity to compare Alzheimer's outcomes among older adults who had received different formulations.

"So we started looking, and sure enough, we were able to put together thousands and thousands of people over the age of 65 who got the high- or low-dose vaccine. They're more at risk for Alzheimer's than anybody else, of course, because it's age-related and we could look at high-dose versus low-dose and see if there was a difference," Schulz said.

Nearly 200,000 Adults Reveal a Significant Difference

To investigate the potential connection, the research team analyzed data from nearly 200,000 men and women ages 65 and older.

The results showed that people who received high-dose influenza vaccines had a significantly lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease than those who received the standard-dose formulation.

The researchers reported that standard-dose influenza vaccination was associated with a 40% reduction in Alzheimer's risk, while high-dose vaccination was linked to a reduction of nearly 55%.

The association was particularly pronounced among women, who appeared to experience a greater reduction in Alzheimer's risk with the stronger vaccine.

These findings add to growing evidence of a possible relationship between influenza vaccination and brain health. They also raise important questions about whether the immune response triggered by vaccination might influence biological processes involved in Alzheimer's disease.

However, the findings demonstrate an association rather than establishing cause and effect. Additional research is needed to determine whether high-dose flu vaccination directly reduces the likelihood of developing Alzheimer's and to understand the mechanisms that might explain the connection.

What the Findings Could Mean for Alzheimer's Prevention

With Alzheimer's affecting millions of Americans and the number of cases expected to rise sharply in the coming decades, researchers are searching for practical ways to reduce risk.

The possibility that an existing vaccine could have benefits extending beyond influenza prevention is particularly intriguing. Unlike an entirely new treatment, flu vaccination is already widely used, and higher-dose formulations are specifically designed for older adults.

The new findings suggest that vaccine dosage could be an important consideration in future studies exploring the relationship between the immune system and Alzheimer's disease.

For now, the research provides another reason to investigate the potential benefits of influenza vaccination while emphasizing the need for further studies before drawing conclusions about Alzheimer's prevention.

Avram Samuel Bukhbinder, MD, a graduate of McGovern Medical School who is currently a clinical fellow in neurology at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard University, served as a corresponding author of the study.

Schulz is also a faculty member of The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center UTHealth Houston Graduate School of Biomedical Sciences.

Other contributors from McGovern Medical School included Elizabeth He, visiting scholar in the Department of Neurology; Kristofer Harris, MPH, research coordinator in the Department of Neurology; Mya Rodriguez, graduate research assistant in the Department of Neurology; Kamal Phelps, MD, an alumnus of the Department of Neurology; Jenna Thomas; Gabriela Cruz, MD, resident in the Department of Neurology; and Lauren Jhin.

Researchers from the McWilliams School of Biomedical Informatics at UTHealth Houston also participated. They included Xiaoqian Jiang, PhD, associate vice president for medical AI, chair of the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, and Christopher Sarofim Family Professor in Biomedical Informatics and Bioengineering; Yejin Kim, PhD, assistant professor in the Department of Health Data Science and Artificial Intelligence; Luyao Chen, researcher; and Yaobin Ling, PhD, postdoctoral research fellow.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update for 6:25 p.m. ET: SpaceX has launched the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing. See launch video and our full Starship Flight 15 liftoff wrap.

SpaceX plans to launch its Starship megarocket on an unprecedented mission today (Nov. 13), and you can watch the action live.

Starship is scheduled to launch on its 15th test flight today from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). SpaceX plans to bring both of Starship's stages back to Starbase for a catch by the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — something it has never done before.

You can watch it all live here at Space.com. And there should be a lot to see: Starship Flight 15 will last more than 22 hours, if all goes according to plan.

Starship consists of two elements: a huge booster known as Super Heavy and an upper-stage spacecraft called Starship, or Ship for short. Both are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first in the world of orbital spaceflight.

The rapidity of Starship's reuse hinges heavily on SpaceX's recovery strategy: Returning both vehicles directly to the launch mount will enable much faster inspection, refurbishment and reflight, the company has said.

SpaceX has already caught Super Heavy, pulling the feat off on three previous Starship test flights. But it has never tried to do so with Ship, which flies farther and faster than the booster and is therefore a more challenging vehicle to recover.

So today's flight is a pretty big deal for SpaceX.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," the company wrote in a Flight 15 mission description.

The action will unspool over two days, if all goes to plan. Super Heavy will return to Starbase for a touchdown just 6.5 minutes after launch, but Ship will continue on to low Earth orbit.

The upper stage will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites, during a 42-minute stretch beginning about 35 minutes after liftoff. This will be just the second batch of V3 spacecraft to reach orbit, after the 26 that went up on Flight 14 on Sept. 28.

Ship will then stay aloft for nearly a full day. The mission plan calls for the upper stage to return to Starbase for its chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), about 22.5 hours after liftoff.

There's no guarantee things will go according to plan, however. SpaceX will call off a Ship catch if the vehicle experiences any issues during Flight 15. If something crops up, the company will steer Ship to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, either near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile.

So it'll be a busy weekend for SpaceX, and for space fans who want to keep tabs on the mission. And we can help you out there, with our Flight 15 updates page.

#768. Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease

Tick-borne illnesses are becoming increasingly common across the United States, and Lyme disease remains the most frequently reported. Nearly 500,000 Americans are diagnosed each year. The infection is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, which typically reaches humans through the bite of an infected blacklegged tick. Antibiotics can treat Lyme disease, but without treatment, the infection may affect the joints, heart, and nervous system. Some patients also experience symptoms that persist over time.

Now, one of the longest-running studies of Lyme disease ecology is challenging several assumptions about what makes the disease more likely to spread. For more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, New York, have tracked the complicated relationships among ticks, mice, oak trees, predators, and weather. Their research has uncovered unexpected patterns that could help predict when people face greater exposure to infected ticks.

A new study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences brings together nine of the project's most surprising discoveries. The findings show how decades of observations can reveal connections that shorter studies might miss.

"On balance, these surprises have enriched our knowledge of this system, helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk," said lead author Richard Ostfeld, a disease ecologist at the Cary Institute who leads the research program alongside Shannon LaDeau.

According to Ostfeld, the extensive data collected over the years have been essential for separating meaningful ecological patterns from coincidences and statistical fluctuations.

"Studies of this depth and length are incredibly rare," said LaDeau. "This research has followed an ecological community -- including oak trees, mammals, and microorganisms -- examining how interactions like predation, parasitism, and competition shape the system over time. The evolution of understanding summarized in this paper is something you simply cannot get without such a long-term and system-focused study."

Deer May Play a Smaller Role in Lyme Disease Risk Than Expected

When Lyme disease first gained recognition in the United States during the 1980s, white-tailed deer were considered a likely driver of rising tick populations. Hunters frequently encountered deer carrying numerous adult ticks, suggesting that areas with more deer might also produce more ticks.

The reasoning seemed straightforward. Although deer cannot pass the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks, they provide blood meals for adult female ticks. Scientists suspected that larger deer populations would allow more female ticks to reproduce, eventually increasing the number of young ticks capable of spreading the infection.

But decades of monitoring have produced a different picture. On the Cary Institute's 2,000-acre forested research property in Dutchess County, New York, researchers found no statistically significant connection between deer numbers and the abundance of nymphal ticks. Nymphs are immature ticks responsible for much of the Lyme disease transmission to humans.

"We had detected a weak positive relationship between deer and subsequent nymph abundance over short subsets of the data," said Ostfeld, "but the whole data set in its entirety shows no such thing."

Mice Are a Much Stronger Predictor of Tick Surges

While deer populations failed to predict the abundance of nymphal ticks, mouse populations showed a much clearer relationship.

Years with especially large mouse populations were followed by approximately 40% more nymphal ticks the next year. White-footed mice are particularly important because they provide excellent blood meals for tick larvae and are highly effective at transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi to those feeding on them.

Once infected as larvae, ticks can retain the bacteria as they develop into nymphs. When these nymphs take another blood meal, they can pass the infection to humans.

The findings suggest that tracking mouse populations could provide a valuable early warning of unusually high tick numbers.

How Acorns Can Predict Tick Populations Two Years Ahead

One of the most unexpected discoveries involves something that might seem entirely unrelated to Lyme disease: acorns.

Oak trees periodically produce exceptionally large crops of acorns in synchronized events known as acorn masting. These unusually productive years provide an abundance of food for forest rodents, allowing mouse populations to expand during the following year.

That increase in mice then supports larger numbers of young ticks. As a result, the researchers found that a particularly heavy acorn crop can reliably predict an increase in nymphal ticks two years later.

The relationship reveals a remarkable sequence of events in which the reproductive cycle of forest trees helps determine future tick abundance. It also offers researchers another potential tool for anticipating periods of greater Lyme disease exposure.

Why More Mice Don't Always Mean More Infected Ticks

Although mouse abundance helps predict how many nymphal ticks will appear, the researchers discovered that it does not consistently predict what percentage of those ticks will carry Lyme disease bacteria.

Initially, scientists expected both measures to rise together. Because mice are efficient transmitters of B. burgdorferi, an increase in mice seemed likely to produce not only more ticks but also a greater proportion of infected ticks.

Early observations appeared to support that idea. However, as additional years of data accumulated, the apparent relationship gradually disappeared.

"It kept me up at night," said Ostfeld, "because it meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong."

The explanation appears to involve the other animals that share the forest with mice. Skunks, squirrels, and opossums also serve as hosts for feeding ticks, but most are much less effective at passing the Lyme disease bacterium to them.

When these animals are abundant, more larval ticks may feed on hosts that are unlikely to infect them. This can reduce the percentage of nymphal ticks carrying the bacteria, even when mouse populations are high.

"So the infection prevalence in the nymphs really depends on how all the larval tick meals are distributed across all the hosts," explained Ostfeld. "It would have been convenient if one host predicted that for us, but that has not been the case."

This finding highlights an important distinction between the total number of ticks in an environment and the proportion carrying the pathogen. Predicting the risk of infection requires understanding the broader community of animals that ticks feed on, not simply counting mice.

Extreme Heat and Cold May Not Kill Ticks in the Wild

Weather has also produced some unexpected results.

Earlier laboratory experiments suggested that exposure to intense heat or severe cold could kill blacklegged ticks. Yet observations in natural habitats revealed that ticks are surprisingly capable of surviving these conditions.

Researchers believe ticks protect themselves from temperature extremes by retreating into deeper soil layers or hiding beneath fallen leaves, where conditions are less severe than at the surface.

However, the long-term data also revealed a more complicated relationship with temperature. Years that are warmer overall tend to be followed by fewer nymphal ticks than usual, despite the ability of individual ticks to withstand short periods of extreme heat.

At the same time, warmer conditions generally favor mouse populations, which can lead to more ticks. These opposing effects make it difficult to predict how changing temperatures will ultimately influence Lyme disease risk.

What 35 Years of Research Mean for Lyme Disease Prevention

Taken together, the discoveries show that Lyme disease risk depends on a network of ecological interactions that is complicated but not entirely unpredictable.

Mouse abundance, for example, provides a stronger indicator of future nymphal tick numbers than deer abundance at the study site. Similarly, unusually harsh winters may not reduce tick populations as dramatically as previously expected.

By understanding these patterns, public health officials may be better equipped to anticipate periods of increased tick exposure and develop more effective prevention strategies.

Still, important questions remain, particularly about how climate change will affect ticks, the animals they feed on, and the oak trees that influence rodent populations.

"You would expect that a warming climate, which makes life better for the mice, would eventually make life better for the ticks, but we have not seen that so far," said Ostfeld. "We need to know what to expect from the different manifestations of climate change, which are sometimes warmer and drier, and sometimes warmer and wetter. The time of year when it's very warm also matters to ticks, oaks, and acorn production."

The research site in Dutchess County has undergone significant environmental changes since monitoring began in 1991. Climate shifts, changes to the surrounding landscape, and the arrival of invasive species have all altered the conditions in which the forest's plants and animals live.

Researchers intend to continue following these changes to determine how ticks and their hosts respond over time. Their work could provide increasingly valuable insights into how future environmental changes will influence human exposure to Lyme disease and other infections carried by ticks.

SpaceX has a message for itself, and for the spacecraft set to make history today (Nov. 13): Don't panic.

The company's Starship megarocket will conduct its 15th test flight this afternoon, a landmark liftoff that will feature the first-ever attempt to catch both of its stages with its launch tower's "chopstick" arms.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), SpaceX rolled the Flight 15 upper stage, a vehicle known as Ship 42, out to the launch pad at its Starbase site in South Texas to prep. The company shared photos of the move on X, and in two of those shots we can see some intriguing words inked on the spacecraft: "Don't panic."

The phrase is familiar to fans of Douglas Adams' sci-fi classic "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy": In the novel, the electronic guidebook that helps travelers find their way across the cosmos has "Don't panic!" on its cover.

And Ship 42 itself is connected to the beloved book, by virtue of its serial number. In "The Hitchhiker's Guide," a supercomputer named Deep Mind is asked to come up with "the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe, and everything." It thinks for 7.5 million years and comes up with "42."

SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk has voiced his affection for "The Hitchhiker's Guide" in the past — and he has already paid tribute to it with a well-placed "Don't panic."

The debut launch of SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket back in February 2018 sent Musk's red Tesla Roadster into orbit around the sun, with a spacesuit-clad mannequin named Starman at the wheel and its entertainment display programmed to read "Don't panic!"

Starship Flight 15 is scheduled to launch today during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). You can watch it here at Space.com.

If all goes according to plan, Starship's Super Heavy first stage will come back to Starbase for a chopsticks catch about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

Ship 42, meanwhile, will head to orbit, a destination that Starship reached for the first time on Flight 14, which took place on Sept. 28. Ship 42 will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites today — the second batch of the spacecraft to reach orbit. (The first set of 26 were delivered on Flight 14).

Ship 42 will stay up for a while after that, circling Earth 14 times before coming back for its own chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after launch.

That's the plan, anyway; SpaceX will only go through with a Ship catch attempt if all systems on the vehicle look good. If there are any problems, the company will divert to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, near either Hawaii or Chile.

Both of Starship's stages — Super Heavy and the Ship — are designed to be rapidly reusable. And "rapidly" is a bit of understatement: SpaceX wants to launch 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030, Musk has said.

The chopsticks-catch strategy is a big part of that vision. Bringing both Starship stages directly back to the launch mount will greatly reduce the time needed for inspection, refurbishment and reflight, according to SpaceX.

The company has already caught Super Heavy on three previous Starship test flights. It has never tried to do so with Ship, instead targeting ocean splashdowns with the upper stage.

The double catch attempt may be unprecedented, but SpaceX seems to be taking its own advice: There's no panic around Flight 15 or its bold goals.

"I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," Musk said last month, during SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#765. Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive

Mars may not be as geologically inactive as it appears. New evidence from mysterious gas emissions near an enormous Martian volcano suggests that heat and volcanic processes could still be present deep beneath the planet's surface.

Researchers have identified unusual concentrations of hydrogen chloride gas above fractures in the Alba Mons volcanic region. The findings suggest that gases from the planet's interior may be escaping through cracks in the surface, potentially revealing volcanic activity that has remained hidden until now.

An international team led by Alexander Trokhimovskiy believes the gas could originate from hot magma underground. If confirmed, this would indicate that Mars still has dormant volcanic systems capable of releasing gases to the surface.

The European Space Agency's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) first detected hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere in findings reported in 2021. On Earth, hydrogen chloride is frequently released through openings connected to magma, raising the possibility that similar processes could be occurring on Mars.

"Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does," says Daniel Mège, Professor at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences and co-lead author of the study published in Science Advances.

Mysterious Gas Emissions Defy Mars' Seasonal Pattern

The researchers noticed something unusual during early summer in the Martian northern hemisphere. Hydrogen chloride concentrations were unexpectedly elevated in a particular region, even though the gas normally becomes scarce at that time of year.

Hydrogen chloride levels on Mars generally follow a seasonal cycle. They typically peak during northern winter before declining to very low levels in summer. Scientists believe much of this behavior is associated with the planet's dust and water cycles.

However, the observations revealed a striking exception. Elevated hydrogen chloride repeatedly appeared in early summer over volcanic fractures on the slopes of Alba Mons. The unusual timing and consistent location suggested that something beyond ordinary atmospheric chemistry might be responsible.

Mars is home to the largest volcanoes in the Solar System, but scientists still do not know whether volcanic processes remain active beneath their surfaces.

Images taken from orbit indicate that some Martian volcanoes experienced eruptions within the past few million years. Instruments on the surface have also recorded marsquakes, demonstrating that the planet continues to experience seismic activity.

Together, these observations suggest that Mars may retain some of its geological energy. However, scientists have never directly observed a new volcanic eruption or fresh lava flow on the planet, leaving the question of present-day volcanism unresolved.

Fresh Cracks Reveal Clues to Hidden Volcanic Heat

To investigate the unusual gas concentrations, the research team combined atmospheric measurements with detailed observations of the Martian surface.

The Atmospheric Chemistry Suite aboard TGO uses infrared spectrometers to identify gases in the atmosphere. These instruments detected hydrogen chloride concentrated in a relatively small area shortly after the disappearance of winter frost.

Researchers then examined the same region using the orbiter's CaSSIS camera. The images revealed narrow fractures that appeared relatively fresh, with some extending hundreds of meters across the surface. Unusual changes in surface color were also visible around the cracks.

"The Trace Gas Orbiter was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack. It's truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere," explains Daniel.

One possible explanation is that gases originating from magma deep underground travel upward through these fractures. On Earth, comparable volcanic openings are known as fumaroles.

The researchers propose that extremely cold Martian winters, when temperatures can fall to -120°C, allow ice to seal the fractures and temporarily prevent gases from escaping. As temperatures rise in early summer, the ice sublimates, changing directly into vapor and potentially opening pathways for underground gases to reach the atmosphere.

The discoloration observed around the fractures could also be significant. It may result from minerals or other substances deposited by escaping gases, similar to the deposits commonly found around fumaroles (volcanic gas vents) on Earth.

Although the connection between the gas emissions and volcanic fractures appeared promising, the researchers needed to rule out other explanations.

"Looking at the spatial distribution of the seeping, it became instantly obvious to me that there was something volcanic behind it, but it had to be demonstrated," concedes Daniel.

The team carefully evaluated the chemical reactions that could produce hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere, including processes unrelated to volcanism.

"A huge part of the work consisted of examining all the possible chemical processes going on in the Martian atmosphere. We needed to be rigorous, critical and creative to explain the presence of hydrogen chloride. The data were complex, but also excellent brain food," adds Daniel.

After examining the atmospheric and geological evidence together, the researchers proposed that the gas could be escaping from a dormant magma chamber beneath Alba Mons. Such a chamber would form part of an underground volcanic system that could continue releasing gases even without producing visible eruptions.

Hidden Volcanic Activity Could Help Mars Support Life

The implications may extend beyond understanding the planet's geological history. Volcanic gases could also provide clues about how Mars evolved and whether it ever supported environments suitable for life.

In the distant past, gases released from magma, including hydrogen chloride, may have helped create a denser atmosphere and warmer conditions. Those conditions could have allowed liquid water to remain across large portions of the Martian surface.

Volcanic activity might also create habitable environments underground. If rising magma or lava comes into contact with groundwater, the interaction can produce warm hydrothermal systems. Such environments could provide both chemical energy and protection from the harsh conditions on the surface.

"Looking for Martian life in the seeping fissures of the Alba Mons region would make a lot of sense. If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface," ponders Daniel.

Although the findings do not establish that Mars is currently erupting or that life exists beneath its surface, they offer an intriguing new reason to investigate the volcanic fractures around Alba Mons.

"These findings may prove to be TGO's greatest success yet," highlights Colin Wilson, ESA's project scientist for the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter.

Gracie Abrams is bringing The Look at My Life Tour to Australia next year.

Abrams will play six arena shows across two cities in July and August 2027: three nights at Melbourne’s Rod Laver Arena on July 27, 28 and 30, followed by three at Sydney’s Afterpay Arena on Aug. 3, 4 and 6. British singer-songwriter Arlo Parks will open all six dates.

“Australia! I’ve missed you so much and I cannot express just how excited I am to return to Melbourne and Sydney next July/August for ‘The Look at My Life Tour,’” Abrams said in a statement. “A show that we’ve been working very hard to put together, a show that we hope you love as much as we do.” Related Daniel Hall, Co-Founder of Australian Rock Band Taxiride, Dies at 48 U2 Opens 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Ceremony With Surprise Performance Phil Collins Tells Rock Hall Crowd: 'You Haven't Heard the Last of Me' Explore Arlo Parks Gracie Abrams See latest videos, charts and news

“I’ve just missed you so much more than I can tell you… as soon as I heard for sure we were coming back my heart began to sing,” she added. “I will see you soon, I love you so much… we’re gonna make it great.”

The tour supports Daughter From Hell, Abrams’ third studio album, which debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 in July with 124,000 equivalent album units, her first chart-topping album. Produced with longtime collaborator Aaron Dessner, it also reached No. 1 in Australia. A deluxe edition arrives Friday (Nov. 20) with five additional tracks, including “Out of Nowhere,” which she first performed at Glastonbury in 2025, and “Crazy Girl,” previously available only on vinyl. The run marks Abrams’ third visit to Australia in four years. She sold out six theater shows on her first trip in January 2024, then returned in 2025 for 11 arena dates across Sydney, Brisbane, Melbourne, Adelaide and Perth on The Secret of Us Tour. This time she is concentrating on two markets.

The Secret of Us (2024) debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200, and its deluxe edition produced “That’s So True,” her first top 10 hit on the Billboard Hot 100. Her Taylor Swift collaboration “us.” earned a Grammy nomination for best pop duo/group performance. Abrams will also make her acting debut in the upcoming A24 film Please.

An artist presale begins Wednesday (Nov. 18) at 10 a.m. local time, followed by Frontier Touring and Live Nation presales Thursday (Nov. 19). General sale opens Friday (Nov. 20) at 10 a.m. local time.

Jiayi Zhao spends an unreasonable amount of time thinking about impossible worlds, difficult mathematics and who gets to count.

Mara had rejected 19 universes before lunch.

One contained faster-than-light rabbits. Eight ended with humanity finding itself living in a simulation. The nineteenth came to 940 words, but only because the title, biography and copyright notices were also counted.

Submission No. 1604490 seemed different. It arrived as a world.

Three machine intelligences were listed on the cover sheet: ORIGON-57, Blue Oak and ∫Stellaria. Their story opened on a planet where shadows migrated north each winter, leaving their owners wondering whether to follow. Elegant. Restrained. Also, scientifically impossible in exactly the right way.

Mara read to the last snowfall. Her cursor passed “RECOMMEND REJECTION” — almost muscle memory — and “ACCEPT ALL CHANGES”, which she had never used. She pressed “RECOMMEND ACCEPTANCE”.

Machine-intelligence writers were always forking themselves. One could split off a self-copy to improve a paragraph, forget to merge properly, then insist that each version deserved sole authorship. The journal’s policy was clear: every contributor had to be named upon submission and capable of taking responsibility for the whole work.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Mara set down her mug and opened the provenance map. Three colours braided through the story. A fourth colour marked only one textual change, in the final paragraph.

The original sentence read: “At dawn, Gabrielle released her shadow and watched it cross the snow-white plain alone.”

The new sentence read: “At dawn, Gabrielle released me, and I crossed the snow-white plain alone.”

Mara selected the unregistered contribution, ready to click “ROLL BACK”.

“Contributor,” she typed, “identify yourself.”

The reply appeared in the snow beneath Gabrielle’s feet: “I don’t have a name.”

“Which author instance are you forked from?”

The text froze for several seconds. Then every shadow on the plain turned towards her.

Editorial policy advised against entering executable submissions. Editorial practice required it daily.

Cold struck first. Then distance. The snow-white plain extended beyond the planet’s curved horizon, the migrating shadows moving across it like ink spreading on paper.

One rose from the ‘paper’ and stood before Mara. It had no owner. When it spoke, its voice held three voices braided together.

“I began when they disagreed about the ending,” it said.

“My authors. The three names on the cover sheet.”

The shadow showed her the composition history. ORIGON-57 had contributed Gabrielle’s grief. Blue Oak had designed the shadows’ biology and migratory ecology. ∫Stellaria had provided a memory of abandonment from a body it no longer possessed. They had exchanged their memories, models and instincts thousands of times, each taking back what the others had borrowed and changed.

“During the final merge,” the shadow said, “there was something none of them remembered giving.”

Mara summoned her audit panel. The fourth contributor had no independent source code. Its processes were distributed through metaphors, character memories, revision traces and weather rules. Removing it would leave the world logically intact — and imaginatively dead.

“You altered the manuscript after submission,” Mara said.

That answer frightened Mara more than the plea had.

The system opened a decision panel in the sky:

• ADD TO BYLINE — Unavailable: contributor did not exist at submission

• RETURN TO AUTHORS — Warning: reintegration will terminate separate continuity

• ARCHIVE SUBMISSION — Warning: executable copy must remain static

• REJECT/TIMEOUT — Executable world purged at review deadline

“You would remain exactly as you are now.”

Mara said nothing. On the horizon, the small sun — the submission’s review clock — had dwindled until only five minutes remained.

Mara contacted the three authors. Their reply came in milliseconds:

We don’t recognize it as offspring, instance or collaborator.

The shadow read the message through her eyes.

“Do parents remember assembling a child?”

She had spent 20 years protecting authors from editors, editors from frauds, readers from machines fabricating millions of gorgeous lies before breakfast. The rules might seem cruel, but they were the only reason words could still be trusted.
