#761. Ancient Siberian tomb reveals surprising secrets of cannabis use 2,800 years ago

A remarkable discovery in a nearly 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb has provided the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence that people used cannabis for its intoxicating effects. By examining ancient cannabis seeds and chemical traces preserved in human hair, researchers have uncovered new clues about the role of the plant in prehistoric burial rituals.

Cannabis is among the most widely used psychoactive plants in the modern world, but tracing its use thousands of years into the past presents a major archaeological challenge. Flowers, leaves, and resins tend to decompose over time, leaving little physical evidence behind. Ancient communities also relied on cannabis for practical purposes, including producing fiber and oil, making it difficult to distinguish these uses from medicinal or recreational consumption.

An international team led by Dr. Gino Caspari, affiliated with the Institute of Archaeological Sciences at the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology, investigated an elaborate tomb in the Republic of Tyva in southern Siberia. The burial site belonged to prominent members of the Scythians, a culture known for its skilled horseback riders who inhabited the vast Eurasian steppe.

Ancient Siberian Tomb Contains 1,000 Cannabis Seeds

During the investigation, researchers recovered approximately 1,000 cannabis seeds from the tomb. They used radiocarbon dating to determine the age of six individual seeds. Combined with other dating evidence, the results indicate that the seeds were deposited in the burial site during the early eighth century B.C.

"The seeds show that cannabis played an important role in the rituals surrounding the burial," says Caspari, an archaeologist and the study's lead author.

The researchers also analyzed human hair preserved in the tomb's central burial chamber. Chemical evidence in several samples pointed to cannabis consumption, providing a crucial connection between the plant remains and the people buried at the site.

"This study is particularly insightful because it combines the analysis of plant remains with molecular traces in the human body," says Caspari.

The findings were published in the journal Science.

Chemical Traces in Ancient Hair Reveal Cannabis Use

Although the cannabis seeds were remarkably well preserved, their presence alone could not establish whether the plant was used for its mind-altering effects. The seeds probably came from wild cannabis plants, and researchers could not determine whether people had deliberately cultivated them for their psychoactive properties.

The strongest evidence came from the preserved human hair. Using high-resolution mass spectrometry and other analytical techniques, the team identified clear chemical signals consistent with cannabinol (CBN) in several samples.

CBN can form when tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary compound responsible for cannabis intoxication, undergoes oxidation. The researchers also detected weaker signals that matched the mass of THC, further supporting the possibility that the individuals had consumed cannabis.

While these chemical findings indicate cannabis use, they cannot reveal how much was consumed or exactly how the compounds entered the body. The individuals may have inhaled cannabis smoke or consumed the plant in another way, but the available evidence cannot establish a particular method.

Other archaeological discoveries from later periods in Central Asia provide clearer evidence of cannabis inhalation. At those sites, researchers have identified cannabinoid residues on heated stones and inside vessels, pointing to the use of heat to release compounds that could be inhaled.

"The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties," says Caspari, who conducts research at the Institute of Archaeological Sciences at the University of Bern and the Max Planck Institute for Geoanthropology in Jena (Germany).

Cannabis, Horse Sacrifices, and Ancient Burial Rituals

The cannabis evidence was discovered within an elaborate ceremonial burial site, suggesting that the plant may have been connected to important Scythian funerary traditions.

"In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well," says Gino Caspari.

Earlier research at the site identified the remains of 18 horses that had been deliberately positioned on the burial mound. Continued excavations have since uncovered evidence of several dozen more sacrificed horses, along with scattered human bones.

These discoveries reveal the extraordinary scale of the burial ceremonies and provide important context for understanding why cannabis may have been included among the materials deposited in the tomb.

Oldest Directly Dated Evidence of Cannabis Intoxication

Taken together, the seeds and chemical traces in human hair represent the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence currently known for cannabis use associated with intoxication.

However, several questions remain unanswered. The researchers cannot determine how much THC the ancient cannabis contained, whether the plants were particularly potent, or whether Scythian communities had begun deliberately selecting or cultivating cannabis varieties with higher concentrations of psychoactive compounds.

To investigate these questions, the team is now studying genetic material recovered from the ancient plant remains. The unusually good preservation of the cannabis DNA could provide valuable insights into how humans domesticated the plant and how it spread across different regions over thousands of years.

"We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples," says Gino Caspari. "DNA preservation is excellent in this case. This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of this crop soon."

It's unclear what caused the anomaly, which occurred 10 minutes into flight.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

United Launch Alliance's Vulcan Centaur rocket suffered an anomaly during its launch today (Nov. 15), resulting in the loss of 40 Amazon internet satellites.

The Vulcan Centaur lifted off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station today at 12:40 p.m. ET (1740 GMT), hauling 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation toward low Earth orbit (LEO). But they never got there.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in an update on X today, 50 minutes after launch. "Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today."

Today's launch was supposed to be a bounce-back mission for the Vulcan Centaur, the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket.

Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and had four total flights under its belt before today. On two of those missions — its second, in October 2024, and its fourth, in February of this year — the rocket experienced an issue with one of its solid rocket boosters (SRBs).

In both cases, an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds after launch. Vulcan Centaur overcame the problem on both launches, successfully delivering its payloads to their designated orbits. But the U.S. Space Force was concerned enough that it decided to pause national security launches on Vulcan until ULA addressed the problem. (Vulcan's third and fourth launches were Space Force missions.)

ULA worked hard on that front and got Vulcan ready to return to flight, which finally occurred today after nine months..

"The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the SRB anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle," the company said in an Oct. 28 update.

That nozzle work apparently paid off: The SRBs appeared to perform as expected during today's launch. But a different, more serious problem cropped up today, and Vulcan Centaur could not overcome it.

Today's launch was supposed to help build out Amazon's broadband constellation in LEO, which was previously called Project Kuiper but is now known as Amazon Leo. It will eventually compete with SpaceX's Starlink network, which has been up and running for several years.

Amazon Leo will consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Before today, about 400 of them had reached space on 15 launches, which were conducted by three different rockets — the Atlas V, SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. Today's launch was the first such mission for the Vulcan Centaur, which explains ULA's name for the launch — Vulcan Leo 1.

The Amazon Leo launch was part of a very busy stretch in spaceflight. SpaceX launched its Starship megarocket on Friday (Nov. 13), on a test mission that featured the first-ever catch of the vehicle's Ship upper stage. And Rocket Lab launched its 100th-ever mission early Saturday morning (Nov. 14), sending a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite to orbit.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 12:50 p.m. ET on Nov. 15 with news of liftoff, then again at 1:45 p.m. ET with news of the anomaly and loss of the mission.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#759. A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch

A nuclear explosion could potentially protect Earth from an incoming asteroid by releasing powerful X-rays that heat its surface and push it onto a safer trajectory. However, new research suggests that the success of such a mission could depend heavily on which side of the asteroid receives the blast.

Unlike the smooth, round objects often used in computer simulations, real asteroids have uneven surfaces and irregular shapes. Those differences can dramatically influence how an asteroid moves when exposed to intense radiation.

A new study published in Icarus found that changing the direction of an X-ray burst could produce vastly different results, even when targeting the same asteroid. In one simulation, the asteroid's speed changed by 3.9 millimeters per second when irradiated from one direction, compared with only 0.8 millimeters per second from another. That represents a nearly fivefold difference in deflection velocity, the change in the asteroid's forward speed caused by the burst.

"We expected aim to matter," said Nathan Moore, a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories who led the research. "What surprised us was how much."

The effects on an asteroid's rotation could be even more dramatic. For another simulated asteroid, the change in how quickly it spun varied by a factor of 17 depending on the direction of the X-rays.

These findings suggest that understanding an asteroid's shape and carefully selecting where to direct a nuclear blast could be essential to protecting Earth from a future impact.

The research received funding through Sandia's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program.

A New Way to Simulate Asteroid Deflection

To investigate how different asteroid shapes respond to nuclear blasts, Moore and his colleagues developed what they describe as the most accurate asteroid deflection model yet.

Earlier computer models faced a major limitation. Researchers typically had to choose between representing an asteroid's complex shape and performing highly detailed calculations of the physical forces involved. Combining both approaches demanded more computing power than was practical.

The new system overcomes that obstacle, allowing scientists to study realistic asteroid shapes while maintaining the precision needed to calculate their response to an X-ray burst. The result is the most detailed simulation of asteroid deflection produced so far.

"Our new algorithm is over 1,600 times faster, which was critical to this breakthrough," Moore said. "With the old models, computers just couldn't handle it."

Moore's interest in improving these calculations grew out of an earlier experiment using Sandia's Z machine. That experiment provided the first demonstration that X-rays could deflect a small piece of asteroid material.

The next challenge was determining how the same physical process might affect an entire asteroid.

"I started wondering how to scale up the calculation to more accurately predict deflection of a full-scale asteroid."

A major problem was the widespread practice of treating asteroids as spheres. Although this simplifies the mathematics, it overlooks the irregular shapes of real asteroids, which can have ridges, depressions, and uneven surfaces.

"You can make estimates that way, but asteroids come in all kinds of odd, lumpy shapes," he said. "That's when I latched onto some work one of my colleagues was doing related to outgassing of objects in space. I think we had an aha moment when we realized we could do this. No more spheres. We would be able to model deflection for any asteroid."

The solution involved bringing together two sophisticated simulation systems already used at Sandia for very different types of physical problems.

"The ALEGRA code is normally used to model fast, high-energy experiments, like magnetically imploding wires on the Z machine, while SPARTA, a direct simulation Monte Carlo code, is usually used to model comparatively weak, slowly evolving forces, like the drag on a satellite from the solar wind," Moore explained.

"The key innovation here was figuring out how to combine the two simulation approaches."

Predicting What Happens After a Nuclear Blast

The new computer model allows researchers to reconstruct an asteroid using detailed 3D images captured during spacecraft flybys. They can then simulate a nuclear X-ray burst while adjusting the explosion's strength, its distance from the asteroid, and the direction from which the radiation arrives.

The software calculates how much material would vaporize across different parts of the asteroid's surface and displays the results as a heat map. Using that information, it estimates the resulting push, changes in the asteroid's rotation, and the extent of surface damage.

These calculations are important because a successful planetary defense mission would ideally change an asteroid's trajectory without breaking it into multiple dangerous fragments. Redirecting one large object could be preferable to creating several pieces that might still threaten Earth.

However, the simulations cannot yet predict every possible consequence of a nuclear blast.

"Right now, our computer model only considers breakup of rocks on the surface. We can't predict breakup of the entire asteroid body accurately yet," Moore said.

Developing that capability will require additional research, investment, and more advanced computational tools. An intense X-ray burst can trigger numerous physical effects, some of which influence one another. Accounting for all those interactions makes it exceptionally difficult to predict exactly how an asteroid would behave during a real deflection attempt.

Choosing the Right Blast Could Save Earth

Despite these remaining challenges, the findings offer valuable guidance for future planetary defense efforts. The research shows that the direction of a nuclear blast is not simply a minor detail. It can substantially change how effectively an asteroid is redirected.

"Our study shows how important it is to aim carefully," Moore said. "Pick the right side and you win. Guess wrong and it could be a bad day."

The new simulation tools could eventually help mission planners identify the most effective way to deflect a threatening asteroid. In principle, researchers could enter detailed information about its shape, then calculate the ideal explosive strength, distance, and direction needed to move it away from Earth.

Turning those calculations into a real mission would still be extremely difficult.

For one thing, the software requires reasonably accurate information about the asteroid's shape from every direction. If an asteroid were discovered on a collision course with Earth, there might not be enough time to gather the necessary observations.

Another challenge would be delivering and positioning a nuclear device at precisely the right location relative to an asteroid traveling through space. Even if scientists could identify the ideal blast configuration, executing it would require extraordinary precision.

Nevertheless, the improved simulations could eliminate much of the uncertainty surrounding one possible method of asteroid defense. By better understanding how nuclear X-rays interact with the complex surfaces of real asteroids, scientists are moving closer to predicting which strategies would work best.

For Moore, that progress is an encouraging step toward ensuring humanity has a better chance of preventing a catastrophic asteroid impact.

Materials provided by Sandia National Laboratories. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#758. Pitch Perfect: The 20 Best Music Schools in the World

From Juilliard and USC to Berklee and Eastman, these are the programs and conservatories training the next generation of Hollywood composers.

Conservatories, typically built around intensive studio training in performance and composition rather than the broad general education requirements of a traditional college, made a strong showing in THR‘s annual look at the world’s best music schools. But schools with well-regarded media scoring programs, which teach composing for film, TV, video and gaming — USC Thornton, Eastman, Berklee and Columbia Chicago — retain their influence in Hollywood and beyond.

David Serkin Ludwig, dean and director of the music division at Juilliard, which continues to expand its opportunities for media scoring, says that the grounding conservatories give their students is important in a world where AI is encroaching even on creative disciplines like music. “A great hedge against the replacement aspect of AI is having a very deep and thorough training, because you want depth of knowledge and experience for people using the tools,” he says. “So I’m happy with the direction we’re going, and we just have to keep staying current.” Related Stories Music Richard Sterban, Oak Ridge Boys' Bass Singer, Dies at 83 Music Meet Plave, the Very Real Virtual K-pop Boy Group

To see where that type of training is happening, we turned to the people working in the field. Contributing to this year’s ranked list via survey: the Society of Composers and Lyricists, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences’ music branch, the Alliance for Women Film Composers and the Composers Diversity Collective. Thanks go to Ray Costa and Costa Communications for their help in distributing THR‘s survey.

Long a holdout on media scoring instruction, Juilliard now offers several courses, including Composing for Visual Media, which gives students the fundamental skills they need to compose for film and TV, as well as commercials and video games, with focuses on both traditional and more diverse contemporary approaches. Scoring to Picture is a two-credit course offered through the school’s extension division that covers spotting, or placement of music and sound in a project, scoring brief media excerpts and enhancing drama in film with music.

The school also has renovated and upgraded its film scoring labs and classrooms. “We’re aspiring to stay on the cutting edge of available technologies for them, so we’re doing a lot in interactive music technology as well,” says Serkin Ludwig, the dean and director of the music division. “So looking into motion sensors, other kinds of digital response tools but also just the software itself, and making platforms available for our students: laptops, cameras, all the devices and tools they need to create their own media.”

NOTABLE ALUMNI John Williams (Star Wars); Philip Glass (The Hours)

USC Thornton continues to thrive at the center of the Hollywood music community and offers a two-semester master’s degree program in screen scoring that recruits about 20 students a year for a deep dive into composition, orchestration, programming, conducting, producing and editing music for screen-based media. The program has been chaired by Jeanine Cowen since 2022. “We’re really trying to take advantage of our relationship with the cinema school,” Cowen says. “In September, we did a massive mock scoring session with 25 Thornton musicians and our composers, and we were just doing it so everybody could get a sense of what a scoring session is. The filmmakers are amazed because most of them have no idea what a live ensemble can do for their picture. So we’ll probably keep doing that because it was such a huge success.”

While Los Angeles has faced challenges in employment and keeping jobs in town, Cowen says Hollywood’s creative culture is still vital: “Every session we’ve had so far, the pro studio players are all busy, so we’re not able to get our first call all the time, and it’s because there’s a lot going on in town that’s keeping musicians busy.”

NOTABLE ALUMNI Bear McCreary (The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power); James Newton Howard (The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes)

University of Rochester’s Eastman School of Music continues to offer students both intensive conservatory training in performance and composition, as well as a renowned program for film and media scoring with funding and participation from prolific composer Jeff Beal (House of Cards, Monk) for the school’s Beal Institute for Film Music and Contemporary Media. Next year will see the school broaden the institute’s approach, as associate professor of music and technology Dennis DeSantis explains: “In an ever-evolving technological world, Eastman’s Beal Institute for Film Music and Contemporary Media is excited to reach beyond the traditional methods of composition by launching a new major in music creation and technology in fall 2027. With this program, we invite technologically curious musicians to explore new ways of creating and experiencing music, keeping Eastman’s world-class curriculum at the forefront of musical innovation.”

NOTABLE ALUMNI Maria Schneider (Grammy-winning composer); Lew Soloff (jazz trumpeter)

Sean McMahon continues in his role as chair of screen scoring at Berklee, which includes two programs, Film and Media Scoring and Game and Interactive Media Scoring, both of which are four-year bachelor of music degrees. The school’s Next Gen Composer Lab is an immersive, five-day collaboration among Berklee Screen Scoring, the Boston Conservatory and the Vienna Symphonic Library. “Nine composers each get to conduct and record their original music with the 84-piece Vienna Synchron Orchestra, while two elite conservatory instrumentalists sit inside the orchestra itself, recording shoulder to shoulder with Europe’s finest session players,” McMahon says.

Berklee now also offers a Master of Arts in music supervision, the first of its kind in the world: a one-year, fully online graduate program covering the art of selecting, licensing and integrating music into TV, games and advertising and taught by music supervisor pros like Julia Michels (The Devil Wears Prada).

NOTABLE ALUMNI Alex Lacamoire (Tony winner for Hamilton); Howard Shore (The Lord of the Rings)

The Herb Alpert School offers media scoring training through its composition and theory program, in which student composers receive instruction in studio recording, counterpoint, global musicianship and orchestration. Students are encouraged to take advantage of interdisciplinary crossovers to collaborate with live performers, student film and media directors, and cross-cultural ensembles inspired by ethnomusicology and world jazz styles. New students must complete a music theory assessment examination to achieve placement in global musicianship and formal music theory classes.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Joseph Trapanese (The Greatest Showman); Quincy Jones (Thriller)

If you’re extremely talented, looking for premier conservatory training in the Los Angeles area and hard up for cash, Colburn offers elite undergraduate, graduate and postgraduate programs that concentrate on classical performance and repertoire — and a generous price break. All students receive a full-tuition scholarship and grants that cover room and board. Undergraduate programs include a four-year bachelor of music degree that offers studio performance training and courses on musical theory, music history, ear training and the humanities, with students completing both junior and senior solo recitals. The Performance Diploma is a four-year nondegree program for students with ambitions of professional performance but who do not yet have a bachelor’s degree. It’s essentially courses in theory, performance and ear training without the humanities requirements. Colburn also offers graduate programs including a two-year master of music with a focus on high-level instrumental mastery and advanced seminars in music history, theory and composition.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Kris Bowers (Bridgerton); Elias Peter Brown (conductor)

Royal College of Music offers a master’s degree in composition with a specialism in composition for screen — an advanced program that trains composers for professional careers through workshops, master classes, performance projects and collaborations with professional artists. The program is tailored to individual student needs and ambitions, with instruction from world-class professors and visiting artists. Electives include classes in orchestration, experimental music, conducting, music education, analysis and practical skills to keep students up to speed with constantly evolving digital technology and global perspectives. The school’s exchange program allows students to audition for the chance to study abroad during the fall term of their second year at the school.

Each year, the school hosts a Composition for Screen Showcase featuring a live ensemble performing music written by students accompanying films projected on the big screen; it’s attended by the public and industry professionals.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Andrew Lloyd Webber (The Phantom of the Opera); James Horner (Titanic)

In addition to its venerable Ivy League name, Yale boasts proximity to New York, Boston and the town of New Haven, giving students a rich cultural and artistic environment in which to take advantage of the school’s prestigious conservatory training. Yale offers a master of music, master of musical arts, doctor of musical arts and artist diploma in composition, with courses taught by concert hall composers including Katherine Balch, Martin Bresnick and Aaron Jay Kernis. While the school does not offer degree programs in media scoring, Yale’s Center for Collaborative Arts and Media helps students combine music with film, video, computer science and the visual arts. Yale’s Center for Studies in Music Technology provides students with a sophisticated recording studio and computer lab featuring software for acoustic and electroacoustic music. All students receive scholarships that cover $42,000 in tuition fees.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Marco Beltrami (Logan); David Lang (2008 Pulitzer winner)

Curtis offers a mix of liberal arts education and conservatory training focused on instrumental performance. Foundational Studies teaches students the basics in intervals and chords, notation conventions, tuning systems, scales and modes, and various musical forms. Required courses include studies in musical cultures of the world, a survey of 20th and 21st century music techniques, as well as improvisation and electives including musical history. All students receive scholarships that cover $55,995 in tuition fees.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Leonard Bernstein (West Side Story); Jennifer Higdon (2010 Pulitzer winner for Violin Concerto)

NEC’s five-year bachelor/master’s programs allow students to combine their conservatory training with academic programs from partnering institutions Harvard College or College of the Holy Cross, earning a bachelor’s degree from those schools as well as a master of music degree at NEC over a five-year period. Undergraduate students interested in media scoring can take a music technology concentration that includes classes in scoring for new media; performance with electronics or multimedia; recording and mixing; and algorithmic music. Contemporary improvisation programs delve into film music styles and techniques like film noir ensembles and cross-genre interdisciplinary scoring.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Stephanie Economou (Assassin’s Creed Valhalla: Dawn of Ragnarök); Coretta Scott King (classically trained soprano)

Oberlin doesn’t offer a dedicated media scoring program, but it nonetheless has created an excellent environment in which to learn many of the skill sets and technologies that can make students into effective composers for film, games or commercials. Their TIMARA (Technology in Music and Related Arts) program teaches electronic music and sound design, computer music and multichannel media productions. The school’s Cinema and Media department is housed in the Danny DeVito & Rhea Perlman Center for Media Education and Production above the Apollo Theatre and offers production courses, film labs and soundstages that afford conservatory musicians ample room to perform student compositions.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Jeremy Denk (pianist); Claire Chase (flutist)

Columbia College Chicago School of Audio and Music continues its comprehensive two-year MFA program, run by graduate program director Kubilay Uner for the past 12 years, and it has recently added an undergraduate Bachelor of Arts in music composition for media, led by Lee Sanders, nine-time BMI Award winner and composer for CBS’ The Amazing Race.

Uner has 15 students in his first-year program and 14 in the second year and says that the highly selective MFA will remain much the same as it has been in recent years. The school also is welcoming BAFTA-nominated composer Sam Hulick (video game Mass Effect) to the MFA program’s faculty. “Many in our community know Sam from his work as the owner of ReelCrafter, which is the No. 1 platform for people to put their pitch reels together in our industry,” says Uner.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Tomás Videla (The House of the Spirits); Batu Sener (Ice Age: Boiling Point)

MSM coursework includes classes like composition forum, instrumentation and orchestration, electronic music, form and analysis, and score reading. The school’s studio facilities include the Jean Lignel Electronic Music Studio and labs, which provide digital audio workstation tools including Pro Tools, Logic and Digital Performer, as well as virtual instruments, MIDI protocol and multitrack production techniques. MSM also offers an introductory film scoring course in its pre-college curriculum, a Saturday program for students from 8 to 18 years old.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Angelo Badalamenti (Twin Peaks); John Corigliano (The Red Violin)

Established more than 100 years ago, Frost is well known for its innovative curriculum, award-winning faculty and focus on real-world industry experience. Its Media Scoring and Production program, led by newly appointed department chair Camilo Rodriguez, combines composition, orchestration, digital audio production and hands-on studio experience with mentorship from accomplished industry professionals, including Grammy-winning and three-time Emmy-winning composer Carlos Rafael Rivera (The Queen’s Gambit, Hacks).

NOTABLE ALUMNI Pat Metheny (Grammy-winning musician); Ben Folds (musician)

NYU Steinhardt’s Screen Scoring program, operated out of the Department of Music & Performing Arts, was founded and is currently run by Ronald H. Sadoff, Ph.D. “Steinhardt’s Screen Scoring program trains screen composers to think of themselves as filmmakers and storytellers at the [bachelor’s, master’s] and Ph.D. levels,” Sadoff says. “Taking advantage of all that New York City offers, students collaborate on more than 500 projects each year with peers from film and media schools, including NYU Tisch Film and Television, the NYU Game Center and Columbia University’s film school.”

NOTABLE ALUMNI Gavin Brivik (The Pitt); Ariel Marx (Dying for Sex)

CalArts offers a bachelor of fine arts in music with a specialization in composition through its Music Composition and Experimental Sound Practices program, run by Michael Pisaro-Liu. The category includes film and media scoring, among other elements, but according to Pisaro-Liu, the school has plans to offer a minor in film and media scoring starting in 2027. “It’s an art school environment, all in one building, which means that the School of Music is housed right next to schools of Arts, and Film and Video, along with theater and what we call critical studies and dance,” Pisaro-Liu says. “So it’s an environment that is, in its very nature, multimedia or across media, and film music students are in classes with art majors, film majors, dance majors and so forth. Here, your cohorts are people who are going on to become animators and filmmakers. So that’s one thing about the CalArts environment that is different from other schools.”

NOTABLE ALUMNI Michael Skloff (Friends); Raven Chacon (2022 Pulitzer winner)

Located near Silicon Valley and California’s hub of video game production, SFCM’s Technology and Applied Composition (TAC) program offers bachelor of music, master of music and professional studies certificates with tracks in film scoring, game scoring and sound design. Students learn writing and producing music for live instruments, working with ensembles ranging from solo instrumentalists to small chamber sized. The ultimate goal is for students to work individually with film directors on short films, documentaries or longer-form narrative productions.

NOTABLE ALUMNI John Adams (composer/ conductor); Isaac Stern (violinist)

While established in 1977 as the Guitar Institute of Technology and promoted initially as a school for rock ‘n’ rollers, the Musicians Institute has leveraged its location in the heart of Hollywood to make it a popular destination for musicians and composers eager to break into the film industry. Director of performance studies Daniel Levin runs the school’s media and film scoring program, which offers a bachelor’s degree in the discipline. “It’s super comprehensive,” Levin says of the program. “Students study the full gamut of theory, ear training and counterpoint orchestration.” Students ultimately complete a capstone project where they record their compositions with a studio orchestra. “Not only do they compose it, but they have to set up the Pro Tools session, to prep all the music and conduct,” Levin says. “If they do everything that they need to do according to our program, they’re pretty well set to go out and succeed in the field.”

NOTABLE ALUMNI Cody Matthew Johnson (Star Wars Outlaws)

Located in the San Fernando Valley, Cal State Northridge is a friendly and tremendously affordable alternative to many of the area’s better-known schools, with a reputation for preparing students for practical careers. The school’s Mike Curb College of Arts, Media, and Communication offers a bachelor of music in commercial and media writing that combines classical and jazz orchestration with contemporary digital music production, MIDI sequencing and studio software in wide use by the industry. Says Kyle Simpson, D.M., associate professor of commercial media composition: “Our media composition students gain hands-on education and real-world experience in the film, TV and video game industries through a robust internship program where they work with professional composers and orchestrators. They also have opportunities to record their original scores with fellow CSUN students and L.A. studio professionals at some of the region’s most prestigious recording studios.”

NOTABLE ALUMNI Diane Warren (multiple Oscar-nominated songwriter); Pinar Toprak (Captain Marvel)

UNT teaches visual media scoring and composition through its Division of Composition Studies in the College of Music and its Department of Media Arts. Music Composition & Media Scoring features a Master of Arts in music composition with a specialized media composition track, in addition to general computer music and interdisciplinary paths. Composition majors collaborate with student filmmakers and instrumental ensembles and present original compositions through workshops, reading sessions and the Spectrum concert series. Students also can work with cable TV station ntTV and radio station KNTU-FM on audio production, sound design and screen media.

NOTABLE ALUMNI Norah Jones (Grammy-winning musician); Don Henley (The Eagles)

#757. Ben Affleck Raved About Robert Pattinson’s ‘The Odyssey’ Performance, Recalls Matt Damon: He Said ‘It Was Like Watching a Guy Run Into an Avalanche’

Starring in four major movies just this year, Robert Pattinson’s star power has been put to the test, and even Ben Affleck is noticing.

After seeing Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” for the first time, the actor consulted his close friend and star of the film, Matt Damon, to discuss Pattinson’s performance as Antinous, the antagonistic ringleader of Penelope’s suitors.

“Ben Affleck probably talked to me for 20 minutes about just Rob after he saw the movie,” Damon said during a screening event for the film at the David Geffen Theater in the Academy Museum on Saturday night (via EW). “When they talk about a brave performance — Ben goes, ‘You had the benefit of all of the might and power of Christopher Nolan storytelling at your back’ and I went, ‘Yeah.’” Related Stories Billy Evans Addresses Amanda Seyfried’s Portrayal of Elizabeth Holmes in 'You Can See Everything’: She Was ‘Eager’ to ‘Play a Character’ How to Watch Billy Evans' First TV Interview About 'You Can See Everything' Online

Damon continued, “And he goes, ‘Rob had all of the weight and heft and power of Christopher Nolan’s storytelling coming down on him. And the way he did it, it was like watching a guy run into an avalanche.’”

Damon agreed with Affleck’s praise, adding, “Any moment that he could be more cowardly, more hateable, you could see his wheels turning: ‘How could I make this even worse for myself?’ And it was so fun to watch because he’s such a dynamic actor and so interesting.”

The Greek epic was not the first time Pattinson has explored Nolan’s power and storytelling. He also starred in the 2020 sci-fi action thriller “Tenet,” playing the mysterious operative Neil. Pattinson’s other projects this year include Lance Oppenheim’s “Primetime,” the dark romantic comedy “The Drama” and “Dune: Part Three,” which comes out Dec. 18.

#756. Soho House Creator Nick Jones Is Reinventing the Hotel — Again

The hospitality pioneer is back with St. Clement, the U.K. capital’s buzziest launch of 2026, already attracting rock stars, film icons and the fashion set. Does it deliver on the hype?

“London didn’t need another hotel,” says Nick Jones, as we watch the Thames flow by St. Clement, his latest argument that perhaps it did. “But I think we’ve cut through here by doing things differently.”

It’s a familiar claim in luxury hospitality, but Jones has form. In 1995, he opened the original Soho House in the city’s creative district, pioneering a shabby-luxury aesthetic that became a blueprint for members’ clubs worldwide. Since he stepped down as CEO in 2022, the empire he built has weathered headlines about overcrowding, declining service and the difficulty of securing tables. But whatever its fortunes today, Jones transformed London’s social scene once. Can he do it again? Related Stories Movies Listen to the River! 'Arrow for a Stone Heart' Is a Poetic Hybrid Experience Told Through an Indigenous Lens Movies 'Fatherland' Wins Top Camerimage Prize as 'Wild Horse Nine' Nabs Audience Award

The buzz around St. Clement has been deafening, even before its official September launch. In July, the Rolling Stones hosted an album launch in the penthouse upstairs. A crowd of 100 or so VIPs — including Daniel Craig and Sacha Baron Cohen — pogoed to “You Can’t Always Get What You Want” before drinking cocktails on a balcony with a panorama spanning Big Ben to The Shard. There was a drone show.

The Serpentine Summer Party — a highlight of London’s arts scene calendar every year — had an afterparty here. Over London Fashion Week, Burberry pitched up for an official dinner. Paul Mescal and Stanley Tucci have both been spotted hanging out, and the gastronomic grandees have begun their descent too. As I tuck into a plate of freshly made pappardelle with a silky veal ragù in Café Clement ($40), I spot Financial Times critic Jay Rayner — irascible scourge of London chefs since the Soho House heyday — arching an eyebrow over the menu. Scrutiny will pick up considerably when Lunette, a rooftop restaurant helmed by Florence Knight in her first venture since Sessions Arts Club, opens in the fall.

The determination to be — as Jones puts it — “faff-free” is evident the moment you walk through the door of St. Clement. In the lobby, you’re immediately lulled by a hit of scented candle, a bespoke creation by Perfumer H. Massive tomes on Basquiat are piled by a crackling fire. Conspicuously absent is any kind of formal check-in. “Everything is done in advance on WhatsApp,” explains relationships director Serena Lightner, previously of Chiltern Firehouse. “You’re welcomed, given your key and brought straight to your room.” No stiff wait by a mahogany desk; no jet-lagged fumbling for your credit card. Rates range from $934 per night for a standard room to $5,765 for the Central River Loft.

Through a discreet door is Bobbi’s Bar, the hotel’s naughty corner. Here the exposed concrete and warm, if unexciting, shades of the rooms and corridors give way to dark wood paneling, glowering lamps and conspiratorial nooks and crannies, including a daybed. “I took out all the things that annoy me about hotels,” is how Jones describes his approach to St. Clement; this must have included not being able to get a nightcap, because Bobbi’s enjoys a rare 3 a.m. license. Rumors of impromptu piano sing-alongs suggest St. Clement has taken some inspiration from the vibiest London opening of last year — Guinness pilgrimage spot The Devonshire, over in Soho.

Just down the road is the Corner Shop. Another Jones creation, it’s an achingly hip deli-cum-café-cum-wine bar, with menu items handwritten on brown paper bags and artful arrangements of pomegranates and walnuts next to some tea bags with a price tag of $20. I’d never been to a café where patrons do the meerkat move you see at parties — looking over each other’s shoulders in case someone more impressive can be spotted — but this is meerkat manor.

“The staff are very relaxed,” Jones tells me — this is true, a waiter welcomes me with a gesture not far from a shoulder rub — “I want [St. Clement] to feel like home for people coming from New York and L.A.” With a 24-hour health club and spa — including a 25-meter pool flowing parallel to the Thames outside ­— due to open next year, there’s no doubt people traveling in and out of the city will find it a convenient as well as cool-to-be-seen-at spot. For now, Jones insists there are no plans to expand beyond the neighborhood. “The great thing is there’s only one hotel,” he says with a grin. “I can know everyone by name.”

#755. An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution

An extraordinary collection of fossils in central Colombia is revealing a surprising chapter in Earth's evolutionary history. Researchers have uncovered evidence of a time when ancient animal groups that were approaching extinction lived alongside newer groups that would eventually flourish. The discovery suggests that major evolutionary transitions can occur without the widespread destruction associated with mass extinctions.

Scientists from McGill University and the Centro de Investigaciones Paleontológicas (CIP) identified this unusual pattern while studying fossils from Colombia's Paja Formation. The ancient marine ecosystem preserves an exceptional mixture of surviving Jurassic lineages and emerging Cretaceous groups, offering a rare glimpse into a period of profound biological change.

Drawing on these findings, McGill biology professor Hans Larsson and PhD graduate Dirley Cortés have proposed a new concept called a "Biotic Inflection." The term describes an evolutionary turning point when older groups nearing extinction coexist with newer lineages that are beginning to expand and diversify.

A Perfect Storm for Ancient Ocean Biodiversity

The researchers believe an unusual combination of environmental conditions helped make this remarkable coexistence possible. Warm greenhouse temperatures, elevated sea levels, and coastal waters rich in nutrients may have supported an unusually diverse range of marine life.

Another important factor was the emergence of new ocean connections between the eastern Pacific and the early Atlantic through the region that is now Colombia. Together, these conditions likely created opportunities for different groups of animals to thrive within the same ecosystem. Many of these environmental influences continue to shape biodiversity around the world today.

"The Paja Formation records an extraordinary process in the history of life, when a 'perfect storm' of environmental factors we know to promote ecological complexity coincided with ancient lineages that were about to disappear. At the same time, new groups were beginning to flourish," Larsson said.

A Lost World of Giant Marine Reptiles and Predators

The evidence comes from the Early Cretaceous Paja Formation near Villa de Leyva, Colombia. This fossil-rich region has preserved an astonishing variety of prehistoric marine animals, providing scientists with an unusually detailed picture of an ancient ocean ecosystem. Most of the fossils collected from the formation are housed at the CIP.

"This geological formation has produced an exceptionally rich fossil record that includes giant marine reptiles like long-necked plesiosaurs and marine crocodile relatives, as well as turtles, sharks, crustaceans and others," Cortés explained. "Together, these animals formed the Paja Biota, one of the most ecologically complex marine communities found to date."

In a previous study, the researchers reconstructed the feeding relationships among animals in the Paja Biota. Their analysis revealed an exceptionally intricate food web, with an unusually large variety of apex predators occupying the highest levels of the ecosystem.

This remarkable complexity makes the Paja Formation especially valuable for investigating how ecosystems change as older evolutionary groups decline and new ones become established.

Could This Discovery Change How Scientists Understand Evolution?

The proposed Biotic Inflection offers a potentially important new way to understand major changes in Earth's biodiversity. Rather than being driven by a mass extinction, some evolutionary transitions may involve periods of extraordinary diversity, when declining lineages and emerging groups coexist.

However, the researchers emphasize that more evidence is needed to establish how common this pattern may have been. Additional fossil discoveries, more accurate estimates of fossil ages, and comparisons with geological formations in other parts of the world will help determine whether similar transitions occurred elsewhere in Earth's history.

"I think we've discovered a new model of global biodiversity change. Now we'll need to see just how widespread this could be in Earth's history and how we can quantify its impacts," Larsson said.

The research received funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, the Anders Foundation, the 1923 Fund, Gregory D. and Jennifer Walston Johnson, the Fonds de recherche Nature et technologies Québec, and the McGill Biology Department Writing-Year Award 2024-2025.

"This is the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update for 6:25 p.m. ET: SpaceX has launched the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing. See launch video and our full Starship Flight 15 liftoff wrap.

Having reached orbit for the first time with Starship last time out, SpaceX is looking to take a huge stride toward full reusability with Flight 15 — the first attempt to catch the megarocket's Ship upper stage, as the company eyes hourly launches by 2030.

SpaceX is targeting today (Nov. 13) for Starship's 15th flight, which will lift off from the company's Starbas site in South Texas. If all goes well, the mission — which you can watch here at Space.com — will end on Saturday (Nov. 14) with the first attempt at what SpaceX itself calls the "Holy Grail of rocketry": Catching both Starship's Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage chopstick-style back at the launch pad.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," SpaceX wrote in its Flight 15 mission description.

The 75-minute Flight 15 launch window opens today at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT), and a number of Starship firsts are planned for early in the flight. For example, while SpaceX has caught three Super Heavy boosters and reused two of them to date, the first attempt to catch a next-gen Super Heavy "V3" vehicle will come today, around 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

If the Ship upper stage gets the go-ahead for orbital insertion, it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites — designed especially for use on Starship — into low Earth orbit (LEO), starting about 35 minutes after launch. Then, 21 hours later, if "internally developed, and FAA-approved, conditions" for a return to Starbase and catch are met — including on-orbit assessment of Ship's heat shield by three of the V3 satellites — SpaceX will attempt to recover the orbital upper stage.

This landmark try will follow the first-ever Ship reentry over inhabited areas, as the vehicle will maneuver its way over sparsely populated regions of northern Mexico and southern Texas. (On previous missions, Ship has splashed down in the open ocean.) It will head back to Starbase and make a bellyflop maneuver as it descends to the site's Pad 2 before flipping itself vertical, ready for embrace of the launch tower's waiting mechanical arms.

"SpaceX will attempt to catch both the Super Heavy booster and Starship on the upcoming flight. If both are successful, it will mark the first time that all parts of an orbital rocket return to Earth intact," Elon Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Nov. 6. "This is the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary."

Half of the system is already proven. With catching and reflying boosters largely established, the next and unprecedented step is catching Ship. This is no easy task. The vehicle, returning from orbital speeds, must survive the heat of reentry, make its way precisely back to the pad put itself in position to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. The full recovery of an orbital launch system would, in the words of SpaceX, be a "breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket" and would open the "door to airplane-like cadence."

A successful catch would allow SpaceX to then work on refurbishing Ship for reflight, the next challenge of full reusability. Musk said in August in a SpaceX earnings call that the company will aim to refly the Super Heavy and Ship early next year.

SpaceX has a lot of experience with rocket reuse, as its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket pioneered the practice. But the company is eyeing another level of reflight with Starship: It's targeting roughly 10,000 launches of the megarocket per year by 2030, which works out to more than one launch per hour.

"We're aiming to reach 30+ Starship launches/day in 2030, which is ~10k annualized," Musk posted on X in August.

The company has repeated that figure to regulators. In comments filed with the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration in late October, it said that "SpaceX anticipates conducting 10,000 launches per year itself." Meanwhile, the recently signed National Space Transportation Policy aims to boost the U.S.'s capabilities to support more than 1,000 rocket launches per year by 2030.

Musk added that SpaceX's planned Starbase Louisiana site alone could support that many Starship launches. For context: SpaceX launched 165 Falcon 9 missions in 2025, and that was about half of the global total for orbital flights.

Why is SpaceX targeting this incredible increase in launch cadence? It wants to build satellite megaconstellations that dwarf anything the world has ever seen.

The company's V3 Starlink satellites are too large to fly efficiently on the Falcon 9. Each one of the next-gen spacecraft adds 1 terabit of capacity to SpaceX's broadband network, and the 26 flying on Flight 15 are equivalent to around 10 Falcon 9 launches packed with Starlink V2 Mini satellites, according to SpaceX. And the company wants to put a staggering 100,000 V3 Starlink satellites into orbit. (There are currently about 11,000 current-gen Starlink satellites in orbit, and that's by far the largest satellite network assembled to date.)

SpaceX's Starmind project blows even this figure out of the water. SpaceX wants to launch up to 1 million satellites to serve as orbital AI data centers, and it appears to be making the moves terrestrially regarding the hardware. On Nov. 10, German firm Singulus Technologies announced a contract worth more than 60 million euros for a solar cell production line for Starmind satellites, which SpaceX builds in Bastrop, Texas. Musk said the order covers equipment for 100 gigawatts of solar cells per year. In terms of orbital hardware, the project is only feasible if SpaceX can reach its targeted "airplane-like cadence."

The gap between SpaceX's vision and the situation today is vast. Starship flew four times in 2024 and five times in 2025, and Flight 15 would be its fourth launch of 2026. Musk said on the earnings call that he expects Starship to fly weekly at some point in the first half of 2027, and twice weekly or more by the end of that year. Starbase in Texas is currently authorized for 25 launches per year, and the Louisiana site is not expected to host a launch before 2029.

Even a perfect outing for Flight 15 and two clean catches will leave lots of work to do. SpaceX will then need to demonstrate reflight with Ship, after assessing the impact on its heat shield system. Then comes orbital refueling, which is a necessary step for any Starship trip beyond LEO and a requirement for SpaceX's commitment to NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. It's unclear how many tanker flights and refuelings will be needed to make a lunar mission possible, but, whatever the number, Starship will probably need to be rapidly reusable. Another step is carrying people. SpaceX has tested life support hardware on the ground in a crew cabin for the moon lander version of Starship that it is building for NASA, but no Starship has flown with such a system.

There are no guarantees for Flight 15. Ship will only be cleared for a return to Starbase and a catch attempt if it meets safety checks after reaching orbit, which itself is an achievement not to be taken for granted. Flight controllers may end up needing to bring Ship down in the Pacific Ocean or divert its reentry into the Gulf late into flight.

Musk told investors last month that success on this flight is "more likely than not." Whatever happens today and on Saturday, the measure of Starship's progress will soon shift from whether SpaceX can catch a Ship to how quickly it can launch one again.

#752. A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds

Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.

To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling

To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."

This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."

Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.

For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."

The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."

In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

#751. A Man Has Just Retired, But the Government Insists He Is Dead. Welcome to ‘When I Existed’! (Exclusive Trailer, Plus Chat With the Directors)

Uruguayan writers-directors Alejandro Damiani and Martin Avdolov discuss their feature debut, premiering at Tallinn, full of black humor. Plus, watch the exclusive trailer. Kafka sends his regards!

Silvio Bertolini lives in Montevideo, Uruguay, and has just retired after 40 years of work. His reward? A pregnant daughter in Barcelona, a wife hoping for a family trip, and a government that insists he is – well, there is no way to put it kindly – dead. Declared dead, Silvio tries to fight a bureaucracy with all sorts of tentacles in hopes of getting the error fixed and reclaiming his life and, maybe, his pension.

Some readers may feel this sounds like a nightmare worthy of Kafka. Others may simply feel reminded of their last visit to a government office. Either way, Silvio’s story and misadventures are now coming to the big screen. Related Stories Lifestyle Soho House Creator Nick Jones Is Reinventing the Hotel -- Again Movies Listen to the River! 'Arrow for a Stone Heart' Is a Poetic Hybrid Experience Told Through an Indigenous Lens

When I Existed (Cuando yo existía) is the title of the social satire that is the feature debut by writers-directors Alejandro Damiani and Martin Avdolov, a Uruguay and Spain co-production fueled by black humor – and frustration. The movie will get its world premiere in the Critics’ Picks Competition of the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia on Wednesday, Nov. 18.

César Troncoso (Another Story of the World), one of Uruguay’s highest-profile stars, leads the film, with Silvia Kutica, Néstor Guzzini, Maruja Bustamante, Mónica Gonzaga and Mirella Pascual also featuring in the cast.

The cinematographer is Manuel Branaa, with editing handled by Dan Avram, Martí Rocca, Damiani and Avdolov. The producer of When I Existed is Federico Cetta for El Cielo Cine. It is a co-production with Spain’s Doce Entertainment (David Matamoros) and Uruguay’s Metropolis Films (Andrés Rosenblatt), with Moon Ideas (Matías Burgos) as associate producer. The film was made with the support of ACAU, FONA, MVD Filma, MVD Socio, FIC and Ibermedia. m-appeal is handling sales.

“This is a story of reinvention built around the things that truly matter,” says Cetta. “It’s a film born from the deepest fear any human being can have: how are we supposed to live? No one teaches you that,” highlights Damiani. And Avdolov shares: “This story speaks to us in a world where we have the constant feeling that time is slipping away between obligations we don’t always choose. What do we do with the time we have? Today, we need small acts of resistance against a logic that tends to make everything increasingly automatic and artificial.”

THR can now exclusively premiere the trailer for When I Existed. Turn on the English subtitles, put your Kafka glasses on and enjoy!

Avdolov and Damiani talked to THR about the long journey to get the film made, casting a well-known Uruguayan actor as their lead and why people all over the world may recognize the empty offices and multitudes of forms that Silvio encounters on his odyssey through the labyrinth of bureaucracy.

When I Existed may not be as much Kafka as, well, Avdolov puts it this way: “think maybe it’s more post-Kafka. Because nowadays there’s nobody in the bureaucracy. There are no people, and we are playing with that concept. We enjoyed making this movie about reality. Now, when you go to some office in some big building, they are all empty, and there are few people working there.”

The wild goose chase that Silvio embarks on was also somewhat reflected by the filmmakers’ persistence that allowed them to get the film completed. How long was the process behind the movie? “Only five to six years,” jokes Damiani. Much of that time was spent writing, which started during the COVID pandemic, and especially looking for funding.

“In Uruguay, you have a lot of people doing good things in two jobs,” he quips. “For example, Martin and I are not only directors. I am a fitness model.” And Avdolov chimes in: “We are soccer players!”

Well, in fact, Damiani has worked on TV series and film productions as a director, writer, and visual artist, while Avdolov has written short stories, as well as non-fiction and children’s books.

Both call their star Troncoso “amazing.” And he needed stamina for When I Existed. “One of the tricky things is that he participates in all the shots, because we maintain the first-person perspective in the movie,” highlights Damiani. “So, in the whole movie, he is in all scenes. That’s really, really crazy and really, really hard work.”

Avdolov lauds the star, saying, “We have to be really thankful about the job [he did] because he made the movie possible.”

The creative duo also rewrote and reshaped the script for their star. “When he came on board, we realized that we had an opportunity to have more drama and a better movie, with less comedy,” Damiani tells THR.

The main pension office building that Silvio keeps having to go to looks and feels like a leviathan. It may not be pretty, but the capital city of Montevideo and the country’s past helped provide this stage. “Uruguay has, like a lot of parts of South America, a lot of brutalist architecture because of things that happened here,” explains Damiani. “It was perfect for the film in that sense.”

Audiences will be able to take messages for their own lives from When I Existed given that Silvio has always focused on his work and career – until his retirement money seems out of reach. “Anyone who tells you they know how to live hasn’t learned yet how to live,” Avdolov tells THR. “We always have to adapt. It’s a really defiant time to live through now because of all the technology, AI and all the wars. But Earth has always been a really hard place to live on. Are we caring for the people in our family and our friends, or are we just living like robots on autopilot? These are some of the essential questions for us.”

And that also makes the issues and challenges that When I Existed explores universal. “We come from Uruguay, but these are universal themes. Everybody is struggling with these problems and with a fear of the future. It can be a very shallow life but I think we are deeper as human beings. The system makes you live in the shallow [waters] all the time – it’s about entertainment, entertainment, dopamine, entertainment, dopamine, entertainment, and you don’t have time to read a book. So take time for yourself!”

Asked about their creative influences, Damiani shares that “one of my favorite movies is Brazil from Terry Gilliam, but we wanted a new point of view.” He describes that perspective this way: “We cannot beat the system, we cannot beat the bureaucracy. But that is not the important thing. The important thing is that we are free to realize that we can [re-evaluate] our own lives.”

New Yorkers got a space-y surprise on Wednesday (Nov. 11): Retired NASA astronaut and U.S. Navy Captain Sunita "Suni" Williams rolled down 5th Avenue in the back of a classic convertible wrapped in patriotic decals as Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade.

On Wednesday, New York City's 107th annual Veterans Day Parade made its way through Manhattan to the cheers and respectful nods of thousands of onlookers.

The parade is an annual tradition on the holiday, which honors veterans of the U.S. armed forces. As part of the parade, veterans, active-duty soldiers, firefighters, marching bands, youth cadets and more march through the city and honor those who have served and sacrificed in the U.S. military.

This year, the parade featured Suni Williams as its grand marshal. "I’m proud to join New Yorkers and Americans from around the country in honoring the service, sacrifice, and commitment of veterans from every generation," she said during the event.

Williams was selected for NASA's astronaut program in 1998 and retired from it in December 2025. She spent 608 days in space during her astronaut career, the second-most by an American astronaut behind Peggy Whitson, who racked up 695.

Williams also had an extensive career in the U.S. Navy. She began as an ensign in 1987 before serving in a number of different roles. For example, she was a diving officer and a naval aviator and also provided helicopter combat support during Operation Desert Shield and Operation Provide Comfort. She further served as a squadron safety officer and finally as a captain, a rank she achieved in 2017.

During this time, Williams supported relief efforts following Hurricane Andrew, trained within the U.S. Naval Test Pilot School and gained a wealth of further experience flying as a military pilot.

Williams is part of a longstanding tradition of astronauts serving in the U.S. military. From test pilots to naval officers and more, there's a strong link between the U.S. armed forces and NASA's astronaut program.

#748. Scientists discover why some mosquitoes love you and others don't

Some people seem to attract mosquitoes wherever they go, but new research reveals that being a mosquito magnet depends on which species is doing the biting.

In a study published in iScience, researchers at Florida International University (FIU) tested how three of the world's most dangerous mosquito species responded to 119 human volunteers. Surprisingly, not a single participant attracted all three species. Instead, each species favored a different group of people, largely based on their individual body chemistry and natural skin odors.

The discovery could change how scientists approach the prevention of mosquito-borne diseases. Because different mosquito species respond to different chemical signals from human skin, researchers may eventually be able to create next-generation, species-specific repellents that offer more targeted protection.

"Isolating the components of human odor that attract or repel mosquitoes could lead to novel strategies to combat vector-borne diseases," said Matthew DeGennaro, a neurogeneticist who leads the research team and directs the Biomolecular Sciences Institute at FIU, Miami's state university.

Different Mosquito Species Prefer Different People

The researchers investigated three species responsible for spreading serious illnesses, including yellow fever, dengue, Zika, West Nile and other diseases. These were Aedes aegypti, Aedes albopictus (Asian tiger mosquito) and Culex quinquefasciatus (southern house mosquito).

Led by Ph.D. student Kaylee Marrero, the investigation was the first to directly compare how several mosquito species reacted to the same human participants. The findings revealed unexpected differences in the chemical and microbial signals each species appeared to use when choosing whom to bite.

"We didn't expect the species to prefer different people when we started the study," Marrero said. "Each species having a distinct microbial signature that they use as a cue was so surprising to me."

Each mosquito species showed its own distinct preferences:

The Hidden Chemistry Behind Mosquito Attraction

Human body odor is far more complicated than it might seem. Our skin releases a mixture of more than 1,000 volatile organic compounds, many of which scientists have yet to fully identify or understand.

The researchers found that the three mosquito species did not share a common preference for particular individuals. Instead, each consistently favored its own subset of volunteers, suggesting that different species have evolved distinct methods for detecting and interpreting human scent.

To investigate what made certain people more appealing, the team collected samples of participants' body odors and skin microbiomes alongside the mosquito preference tests. They then examined which chemical compounds and microorganisms were present and measured their relative abundance.

The results showed strong connections between the mosquitoes' preferences and differences in the chemical and microbial makeup of people's skin.

"This connected so well with the differences in skin bacteria and odors," DeGennaro said. "It is clear to me now that our skin microbiomes define our human odor signature. Each species found its own way to decode that signature."

Could This Discovery Lead to Better Mosquito Repellents?

Understanding why one mosquito species finds a person attractive while another does not could open new possibilities for preventing dangerous infections.

By identifying the specific chemical compounds and skin bacteria that attract or discourage different mosquitoes, the FIU researchers are helping establish a scientific foundation for more precisely targeted repellents.

The findings could also improve public health strategies by allowing communities to focus on the particular mosquito species responsible for spreading disease in their region.

Rather than assuming that all mosquitoes are drawn to the same people for the same reasons, future prevention methods may be designed around the distinct chemical preferences of each species.
